I really wanted to like this. I absolutely love the cover with the hourglass filled with the two realms. When I read the blurb and saw it was about the afterlife, I was even more sold on it. When I finally got to read it.... 
 It makes no sense whatsoever. Seriously. I have no reasons to justify all the biggest portions of this book. First: why doesn't Ten want to decide between the two realms? She's literally withstanding months of degradation and torture, sexual condescension, etc. but for what? I mean, I know that her parents want her to go to Myriad. Ten knows that both places probably aren't the best. Yet instead of choosing the lesser of two evils like most others....she stays in a prison cell (sorry, asylum) stabbing herself in the finger over and over again. Ooookay. 
 Second: the two realms send their "best" people to try and lure Ten to their sides. I'll disregard the fact that in ETERNITY, their best people are random 17 year old guys. Figures. Anyway, why do they send their best people to get Ten? Because Ten is special. Why is Ten special? It takes more than half of the book for us to finally get an answer, and it's a half-assed one. They think another eternity soul fused with hers. Also, she can somehow bring light or dark or something? Which doesn't really make sense because there's been no proof of any magic powers up to this point, only a little bit of science fiction and fantasy with souls traversing different realms. So these guys are pulling out all the stops to drive her to their sides....first by impersonating a girl, then by seducing her, then lots and lots and lots of badgering her. 
 Third: everybody REALLY wants Ten because they're waging a war between the two realms. So...why are they fighting? What is the reason for them to dislike each other so strongly, for them to be at war for eternity. I just don't get it. I mean their fundamental ideas are very different, but that doesn't constitute war. 
 On top of all my constant questions, I get a love triangle and instalove. Dates and kisses and pining for one another. It was ridiculousness on top of confusion. So yeah, this whole time I was just thinking that it is a dramatic disappointment of a book. 
 Oh! I just remembered! There was a random part about how Ten's mother was a 16-year-old mother or something, and it was almost implied that it was normal for everyone to be pregnant around that age. I wish I could find that part to remind myself, but whatever.

As dystopias go, "Darkest Minds" occupies the same tier in my estimation as Divergent and Enclave. It is...fine. Probably will make a swell movie. It follows the young-girl-has-special-powers path, leading her first to one and then another boy, both of whom might hurt her, both of whom she holds back from because she might hurt them. 
 Unlike the best YA, "Darkest Minds" doesn't have characters that fix my imagination. As I read, I kept wondering about practical matters that seemed convenient but ultimately inexplicable. For example, in a world repeatedly described as in economic crisis, how is it that there's so much stuff - cars, gas, snack food in abandoned stores, clothing - laying about, free for the taking? There are other plot holes that just don't make sense and aren't really explained, just moved on from. And if these are the sorts of threads I'm pulling as I read, I'm skimming the surface. 
 There is an audience will enjoy the categories of psy kids - red, orange, blue, green - and the 'gotta get back to my family' storyline. I won't be reading the next ones.

 I feel bad writing this review, because it's not favorable at all, but I've resolved to write a review for every book I finish, so here we go... 
 If you're someone who loves the second chance romance trope, I am right there with you. It's probably tied with best friend's older brother/older brother's best friend for me in terms of how much I love it. But in order for me to be invested in a second chance romance story, I need to 'buy' their relationship the first time around, and I didn't here. And I think that is in large part to how much I just didn't care about the characters. I wanted to, and I even did manage to like parts of Vaughn. But as a whole, these were not likable people. Vaughn was a tough guy but allowed her father to run him off? Nope. Didn't work for me. I did like that Vaughn was a tortured hero, but he spent way too much lamenting for my tastes, and by the time I got to know River, I was very sad that he didn't think he deserved better for himself. And why do I say that? Well...spoiler alert. 
 River ended up knocked up because she lied to Vaughn and told him she was on the pill. He trusted her (which was obviously a big mistake,) but it was a lie to get him between her legs in a last ditch effort to keep him. Now, I tried to feel sorry for her, I really did, but when you give me the 'town sweetheart' for a heroine who is 'really going places' and she ends up making a stupid move like that, you've told me one thing and showed me another, and you've lost me. It felt very much like the author was trying to put them on even footing by making them both lie, but here's the thing. Two wrongs don't make a right; I would much rather have seen a huge mistake on one's part, and forgiveness from the other.  
 Vaughn was way too wrapped up in his own guilt to even be mad at River for what she did. I would have liked some tension surrounding those events. Her decision was life altering, and then she could never even be bothered to tell him they had a child. And her reasons weren't compelling enough to be believed. It made it really hard to like her. And now, I feel like I'm just beating a dead horse here, but this was a woman who was working two jobs to make a life for her and her child. Now, she had a rock star brother who offered to give her money to help her out, but she refused! I think I was supposed to be like 'Oh, River. Look at how hard she works to support her daughter. Isn't she such a good person?' But, of course, I went the other way straight into 'WTF? Her brother loves her and wants to help her out, giving her an opportunity to spend more time with her daughter and she refuses?' Yeah. That didn't endear her to me at all. I thought it was a selfish decision. Hot dirty talkin' heroes are something I've come to expect from Tessa Bailey, and this aspect of the book fell short for me as well. Some of the things Vaughn said made me shudder, and not in the good way. And I get wanting to be original in descriptions, but when you mention 'corrugated abs,' all I can picture is the Tin Man with a six pack. And the final nail in the coffin for this one was that while Vaughn may have returned to town because he found out about his daughter, it was clear getting River into bed was priority number one for him. It wasn't until 72% that her really became interested in learning about his daughter. So she was basically the forgotten catalyst. Overall, Thrown Down was a miss for me, but as I've enjoyed previous works from this author, I'm hoping this was a fluke. 
 This review was originally posted at Badass Book Reviews.

 Holy Pooperstickers! This book was sooo exciting and chocked full of major events that will impact the rest of the series for good...or bad. The sad part is that I can't tell you most of what happened because it will spoil the book for you but I can tell you that there are some heartbreaking deaths of recurring characters. I just can't tell you who or why. 
 When I read this book for the first time, I didn't really get the significance of some of the things that happened in the book so when I read subsequent books in the series, I couldn't really remember what exactly happened that was important but now that I have the knowledge that certain events are important, I recognized them right away. Does that sentence even make sense? I'll try to explain without giving too much away but this next paragraph will have some spoilers so don't read it if you don't want to know. 
 SPOILER  
 One of the side stories in the book...and this author's side stories are important because they are continued in later books so you have to pay attention to them...is about Nick Gautier who is a Squire. He's gorgeous, fun-loving, kind of geeky, sarcastic and you just can't help laughing at his antics and loving him. He grew up in New Orleans and has a Cajun accent which only adds to his personality and sexiness. He's one of Acheron's closest friends or as close of a friend as Acheron allows himself to have. For those of you who don't know who Acheron aka Ash is he's the star of the series and the leader of the Dark-Hunters. He has a lot of secrets and when certain secrets are revealed to others like the time he turned into something freaky-looking and yielded godly powers, he erases it from everyone's memories. He oozes sexuality and danger. Acheron and Nick get along great together and Nick treats Ash as a regular guy. 
 In this story, Tabitha Devereaux is walking with Simi, Acheron's adopted demon daughter, to the Sanctuary bar. Simi can change shapes and sometimes appears as a sexy goth chick and other times she is downright scary looking like a dragon with horns and wings. She also lives connected to Ash as a tattoo on his torso. He usually keeps a close watch on her because she likes to eat people and demons and such but actually obeys Ash in everything he says, literally. She finds loopholes in some of his orders. Simi is kind of child-like and speaks of herself in the third-person and has a sing-songy voice. She and Tabitha meet Nick outside of the bar. Simi greets Nick like she knows him and Tabitha has an emergency so she leaves Simi with Nick but Simi only knows Nick because she lives on Acheron and hears and sees whatever Acheron does. 
 Nick and Simi end up having sex. For some reason Tabitha thinks Simi is Acheron's girlfriend so when Nick tells Tabitha what happened, she tells Nick that. Nick tells Tabitha that he didn't know any of that and he will confess to Acheron. When Acheron does find out, he freaks out and throws Nick through a wall. He tells Nick that Simi is his daughter and she was never to have carnal knowledge which I thought was weird but whatever. Some fathers are just overprotective. But it's more than that. It has something to do with the way women and even men treat Ash. They all, anyone who has gone through puberty to old ladies, have a sexual connection to him. He seems to have sexual pheromones that attract women and they can't help but feel that way towards him even if they don't want to and I think this bugs him. I think that he believed if Simi never had sex, she would never feel that way towards him. When he tells Simi this, she tells him that he has a mighty high opinion of himself and that she didn't even like the sex so he has no worries. She said it in a way that cracked me up though. 
 Ash is still too mad at Nick and says, "You're dead to me, Gautier. If I were you I'd kill myself to save me from the trouble of doing it later." I never really got the implication of those words until I read later books in the series and by then, I had forgotten the intensity of the moment and Acheron's words. I just remembered that they had fought. My lesson and point is that when Sherrilyn Kenyon writes something and doesn't edit it out, it usually has some significance in future books and storylines. 
 END OF SPOILER  
 Okay...And now I will get to the main storyline. 
 Valerius Magnus is the grandson with the same face and name of the Roman general who tortured and killed Kyrian, the Dark-Hunter from book #1 of the series. Kyrian was a Greek commander who was tricked and drugged by his wife who then gave him to his enemy. Valerius was only five years old at the time but he remembers it well because his father and grandfather forced him and his brothers to watch the torture and crucifixion. Valerius tried to run away but he was beaten and made to return to watch the torture. Even though, Valerius was a boy and had nothing to do with the torture. Kyrian hates him. He hates all Romans but he hates Valerius most of all. 
 When Kyrian received his soul back, the goddess Artemis needed a replacement Dark-Hunter to watch over parts of New Orleans so for reasons only known to her but probably for pettiness and to get back at Kyrian for daring to get his soul back, she replaced him with Valerius. But it seems more of a punishment to Valerius than to Kyrian because unlike Kyrian, Valerius just wants peace between them but Kyrian wants to kill him. 
 Because of his harsh upbringing and because he has so many people who hate him, Valerius has learned to be distant and cold. His Squire says that he has a stick up his butt and thinks he is too good for anyone else and in a way it is true. Valerius is sophisticated. He came from nobility and one of the most respected families in Rome. He has maids and a full staff to run his household and would never think of eating off a paper plate or using a microwave. He even dresses in Armani to go out Daimon hunting instead of looking like a biker like most of the other Dark-Hunters. Yet he has a soft side to him and even though he doesn't show it, hurts that he is alone. 
 Tabitha Devereaux is the twin to Kyrian's wife, Amanda. People think she is crazy because she is a self-proclaimed vampire slayer. She doesn't keep it secret but she knows that most people think she is insane so she isn't revealing any paranormal secrets to other humans. Despite the vampire-slaying part, people generally love her once they get to know her and she has friends all over New Orleans. She has a big heart and helps out her friends whenever possible. 
 Valerius meets Tabitha while out patrolling for Daimons. He sees a woman who looks like a beautiful Amazon warrior fighting with superior skill, surrounded by Daimons and doing a pretty good job of killing them. He goes to help and she accidentally stabs him in the chest as a Daimon slices his back open. When the fight is over, Tabitha gets Valerius to her place to take care of him. She figures out who he is but he has no idea who she is. 
 I practically rolled on the floor laughing when he wakes up and sees a large woman with a pronounced Adam's apple sitting in a chair in the room. He looks around and the room that could only be described as 'tacky' with its nice antiques covered in Mardi-Gras beads, a giant toy-car road map rug and a cuckoo clock with a bird with a red Mohawk. Oh, and he is naked. Then Tabitha asks him if he is hungry and if he wants Italian food. He goes downstairs and she hands him a can of ravioli with a spoon. He sneers at it and goes back upstairs so she made him pasta with sauce. When he goes to take a bite, he notices the pasta is in the shape of penises. Hilarious! 
 They are two people who are opposites in class and sophistication but they fall for each other anyway. The problem is, is that he is a Dark-Hunter who isn't allowed to have a relationship and everyone she knows hates him. Her sister would have a conniption if she ever found out.

 Terms and definitions 
 Apollites - A race of people made by Apollo with the intention that he would one day replace Zeus. He thought that he could create a race superior to humans. Apollites are stronger and taller than humans with psychic powers. Angered by this, Zeus made declared war on them and exiled them to Atlantis. 
 When the Apollite queen became jealous of Apollo's beloved mistress, Ryssa, she ordered Ryssa and her newborn's son to be killed and ripped apart. In sorrow and rage over this, Apollo cursed all Apollites to die painfully on their 27th birthday because that was how old Ryssa was. They also could no longer live in the daylight and had to live only off of Apollite blood. In doing this, he also cursed his son, Stryker. 
 Daimon - some Apollites live longer because they have learned to suck the souls out of humans to extend their lives but they have to keep a steady diet of souls to live. Daimons have black tattoo-like marks on their chests like inkblots where they gather souls. 
 Spathi - warrior Daimons who are stronger and faster than other Daimons. They can be reincarnated after their death since their disembodied essence remains intact. They are Apollymi's guards and pets. They are identified by a mark of a yellow sun with a black dragon inside. Their leader is Stryker. 
 Dark-Hunter - a warrior who sold his soul to the goddess Artemis for a single act of vengeance. They hunt and kill Daimons to protect mankind and are immortal. Each warrior has his own unique power or set of powers such as mind-reading, telekinesis and healing. Because Daimons have animalistic instincts and features such as fangs, so do Dark-Hunters but they do not drink blood. They also cannot go into the sunlight. They cannot marry or have a lover for more than one night. Because Dark-Hunters are so powerful, two cannot be near each other or their powers will drain. They also cannot hurt or kill each other because what one does to the other happens to them also; if one hits and breaks the nose of another Dark-Hunter, his or her nose will break also. 
 Acheron - main character of the Dark-Hunter series. He has lots of secrets and until you get to the book named Acheron, he is shrouded in mystery. He was the first Dark-Hunter ever and is over 11,000 years old. We know he is the son of Apollymi, the Atlantean goddess and he has unimaginable powers but he hides most of them and erases anyone's minds of any events that have revealed powers that he doesn't want anyone to know he has. He also oozes sexuality and danger. 
 Apollymi - also known as the Destroyer, a powerful Atlantean goddess who destroyed everyone else in her pantheon over an event that nearly tore out her heart. After sinking Atlantis into the ocean and practically annihilating the world, the Greek gods imprisoned her in the nether world called Kalosis. She may be contained but she is far from helpless. Nobody wants to piss her off because she will crush them.

I don't know how to label this novel. 
 It's true that it is like a soap opera; it's addictive, highly emotional and deeply disturbing. But soap operas are boring, while 
 Outlander 
 is not. I enjoyed reading about the realities of living in such a primitive time as the 18th century, because it is such a stark contrast to our own century. I know it sounds ridiculous, but I was thinking some of the time, "Wow, none of these characters have any idea that mankind landed on the moon." 
 I have a keen interest in history and often wondered what it must have been like to live in historic times. Well, I think 
 Outlander 
 gave me some idea. I think it was incredibly realistic, and it's a mistake to judge the characters in the book by today's standards. 
 A highly controversial book and not meant for the faint-hearted, it tells of the less pleasant realities of life - to put it mildly - which have happened and do happen whether people like it or not. Of course, I hated those vile things, more precisely Jamie spanking Clare with a belt for putting the clansmen in danger, and later Jamie getting brutally raped and tortured by the same sadistic villain who kidnapped Claire . A lot of people seem to be more deeply disturbed by the former rather than the latter, yet you should take into consideration that there was a distinct difference between domestic violence and what passed for family discipline in those awful times. 
 And I was sorry to find that the subject caused so much wrangle. Like I said, domestic violence happened like that in the past, and it's still happening today in its malicious form and sticking your neck in the sand won't make it go away. Talking about it and standing against it in real life is a better alternative to ignorantly dissing a book for its brutal realism. So if you can't handle the subject, better read a fairy tale instead.

Well! This was highly enjoyable. The writing was fluid, the time period well-researched but not overdone, and the characters memorably drawn. I'd never heard of the Kopp sisters before (and it's not like they're super well-known historical figures), and I think there's a danger with their story that they could've been too passive--a lot of the novel takes place at their farm while they're waiting for updates from the sheriff. Obviously, though, these are not passive ladies, and they take it upon themselves to arm themselves to fight back against their attackers. 
 My only complaint is that the last line of the book needed one other line after it--I turned the page and said "that's it?" But it was still a good ending, and a great book overall. It's rare these days to find well-written historical fiction that actually has (a) a richness to it without (b) being overwrought/over-drawn and (c) lusty, heaving bosoms. I'm pretty done with those. Luckily, there's none of that here. 
 Also, one last note on a plot thing: So I was pleased to see Constance not actively pursuing love until the plot twist of SECRET PREGNANCY, FLEURETTE IS HER DAUGHTER! At the same time, the twist didn't feel added for shock value--obviously, it really happened--and the aftermath was dealt with really quite successfully. Constance has to deal with a lot of conflicting feelings for Fleurette as she does not know who her true mother is, and she wants to mother her "sister". I thought it was really rather artfully done, without veering too heavily into tragedy as historical fiction is wont to do with weird pregnancies. So that was a yay.

It's a good haunted story with immense sense of foreboding. 
 I had very hard time deciding what to rate this book. I don't care about romance and immediately discarded that stuff in favor of something super creepy: the actual paranormal plot. It struck close to home; I used to read a lot about ley lines, the legend of sleeping kings, significance of stone circles, horse hill figures, etc, mainly in Great Britain, but Nazca too, and many other unexplained real world relics and phenomena. It's even more weird that I used to attend a university named after main historical figure of the book (Glyndwr). It was kind of disturbing to read about all these in fiction book form; unsettling once I realized what the kids were doing, and with deep sense of approaching doom towards the end of the book. (It's fiction, so everything bad that could happen would be amplified.) You just don't mess with those things for your own fun. 
 The plot was easy for me to follow, but I can see how it could be too thick and slow paced for someone without background knowledge. While I loved the "lore" part, I couldn't help but feel characters' (mainly Gansey's) motivations were cartoony and simplistic. Wake up sleeping King to ask for a wish? Didn't it occur to him that the King might not appreciate being woken up for petty things?  I hope it'll be explained in next volumes in a more satisfactory manner. 
 Characters were surprisingly good - very varied cast in common roles, but thanks to Stiefvater's superb writing, they came out alive, not just moving cliches. I especially loved secondary characters - the antics of Blue's mother and cousins, Ronan's family issues, even the whimsical Barrington Whelk. The author is amazing with words - the characters and situations she describes are colorful and vivid, but not overdrawn, using little words to convey a lot. 
 I liked the dynamics between characters, but I'm afraid I'm somewhat too old to gush over any of the guys, and I'm certainly not interested in anything that may detract from the intriguing plot at hand - like romance, which thankfully was merely in fledgling stages in this book. 
 All in all, it was a great soft horror, like a huge ghost story, with surprisingly oppressing atmosphere. I doubt this is what the author intended, but I loved the theme of this book and felt thoroughly creeped out while reading it. I'm giving 5 stars for this very pleasant surprise, although I am fully expecting to trash the other volumes where the romance presumably starts for real. Oh well - at least The Raven Boys was a fun ride.

 I really liked this book. It was so different from anything I'd ever read before. As the title suggests, The Suicide Shop is about a store that caters to suicidal people. It stocks things like guns, poison, and nooses. The owners of the shop have 3 children. The elder children are properly depressed, but their youngest child, Alan, is a very optimistic kid. 
 The writing in this book is very simplistic. I don't know if that was a creative choice by the author, or if it's just the translation (this book was originally published in French), but it's a very simple book to read. Each chapter kind of seems like a short story, similar to those of The Little Prince. There is an overarching plot, but this isn't a very plot-driven book. It takes place over a number of years, but each year only gets a chapter or two devoted to it. 
 I really liked the world building in this book. It was barely there. We get the sense that this happens in the future, most likely after some apocalyptic event, but we're never explicitly told what is happening in the world. Obviously a lot of people are depressed and wish to commit suicide, but we don't learn much about the world outside of the shop. We get little hints about the outside world, but for the most part, it's a mystery. 
 I wasn't a huge fan of the ending, mostly because I didn't understand it. I mean, why did Alan jump? Was he suicidal? Did he just want to mess with his parents? Did he feel as though he had no purpose in life now that his family was happy?  I wish this book was more popular. Then I'm sure there would be tons of explanations online. I guess I'll have to re-read this some day; hopefully I'll understand the ending better the second time round.

First impressions: I love a good prologue - it sets the stage, gets you interested, and dives right into the action. Believe me, Martin gives good prologue here. It gave me important information about the northern area of the country, was full of suspense, and made me want to learn more. What else could you ask for? 
 Lasting impressions: This is undoubtedly an epic story. It covers lots of characters over a long period of time in a vast world. At times this was overwhelming, particularly to someone who doesn't read a lot of epic fantasy, but ultimately the story was powerful and satisfying. 
 Conflicting impressions: Having spent so much time lately reading first person intimate narratives, the switch to a more distant third person point of view was a big change up. I was frustrated at times by how Martin seemed to power through difficult moments and present them so matter of factly. Where was all the angst and hand wringing I love? Oh, right. Not that kind of book, so no real points off from me. 
 Overall impressions: I have to emphasize again that I am not normally an epic fantasy reader. That, in and of itself, is a huge reason I did not rate this book higher. It's just not my preferred genre. I love fantasy stories, I love swords and action and betrayal and lots of other fantasy elements, it's just that slogging through 850 pages is not my idea of a good time. It takes me months to get through one of Diana Gabaldon's behemoths, and I love them, but the process itself is a struggle. I have a short attention span. 
 That said, I struggled to get through this one. If it weren't for the HBO premiere, I don't think I would have had the motivation to finish. As much as I liked the characters and the story, it didn't quite move fast enough to keep me engaged. It took me three weeks to read the first half of the book, and the second half I simply forced myself to sit down and read in a marathon 4 hour reading session on Friday night. 
 Am I glad I did? Absolutely. Like I said, it's a great book. The characters were fantastic, and with the revolving POVs, you really get a chance to get to know them individually. My favorites by far were Arya, the 10 year old (I think) daughter of House Stark, and Tyrion Lannister, dwarf brother to the Queen. Arya is a tomboy who only wants to fight and be outside, though custom dictates she must learn sewing and act a lady. Tyrion is called "the Imp" by his countrymen, a nickname he despises, and because of his perceived deformity, is looked down upon by nearly everyone he encounters. 
 The beauty of the story is that all of the characters are deeply flawed, so as events quickly get out of their control, these flaws dictate devastating consequences. Martin is truly not afraid to show the darkest sides of people, nor is he afraid to take things from the characters we love so dearly. This book was frustrating often because I just wanted things to get better instead of get worse, and that is not usually the plan. 
 I highly recommend the book to fantasy fans, although most of them have probably already read it. Although it's not my particular cup of tea, I still enjoyed the story and am glad it is getting a well deserved boost in publicity thanks to the HBO series. For my thoughts on the show, read on.

 *** 
 First question: why offer a portrait photography deal to a woman who takes calender snaps? The security guys arrange her passport in hours. How?  Someone is shooting at them and he takes her to his bulletproof cabin and then doesn't leave to ... I dunno... do his job. They play scrabble instead. And WHY is his cabin bulletproof? For some reason she thinks he can't cook. 
 The housekeeper just called her 'darling' ? 
 You should say 'your highness or your majesty' when speaking to the King. Or whatever title they have asked you to use. Didn't anyone give her an etiquette lesson? She can't google it, she didn't seem to pack her laptop. 
 Over a first course of fine bullion and black rye bread, Helina asked, "What of your family line, Miss Sinclair? Where do they hail from?" (Kindle Locations 2492-2493). 
 They ate gold bars? You mean soup kind of bouillon. 
 There's a lot of errors like this, by the way. Here's another: 
 I'm pissed off at you for negating to tell me who you were, (Kindle Location 2843). 
 That should be 'neglecting' not 'negating'. 
 No editor... again. 
 The story just doesn't make sense. The head of security turns out to be the eldest prince [GOSH!] and he's in love with her. But Mattias has been coming on to her as well but says it was to protect her for his brother... uh huh. 
 She doesn't have OCD, she occasionally lines things up. That's all. She packed up and left home immediately with no OCD overload. 
 She doesn't mourn her parents. It's been less than a year. She blabs about miscarriages at the dinner table. WHY? 
 And she gets caught by dumb traps like notes from people when she has their phone number and she's already fallen for the note trick once. 
 The maid who tried to kill her, said she was doing it for Viia who got dumped but Chey has nothing to do with Viia getting dumped and none of it makes any sense. Murdering your rival will generally throw you out as well. You know? 
 'I'll be safe in my room,' says the girl who's already been attacked several times in her room. The bodyguard shot the maid dead before she could be questioned. Plus, Sander said they had cameras in her room but that's a forgotten story point later. 
 And the sex is meh... 
 Laying her down on the mattress, Sander covered her with kisses from her navel to her throat, and slid between her thighs with an experienced slice of his pelvis. (Kindle Locations 1809-1810) 
 His pelvis is experienced? And it slices? Does it dice, too? 
 I hope she meant 'slide'. 
 I mean... I might believe it if she had some secret royal lineage and they tracked her down deliberately, but to pluck a complete stranger from the streets of Seattle when she doesn't even speak their language is just TOO unbelievable. [I am aware of how odd that sounds. I can believe she's a secret princess but not a commoner. I would believe it, if you told me this was a pull-to-publish fanfiction.] 
 It's Cinderella story gone very wrong somewhere.

 I loved this book and everything about it. Out of the 3 books in the series, this one is my favorite. I knew from the moment we met Quarry as a little guy in the first book that I wanted to know how his story turned out. 
 On The Ropes series is an excellent series about 3 brothers and how they overcome hardships in their lives. Till is the oldest of the three and because of their neglectful parents, he takes it upon himself to raise his brothers. The sacrifice and discipline he endures to make sure his younger brothers are well taken care of are honorable. 
 FIGHTING SOLITUDE is Quarry's story of finding love and success within in the confines of life's obstacles. Quarry "The Stone Fist" Page is my favorite of the three brothers. His story touched me so deeply that I'm still thinking about it days later. While I may not know what it's like to be deaf or to have a close relationship with someone who is, I do know what it's like to watch someone who you love overcome a disability. The willingness to be "normal" and fit in is human nature. 
 The complexities of the story from being raised by his older brother -to- losing someone you love -to- knowing you're going deaf -to- becoming a professional fighter was the right mix of awesomeness. It had everything I had hoped for plus more. I'm not a crier but when I read the notes left behind I couldn't help but break down and cry. 
 This is definitely a favorite book of 2016 for me. I'm excited to see what Ms. Martinez brings us next because if it's anywhere close to being as good as this one... she'll have another winner. 
 SERIES: 
 Each book focuses on one of the three brothers. 
 Book 1 - Till | Book 2 - Flint | Book 3 - Quarry

 "Jackaby took a deep breath, his face leaden. And then he made a deal with the devil." 
 This final installment in the Jackaby series probably sits somewhere in the 2.5 star range for me. There were things I liked and things I didn't like. 
 The best part about this novel, as well as the previous three, is Jackaby himself. He has such a snarky attitude that makes him hilarious. He and Abigail have some great banter during portions of the novel. I just wish there had been more of that. More of the main characters from all of the preceding novels in general would have been nice. 
 I was rather disappointed by the overall tone of this novel. The others were so much fun as Abigail and Jackaby, along with their friends, solved paranormal mysteries. All of those came together for the overarching plot, which was the focus of the novel. And I found it rather lacking. The fun of the others was not as present here. There would be bursts of the same humor and tone, but they never seemed to last long. There was also an influx of new characters that I never felt I got to know or understand. They seemed to pop up to further the plot, without having any other purpose. 
 The final conclusion was satisfactory enough but I still didn't feel fully satisfied. There were little questions I had through the series that were never answered or seemed outright ignored. I had fun while reading it, but never really felt invested. 
 Overall this was just an ok conclusion to the series. I would definitely still recommend them, particularly the first one, but I think that Ritter could have tweaked a few things to make this a stronger ending.

It is finally over! I have made to the end of the series! So what happened? I do not know. It just seemed like a whole lot of nothing! 
 I would like to start this review with all of the positives in this book. 
 I do have to say that Ally Condie can write some very pretty words. Sometimes her words sound like poetry and that is what kept me going for the most part. This is why I gave this book as two stars and not one. 
 What are the other things I liked about this book? I cannot think of anything else. This book is boring! I really do not know how I was able to make it to the end. I hate to give up on a book, and I hate it even more to give up on a series, but I still think that it is a miracle that I was able to get through this book and the whole Matched series. 
 The first book of this series is really not all that bad. It is easy to get through, but it becomes very hard to keep going once you get to the second book in this series. I will warn you that the second book is the worse book of this series, and I could not even finish it. I had only about fifteen pages of the second book left, and I could not continue on. All I did was I looked up what happened in those fifteen pages on the Internet. I knew that I would read the last book in the series even though I did not really like were the series was going (or I should say where the series was not going, because nothing happens in these damn books!). I did make to the end of this book and I think I deserve an award to making to the end. The book did get really interesting about the middle of the book, but that changes quickly. 
 Okay now lets get into what did happen in the book. Warning there is going to be some spoilers. So if you want to read this book for yourself and you want to do so without knowing what is going to happen, then I would advise you to stop reading this review right now. But if you do not care if you know, or if you have no plans on reading the book, but still want to know what happens and you want to save yourself the time, tears of boredom, and sanity, then please continue on reading. 
 I need to talk about the death of Oker . I think this death was so stupid. I do not care that they died, but I honestly would not have cared if every single character would have died in this book. That is because this characters were boring! They had no personality! And I do get it that Society as taken away personality, but can they at least have a little bit. Can we at least seem them start to change towards the end. You know now since they now Society is bad, and they are finally starting to think for themselves. A little personality would have really helped this book (and series) a great deal! But I still feel like this death was not needed. It was just an excuse to drag this book on some more. 
 I am going to go ahead and get all of the deaths out of the way now. 
 Indie's  death was stupid too. I do not care that the character died. I never had any strong feelings for this character. I just think it was too easy. The kiss between her and Ky  was stupid. And I think that is why she died. She was a bump in Ky's and Cassia's  relationship, and so that bump had to be taken care of, but that kiss was not even that big of a deal. It was clear who he was going to end up with. 
 The other death in the book had no impact at all. It was only talked about for a few pages, and I do not feel like even addressing the death. If Ally Condie does not that think that it is important to talk about how this is going to change her characters, then I do not feel like I should have to write about it in my review! 
 Now to the damn cure! 
 Oh, God! This is what most of the book was about! I am not kidding! Trying to find the cure. It was worse than cure storyline in season four of The Vampire Diaries. You would think it would be about the Rising taken over Society. Nope!(But more on that later). This book was about finding a book for those that had been taken down by the Plaque. And I do understand, but does it really have to take the characters 512 pages to find a cure?! Could it had been possible to have half of the book be about finding the cure and the other half be about taking down Society? 
 That brings me to the next thing I want to talk about. The Rising vs. Society. 
 There was no big battle! There was no fighting. It was like a Revolution was not even happening at all, and it kind of true. The Rising and Society are the same  Which is really easy to figure out. I really figured that out a long time ago. Like about four hundred pages before the big secret was revealed, and by that time it was so obvious that was what was happening. It was so obvious that I forgot that the characters did not know that that was what was going on. And there are a lot of things that are left unanswered. Too many things are left unanswered. And the few answers that do get answered are not big deal. There are hundreds of pages that are dedicated to nothing, and big parts only get like one or two pages. It is kind of like the plot of the whole series is just an afterthought. There needed to be more. I was dying for some plot. I felt like I learned nothing from this book. Well I guess I did learn who Cassia picked. 
 And that brings me to the love triangle. 
 I have to say this: I HATE love triangles! They are really stupid. They are stupid because most of the time you can guess who the character at the center of the love triangle is going to pick. There is no mystery to a love triangle. It is just filler. And it is something that has been done a million times. And it was been done about a billion times in YA. And they are usually boring. And the only thing it accomplishes is it divides fans of a series into "teams", and it makes most of the fans feel like they must make T-shirts, posters, and other items to declare whatever "team" that they are on. But I have to stay that I did like Ky a little bit better than Xander in the beginning of the series. But by the end I did not care for a single character. So I did not care who Cassia picked, but it was obvious who she would pick. Like I said before, there is no mystery in a love triangle. I think it would have been a cool idea if Cassia would have picked no one. Because either way she picked who Society picked for her. I will not say who she picked, but either one was what Society had picked for her. Xander was her Match, but Ky's face was the first one that came on the screen. Now I know that Society did not want Ky's face to come up on the screen. I know that Society did not want Ky to be Matched with anyone, but Ky and Cassia was still Matched by using the data that Society thought made a happy couple. So either one makes Cassia both a rebel and not a rebel. If she goes with Ky is rebelling by picking a person that Society said did not have a Match, but Ky still has the best qualities and personality that best that Society thinks best fits Cassia's qualities and personality. And if she goes with Xander is picking the one that does not best fit her by Society standards, but it is the best person for that Society feels is worthy of a Match. Do you see the corner that Ally Condie wrote herself in? That is why the best choice for Cassia would have been neither of them. 
 Now this is the last point I am going to make in my review. And I am going to talk about the writing of this book. 
 Now I know that I said that the writing is the only thing that kept it from being a one star book, and I still feel that way, but some of the writing was horrible. And I was actually shocked by this, because both Matched and Crossed had beautiful writing! I was amazed by how someone could make words sound so beautiful. There is not a lot of action in this series, but Ally Condie someone managed to make nothing sound so beautiful. But this book had places that felt like she was not even trying. There were places were it felt like I was reading the rough draft of this book. The writing just did not flow like it did in the first two books of this series. It was sloppy and many times very cheesy and corny. I had to read a few sentences out loud a few times because the wording of the sentences was awkward. 
 So that is it. That is my review. There was a few good things about this book, but it was mostly just bad. At the end I wondered what just had the characters Reached. 
 Favorite quote: "Words mean what you want them to mean."

YES! YES! YES! Chelsea Cain? The creator of the disturbingly demented Heartsick (the Gretchen Lowell/Archie Sheridan) series? She's back with a new series, you say? COUNT ME IN! And, thanks to the kind folks over at NetGalley, I got a sneak peak of her new book that is set to hit the shelves this August. 
 I really, really tried to hold off reading and reviewing this one until closer to the publication date - but I was supremely unsuccessful in this regard, as I, of course, frantically read it upon receipt of the galley, in the course of a single evening. I was NOT disappointed; Chelsea Cain knows how to write edgy nail-biting novels, and she does it with apparent ease. 
 I thought I would miss Archie and Gretchen's twisted chemistry, but, somehow, Cain manages to create a new Stockholm-y relationship that is just as incomprehensible and twisted. Meet Kick Lannigan, a survivor of five long years of horrific childhood abuse at the hands of an internet-savvy pedophile who systematically trained her to recognize him as her protective, well-meaning father. As a adult, she can admit that she was victimized - but make no mistake - Kick is NOT a victim. In attempting to ensure that she will never fall prey to another predator, she's practically become a lethal weapon. She's trained in martial arts and defensive combat, and she is confident that she can shoot or slash her way out of any dangerous situation. Throughout the years, she's managed to put her own past trauma out of sight and mind. In fact, the man that was responsible for her captivity and torture is behind bars, near the edge of kidney failure and impending death. There's only one slightly unhealthy fixation that Kick indulges in - obsessing over the other, more recent abductions of children in the news. When a handsome, dangerous man named Bishop approaches Kick for her help in stopping a string of abductions, she's pulled back into her past, forced to face the monsters she thought she had left far behind her. 
 Super suspenseful. Super fun - well, as much fun as a book about pedophiles can be. HIGHLY recommended. This book would make for a first-class summer read. Thanks NetGalley for making one girl so darn happy before August ;)

Not only is the reader acutely aware of the struggles and frustrations of Maud and the people she interacts with while dealing with her disease, but she is the ultimate unreliable narrator. Short Review 
 One of the better main story lines of the series so far, set beside one of the worst side plots so far. The Denarians saved this one for me, and made it one of the better installments. Even so, these are really seeming to be a series built for people who already love it and want more of the same old formula. 
 Long Review 
 The world building done in this series, and in this installment in particular, is excellent. Butcher does a fantastic job setting up believable groups with internal political issues, strengths, weaknesses, and limitations. In a genre where it would be extremely easy to deus ex magicka your way out of things, Butcher is superb about setting up constraints on the powers of every faction, monster, and school of magic introduced and holding them to those limits. 
 Butcher's pacing, as it has been consistently so far, is also excellent. I never really felt any lulls (although an issue with the side plot came close, more on that in a minute), and everything kept moving a lot at a good clip like all of his novels have so far. We also get a lot of great new characters like the Archive, Kincaid, Shiro, and Sanya to name to just a handful. 
 It would have been a much better book in my opinion though if the whole Red Court/Ortega/Susan side plot had been left out and we got Ivy in there some other way. Unlike other books in the series, where the secondary problem / investigation always came around to entwine with the main story in some way, the Susan part doesn't. It totally distracts from the main story and in my opinion detracts from it. 
 The sex scene was terribly written. I sincerely hope Butcher never, ever includes another sex scene again in any of the other books of his I'm going to read but I doubt I'll be so fortunate. That's even leaving out the fact that they just basically left Shiro to be tortured to death. I get that it was the vampire stuff making Susan behave that way, but as a reader it seems really callous. 
 Harry's still a sexist asshat. No surprise there. 
 All of Marcone's involvement was excellent though, I enjoyed his expansion as a character. I actually kind of wish the series was about Marcone if for no other reason than because of how so goddamn unlikeable Harry is. 
 Overall, worth it for the side characters and the Denarians (Nicodemus was an excellent antagonist). Could have been a much shorter book though.

MockingJay-- my least favourite. 
 Don't get me wrong. I did still enjoy it, just not as much as 1 and 2. 
  Honestly, a lot of the times I just found everything really depressing. There were a few bright spots here and there, but most of the time, with Katniss wandering around aimlessly and suffering another mental break, it was just sad. 
 My biggest problem with this book is Peeta and Katniss' relationship. To be honest, they could have killed Peeta when he was taken at the beginning and I would have quickly gotten over it. But no, he sticks around. Even when he's a homicidal MANIAC he still sticks around. Yes, I realise that it isn't his fault, that he's been hijacked, but someone choking the life out of you isn't something you just forget. I still am not okay with their relationship. They just seem to be thrown together at the end of the book and Katniss is like: "Okay! Gale's not coming back so let's have babies!" What?! This woman is mentally unstable, and is still unstable years later. The last thing she needs to worry about is having freaking kids with bread boy. It all just didn't sit right with me. It felt like Collins knew she would would have to pair Katniss with SOMEONE, so she just mashed them together. 
 On that note, I want to say that I DO like Peeta. I just don't like the way that their romance was worked out. Too many problems. 
 I enjoyed interactions with Gale, as few and fleeting as they were. Finnick absolutely broke my heart in this book. He's just the type of character you want to protect...but you know no matter how much you like him, something shitty is going to happen to him. 
 The shining moment for me in this book is when BAM! Katniss kills Coin with an arrow that was meant for Snow. I was very proud of her, and felt that maybe she was returning to the girl we met in the first book. The girl that wouldn't back down from what she knew was right.  
 Anyway, for all my complaining, I did still enjoy reading and I still really like the trilogy. I don't think that it would have felt right to read the first two books and neglect this one since I wanted some kind of closure.

I've seen nothing but rave reviews about Never Never since it came out several months ago, but I honestly had no intention of reading it. I've only read one Colleen Hoover book and while I enjoyed it, I still don't quite understand all the hype. However, this book was recently free for a limited time for Nook so I thought, "why not?" 
 The very brief synopsis does not give much away. Charlie and Silas are high school students, a couple, and they both have suddenly lost their memory. The brief story follows them as they try to figure out not just what happened to them, but who they are. They don't tell anyone that they lost their memory and fake their way through several awkward encounters with their friends and family. They slowly discover things about themselves and their relationship, mostly things they don't like. It's not until the final chapter that something is discovered about their sudden amnesia. 
 Alternating first person POV is my favorite and it's done well here. Fisher writes Charlie and Hoover writes Silas. The authors do work well together and while I thought it was obvious different authors were writing the different characters, I liked it because the characters are so different. I liked Silas and his little brother Landon (I hope we get more Landon!). I really didn't care for Charlie at all. She's the stereotypical YA heroine I hate - the one who acts tough to hide her vulnerability, the one who is always pushing people away, the one who more special than she realizes. *Le Sigh* 
 It took several chapters for me to get into the story. I was all ready to give this book 1-2 stars, but then I got to know the characters a little bit more and wanted to know what happens to them. This is a Part 1 of a story that has at least three parts, so there was not a lot of resolution. I have to say that I kind of hate the way this is being published. I wish it would just be one regular sized book instead of several novellas. But whatever pays the bills, I guess. 
 Overall, I liked Never Never more than I anticipated. The story was intriguing, if a bit slow. The characters are well written and I look forward to finding out what happens next. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 3 stars

If you know anything about me, I am completely, madly, desperately in love with Valente's writing. Her prose is poetry, her characters are heart-wrenching, and her words sends shivers down my spine and makes me acutely aware of each heart beat - because her words are about love and life and tragedy. 
 And this book is no different. It is an play on the old Russian tale of Death and his bride. It is magic, tragedy, love, poetry, and the transformation of a girl who sees magic to a naive bride who can only be silent as Death feeds her caviar and bread to a weary commander and finally to someone who decides her life for herself. 
 You know the tale. But you do not know this one. Every single fairy tale keeps its plot set in stone. But it is not the same, it really is not. 
 You will fall in love with Marya and be angry at Koschei. You will slowly warm up to Ivan, despite his foolish nature, and mourn the loss of innocence as Marya fights a never ending war. 
 I write this in my notes as well: 
 "Heart wrenching tragedy. You make me fall in love with a beautiful rusalka and her daughter, and you kill them slowly. You make me long for some sort of salvation of this hungry, cold city." 
 Oh reader, you just have to read this book to understand how desperate I felt for these characters. Russia comes to life. You need not love Dostoevsky or Pushkin or Tolstoy to love this book (but if you, you will love this a million times more as well). We feel the cold, cold city, that the war is always going badly, the rigidity of the Party, and the emotions of the people. By the end of the book, you know this city. 
 This is a book that highlights Valente's strengths. Unfortunately, I think it also shows one of her weaknesses as well. The ending. I don't think she stuck the ending. It ends on an ambiguous, flat note. It is not a "bad" ending. Just one that brings in new and random plot points that have never been explained before, cuts off abruptly, and does not quite wrap everything up. 
 3.5 stars rounded down. It was good to very good. And I would definitely recommend it to everyone and anyone - but especially people who want to read fantasy not in a Western setting, a retold fairy tale, or just beautiful prose in general.

I was stumbling a bit when I read the first few chapters. The writing style is fine. The language on the other hand is something. It took me a while to figure out what 'smatter and chillun are..and also 'yonder which still confuses me sometimes and trust me, there're more. But I think 'Yessum' and 'Nome' is cute. I had to re-read some paragraph to understand what the passage is trying to say. The synopsis mentioned that the book is about a little girl story. I'm not sure what I expected out of the book but it surprised me that it's just a typical story of a little girl growing up. 
 What makes the book a winner is Atticus I must say. I really wanna thank Harper Lee for not ending the story with Scout and Jem all grown up crying at the bed side waiting for Atticus to die in peace. Oh dear God I'm not sure if I can handle that. Thank you Lee for not killing Atticus. It's 2014 and it's still weird as it was back in 1962 calling your father by his first name. At first, I was confused of their relationship until Miss Maudie or is it Miss Rachel mentioned to the children that it's not common to call a father with their first name. But after a while, it's cute. 
 What I love about Atticus is how he handle the kids. How he answers their questions again and again and how he understands them. His wife must be amazing I can tell. I almost cried when they send food to Atticus's home as a sign of appreciation even though he lost the case. 
 The book is mainly about racism between the white and the black. I wonder if it surprises Lee to know that it has been 54 years since he published the book and racism still exist. It's not as bad but it's still there with all its context and crisis. 
 Let's talk about the movie now. I watched the movie right after I finished with the book. It only took too many movies for me to accept the fact that a book-turned-movie will never ever be the same with the book. They deliver different things and you can't expect to receive the same either. The movie of course left some scene but they kept it real down to the lines. Movie-Atticus is a bit different than what I imagined but Gregory Peck played Atticus reallyyy well. His acting is exactly how I imagine Atticus react when I read the book. I'm not a cry baby, really, I'm not but I cried when Atticus came to tell Helen that Tom has died. 
 And Scout is so cute! Jem too! If it wasn't for the book, I would have never watched the movie in a million years hahaha. 
 Ending:  Tom killed himself before they appeal to the court. Robert Ewell tried to kill Jem and Scout on their way home from a school play but they were saved by Boo Radley. Robert Ewell died in the incident but he was not killed by Boo or Jem, he was tripped by something which then he accidentally stabbed himself.

ARC provided by author in exchange for review. 
 I enjoyed this story but expected more of it. It reminds me a bit of the movie "Dangerous Liaisons" with the games of seduction the characters play. 
 I liked the tennis metaphors and their strong presence in the whole story. Quinn was a great character - really broken, cynical, unable to experience real emotions and to connect with anyone. At the same time he was such a confident professional player, both on the tennis court and on college field in twisted game of seduction his frat brothers play. At the same time, he is completely weak and indecisive when it comes to his father, Emilie, even Sebastian. I really hated him for being so weak. 
 On the other hand, Emilie was so strong and sure of her feelings. She went through her own family drama and doubts about the future. I liked that she was not some good innocent girl who managed to save the bad boy from himself. She knew who she was and what she wanted and could get from Quinn.  Cara McKenna has quickly become an auto-buy author for me. I absolutely love how she works her plots. There is never any needless drama-everything that happens in her stories has a purpose, and they never go where I think they are going to. 
 I loved both of the main characters in this story. Annie was a bit shy, but she was also tenacious. She was determined to put her fear aside in order to do her job in a medium security men's prison. Then, later in the story, she would not give up when she didn't feel Eric's freedom was important enough to him. She'd closed herself off from relationships with no intention of ever going there again. Especially with a man who had violence in his past.  
 Eric is almost like an 'anti-anti-hero.' You would think five years in prison would have hardened him and made him less approachable, but Eric has really taken his time inside to reflect on his life and the kind of man he wants to be-or more importantly, the kind of man he doesn't want to be. His moral code has only strengthened in the years since he's been put away. He's an incredibly kind and generous man. 
 "I do know why I like you so much. Beyond the infatuation." 
 "Why?" 
 "You say stuff like that. In your letters...you said the most beautiful things." 
 "You made me see beautiful things again." 
 "See? Stuff like that." 
 While I enjoyed the entire book, I do have to admit the first part was my favorite. I almost felt naughty reading it; my heart raced when Annie's did, and I spent most of that time afraid of getting caught! I loved their written 'courtship.' Eric's initial letter was so honest, and it set the tone for their entire relationship. No matter how hard it was for them, they were (almost) always up front with each other. 
 He flipped to a dog-eared page, and casual as you please, he slid out what had become an absolute fetish object to me-a folded, lined piece of paper. 
 I felt like Annie and Eric needed each other. Annie needed someone who was gentle and kind to show her how she should be treated, and Eric needed Annie to show him that he needed to make himself a priority. It was a nice balance, because I felt like they needed each other equally. 
 I really enjoyed the steamy scenes in this book. Cara McKenna knows how to shake things up without repeating the same scene over and over again! 
 "Kiss me," I murmured, the words thin with desperation. 
 "I only get to do it once, for the first time." 
 "I'm going to die if you don't." 
 His lips twitched and his eyes narrowed, crinkling. "Remind me which of us has been locked up for five years." 
 This story held true to the obstacles of life after prison and worrying about the stigma that was going to be attached to that. As I said before, I felt like everything that happened in this story had a purpose. The characters were real and raw-particularly Eric, and the plot was so fresh and well done. 
 I can't recommend this book enough!

HEIRS AND GRACES by Rhys Bowen (Murder Mystery) Don't Let the Genre Fool You http://www.angelad.me/book-review-hei... 
 HEIRS AND GRACES by Rhys Bowen is the seventh in line in the Royal Spyness series. This historical whodunit has been touted as the book fix for the "Downtown Abbey" fan. Personally, I feel like this characterization pigeon holes this fast paced, fun read into the Historical Murder Mystery genre, when this story is so much more! 
 I don't remember why I picked up the first book of the series, HER ROYAL SPYNESS. I'm sure I read some review that talked about this quirky leading Lady Victoria Georgiana Charlotte Eugenie, 34th in line for the throne and I was hooked. 
 I am not loyal to one genre. If it is fun and well written, I will read it. 
 I love reading about feisty female main characters and you don't typically see them in the Murder Mystery genre. That is what I thought, UNTIL, I started perusing my bookshelf and I realized that a large percentage of the book I read have a murder mystery in them. Books like: OUTLANDER by Diana Gaboldon, DEAD UNTIL DARK (Sookie Stackhouse) by Charlaine Harris, ONE FOR THE MONEY (Stephanie Plum) by Janet Evanovich, NAKED IN DEATH by J.D. Robb. These books are shelved in various places but they do carry that murder mystery element WITH a strong female main character. (I share this because I think there is a contingent of readers (like) me that may not give this series a chance simply because of where it's classified.) 
 Like the previous books HEIRS AND GRACES is a fun excursion to 1934 England. Ms. Bowen's use of language creates this vivid tapestry of time and place, that makes me want to curl up with a nice cup of tea. The humor is a wonderful juxtaposition to the dark undertones of murder and the mystery was a surprise to the very end. 
 The one complaint I have is that compared to the previous books the secondary storyline (ahem! Mr. Darcy) didn't have the same tension it did in previous books. Darcy and Georgie's relationship is progressing but it felt stale and unchallenged. 
 This book is well written, with great historical insights and I would recommend this for readers from teen to adult!

This review is mainly for Assassin's Quest, but also for the Farseer Trilogy as a whole. My final thoughts revolve around how Robin Hobb lets me live out a lot of my guilty pleasures in fantasy literature without guilt. In this book she continues tropes like talking with animals, badass sword-wielding heroines, spiteful pretenders to the throne, and then she adds dragons. Maybe it's because this is a 90s series and makes me very nostalgic for the fantasy lit. of my teenage years, but I kinda dug the world despite cliches. 
 I think I also enjoyed it because it's not an entire cliche. General spoilers, so locking just in case.  One of the best surprises for me was Fitz' relationship with Molly. I have to say that for most of the second book and every time he mentioned Molly in this book, I groaned. It's not that she's an awful character, but she always pulled me out of the story and back into Fitz adolescent romance. Adolescent romance is my least favorite thing to read ever. Give me a phone book; it's more interesting. I like that Hobb recognized it as an adolescent romance, something Fitz had to go through and from which he would mature. They get their happy endings, but not with each other. Fitz doesn't even get a stand-in for Molly (I wouldn't count Starling). He just has to grow up and move on. Not enough fantasy books show that this is often what people (especially teenagers) have to do. 
 Hobb writes animals like nobody's business, and Nighteyes' growth into partly human is more interesting to me than Fitz' wolfish natures. I like the slow transformation, the fact that Nighteyes grows to realize he wants a pack and won't have one among wolves, so he builds one among humans. It's slow and subtle and easily the factor that sets this book apart from all those fantasy tropes. 
 The Fool was a character I grew to love quite a bit more in this book. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed him before, but I enjoyed him in the way all fan favorites are enjoyed. There's no question people will like him; he gets to be the sardonic tongue making fun of the story in the background. This book gives him background of his own, and while I found the White Prophet backstory a little flimsy, his relationship with Fitz more than makes up for it. The Fool gets to be genuine in this book, and it turns out unique and beautiful. 
 Chade, whom I loved for many of the reasons I love the Fool, also gets to be a bit more genuine. I loved seeing him in his prime, and I wished he was present for more of the book. 
 The other characters don't engage me as much. In the second book, I was about done with Fitz. He's more palatable in this one, particularly in the beginning where he's learning to be human again. However, he still gets all Molly, Molly, Molly too much for my taste and too often makes such stupid decisions. He's a believable character, but one I want to smack down nonetheless. Kettricken and Verity are also similarly believable if disappointing. It saddened me to see two of my favorites so weakened, and Verity is used as an emergency save a bit too often. I like Kettricken's steel spine, but I would've liked to see her take more action other than "Gotta find Verity." I wanted to follow her dragon story past the ending. That is my Kettricken. 
 The new characters didn't move me too much. Starling is a bit irritating and Kettle was clearly marked for death from the moment she came on stage, so I don't have much to say about them. Regal remains too simple a villain for my taste. 
 That said: This ending rocked. Very spoilery from here. 
 Hobb gave me all the clues to her ending, but I didn't pick up on a single one of them. Skill-imprinting is such a basic tenant of all the books, but I never expected Fitz to be able to use it. Imprinting Regal to be a fanatical Farseer loyalist is absolute brilliance. I'd also totally forgotten about the little ferret from Blue Lake. What a fantastic comeuppance. My hat off to you, Ms. Hobb. 
 I also enjoyed the Forging reveal. While it's a little bit abracadabra, the idea that Forging is an accidental side-effect of dragon exposure which destroyed a people totally unintentionally is a unique angle. I still think maybe the Redships would have pointed out this was a revenge mission, but then again their perspective is one where sense doesn't factor in. I still don't understand Forging all that well, but the how isn't as important as the why in this case.  
 So final thought-wise, this book isn't for everyone, but it mostly worked for me. You have to have a taste for fantasy tropes and a willingness to deal with a teenage (he might be older now, but he still talks like one) first-person narrator. If neither of those things bothers you, there is a lot to be said for the characters, story-telling, and world building here. It'll probably take me a while to get to the next trilogy in this universe, but it's definitely on my to read list now.

 This is my first of Amy Harmon's books, so I wasn't really sure what to expect. I just glanced over the description, and since the ebook was on sale, I impulse-bought it, and wow, was that one of my better decisions. 
 I think this has become my new favorite book. At least for now. The story is so beautifully crafted. From beginning to end. There were parts that annoyed me, of course, but all in all, the structure and language and development and characters of this story are just fantastic. Literally and colloquially. It's got elements of fantasy, romance, and at times, it feels reminiscent of Beauty and the Beast and, of course, The Little Mermaid. There's so much to this book, and Harmon handles it all so beautifully. 
 Can we talk about Tiras's character development for a moment? Great. So, he starts out as this possessive, kind-of scary, brooding guy, and I just had a bad feeling about him. You know when you're reading a book and the romance is borderline abusive but no one in the book acknowledges that and you're supposed to think it's romantic and sweet and beautiful? I was so afraid we were headed there. Fortunately, so was our awesome heroine, Lark. And she makes sure we aren't. 
 This part of the novel is so important to me because of this specific reason: she still challenges him and doesn't accept his "using" her, but she doesn't miraculously become not a damsel in distress anymore. She's a weak girl: she can't speak, she's never had anyone to confide in, and she doesn't really know how relationships work, so she takes a lot of Tiras's hits at the beginning. Which he gives because he's the king and he had a terrible example to follow--not that that excuses it. BUT Lark punches back in the best way she can. There's no out-of-character moment where she Stands Up To Him(tm) because that's not realistic. Her character is so realistic. She's small and weak and unsure, but she challenges Tiras and together they make each other better and learn how to be better people. He goes from terrifying and fearful to loving and sure, and she goes from powerless and silent to powerful and brave, but they both retain their personalities. He's still an arrogant king, and she's still a small girl, but they make each other better and grow, and I'm probably not explaining this very well at all because I'm so emotional right now but just know that the relationship between these two has some of the best development I've ever read. 
 ALSO can we talk about the biblical references? Ok. I'm still not completely sure what I think about these. I know Harmon has some other novels that are biblical-ish, but I haven't read those so I'm not sure exactly where she stands... 
 Tiras has a lot of similarities to Jesus. He keeps warning his friends that he has to go. He's preparing the way for them for when he leaves. "Where I'm going, you cannot follow." (I mean, that's, like, a direct quote from Jesus.) And then there's that whole scene which, to me, read like a retelling of that time the Pharisees brought the adulterous woman to Jesus and said, "we gotta stone her" and Jesus said, "whichever among you is free of sin may throw the first stone," and they all walked away one by one and then Jesus told the girl "Go and sin no more." I mean, Tiras's thing is he literally says, "Go and do no harm." 
 And then there's the Council of Lords acting as Pharisees trying to actively seek out people to punish for breaking trite laws. Sure, these people (the Gifted) aren't exactly sinners because they're not doing anything wrong, but to me, the idea was the same. They're still people, even if they have the potential to do bad things (like become those creepy Volgar things), and Tiras has mercy on them even though the past rulers of his kingdom did not. The kingdom of Jerusalem? is for all people, as long as they're not evil (like those creepy Volgar things), and Tiras is quite literally willing to die for that. 
 So whether or not we're supposed to see Tiras as a Christ-like figure, I did. I mean, he's definitely not exactly like Jesus. Not so much (or at all) when it comes to his relationship with Lark, but very much so when it comes to how he wants rules the kingdom. I think having those similarities made me think about the message in certain way. Like, to be a good leader and show mercy and understanding to everyone, it takes someone who's willing to be Christ-like, and here's what that looks like. That's just my take on it. 
 Not to mention the whole "God of Words" thing and the literal quoting of the Bible at the beginning... 
 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God 
 To me, this kind of framed the novel in a biblical context, but then again, I do see everything that way, anyway. I liked these references because of the way it made ME think about the story and its message, considering I had all that background information, but I'm REALLY curious as to how other people read into that!! 
 (If you're still reading this by chance and have any thoughts about that, please feel free to comment!) 
 Also, words. I feel like I can't leave that out of my review. Obviously, words are important to this story because our main character can't speak, but she still uses them to become powerful. The central message of this book reminds me of my favorite Margaret Atwood quote: 
 A word after a word after a word is power. 
 And in that respect, this book is really important to me, as someone who is almost always silent, but uses words in a different way, through writing, to use their power. Like Lark does, but different. I think Harmon shows us that you don't have to be a good talker to be powerful, and that words are powerful, no matter what form they take. 
 (And she sprinkles little reminders throughout that the words and the power are God-given. Which I like.) 
 The only thing that really bothered me was the grammatical mistakes. There were So. Many. (EDIT: I have only just now realized that this is a self-published/indie book, so I can be forgiving in this respect, but it still annoyed me.) Apostrophes where they shouldn't have been, misspellings, and inconsistent capitalization of the Gifted (gifted?) drove me NUTS. 
 And I'll also warn those who are, for some reason, still reading this that it starts out... strange. Like I said, the relationship between Lark and Tiras is not exemplary at first, and plot-wise, I wasn't even sure what was going on. I didn't even know what our goal was, but the writing and the characters kept me sucked into the story, and once it clicked for me, I finished the whole thing in one sitting because I could not tear myself away. 
 Over all, I enjoyed this book SO much, and I will definitely be looking into her other work. Harmon has such a creative mind, and this story BLEW ME AWAY with its complexity, its development, its characters, and its heart. 
 I'm giving it a good 4.8 stars, and I would recommend it to anyone who appreciates a beautifully crafted story or a good fantasy--this one's got both!
