(Side note: If it seems I'm mocking Epic Mickey, I'm not. I own it for the Wii. Played it. Loved it. Never beat it. And...now I'm thinking of restarting that game...but NO...reviewing, reviewing, reviewing must be a priority here). While I'm still digressing, I should come out of the closet as a minor RPG fan and sometime video-gamer in my previous life, pre-baby. I really loved the Paper Mario RPGs, played Animal Farm and Harvest Moon, and my brother was (IS) a hardcore gamer - all platforms, most computer games (especially World of Warcraft in its heyday) , Mortal Combat tournaments - the works). So, that said - most of the terminology and video game references we not lost on me, but... that doesn't me that I necessarily LOVED the heavy-handed approach to recaps and in-depth game description. I didn't really LOVE the book, but I did appreciate parts of it. It really captured the wonder and awe that was associated with how video games (and computer technology) changed reality for a whole generation of youth. I was part of that generation. I know. But not to the extent that this author knows - because it's clear he has done his research (if not lived the part). 
 Our narrator Russell is an early middle-aged closet nerd who ran out of opportunities (or personal ambition) in the "real" world of adult jobs. In high school, he ran with a handful of misfit of technies who were grouped together to program a video game for a project and, later, at a computer summer camp. While Russell attempted to pursue a more traditional career (however unsuccessfully or misguided), the others formed a highly successful video game company. With little else available to misguided, middle-aged Russell, he throws himself on the mercy of his former friends and begins a career as a video game designer. This story is his account of settling into this new environment, all the while plagued by the unexplained death of one of his former friends, Simon, the genius behind the company's success. Russell throws himself into his work, attempting to fix a mysterious virus that has started to plague players in unpredictable ways. While the description of the game world became a bit of a drag, the book shone in the passages that dealt with the high school relationship dynamics of the gamers. I wish that there had been more reality - and less virtual reality. 
 All in all, it was so-so. Not good. Not bad. There wasn't enough substance and resolution to the plot. I appreciated the opportunity to read this one even if it wasn't for me.

 About three-quarters of the way through this book, I had to stop reading for a day or two. I just couldn't bear to go on, I dreaded to think what would happen to the man and his son. The dangers are myriad in Cormac McCarthy's post-apocalyptic world, and lie in wait around every corner. It's a bleak book. McCarthy keeps the dialogue terse and the color limited to a palette of gray and ash. Only the boy is described with color. He's golden, carrying the last flame of compassion in his heart. 
 The book is driven by their journey south to the coast, where the man hopes for a warm winter. I had some questions about the ultimate purpose of the journey. But I think it suits McCarthy's purposes symbolically that they are itinerant, constantly vulnerable. We seem to have destroyed our home for good in the apocalypse, so the man and the boy are forever homeless, scrounging, hiding, living on borrowed time. 
 McCarthy's writing, which I found lean in _No Country for Old Men_, seems to have gone on a starvation diet. The language is spare, as if the same disaster that has pared the characters down to their essential motivations has worked on the book itself. The boy asks at one point about their "long-term goals" and the man questions him about where he heard the term. In this world there's no such thing. Survival, the shortest-term goal ever, is the only goal. This makes for a simple, powerful narrative, and compelling--who doesn't want to see good protect innocence and triumph over evil (marauders! cannibals!)? But was that really what was going on? Clearly there were bad guys, but the father's attempts to "protect" the son seem to ensure their isolation as much as their safety. I was left frustrated by the neat, vague ending. It's so easy all of a sudden! It's something to debate with friends, I suppose, whether we are to take this ending at face value or as a dream of death.

So I know there is a TV Series of this out there, like with so many other things. No I have not watched it. 
 My sister would tell me why read it when you can watch it... 
 My answer..."Cause maybe I'm a Freak that would like to have a better background than I know the series will give me." 
 So Alison is at the centre of a circle of five BFF's. They share everything, and Alison (Ali) is the glue that holds them all together, they only became friends because of her after all. They share everything from cloths to secrets and promise to protect one another at all costs. 
 Then one night when the girls have a sleepover to celebrate the start of summer vacation there's an argument. As usual Ali is trying to get them all to do what she wants, everyone reluctantly agrees until Spencer decides she's had enough of being bossed around and kicks Ali out, the minute Ali goes waltzing out the door Spencer regrets it but Ali is gone. 
 On the night she goes missing, no one can find her, has she been kidnapped or murdered. 
 Fast-ward three years later and it's been proven that Ali was the glue that held, Emily, Hanna, Spencer and Aria together as a group. All the girls are now living their own lives separate from any friendship they might once have shared, still at the same school but they pass one another on a daily basis without so much as an acknowledgement. 
 But something sinister begins to happen that might bring the girls back together whether they want to or not. Each begins getting cryptic messages hinting at secrets that only Ali would have known about each of them. Secrets none of the girls shared as a group or with anyone else in our outside of the group. 
 Not only does this person hint at knowing the secrets the girls believed long buried but they seem to know things that is happening to each of the girls now, secrets that no one could know. To make it even worse the messages have all been signed "A". 
 Is it someone messing with them or is Alison still alive? 
 This not a tediously taxing book to read, it's just plain guilty fun. It does keep you guessing, Shepard gives you new suspects all the time that has you wondering who it could be. So it's enjoyable and keeps you reading. 
 Especially because "A" keeps threatening that they knows the biggest secret that all the girls the girls share (or think they do) connecting them to Spencer and Ali's creepy neighbour across the street Toby, and his stepsister Jenna. 
 If anything I kept reading just to find out what the secret was. 
 All the girls lives seems to begin falling apart, was it something that was going to happen anyway or does "A" have a hand in it. 
 Just when the girls believe that A could be Ali come back from the dead, Ali's body is found when the new girl, Maya's family who's moved into Ali's hold house, dig up the old gazebo area to build a tennis court. 
 Is it really Ali's body? If it is and "A" isn't Alison, who is it that knows every secret past and present? 
 All these girls are from fairly well off families, the embodiment of "poor little rich girl" syndrome, everyone of them as a credit card, the designer cloths and of course everyone is buying from Tiffany's or stealing from them.... 
 One reason that I enjoyed the book, even though the girls tend to be a but melodramatic at times, is that it shows that teens lives are not just parties and who's dating who, exam dramatics. They actually do have some serious issues and for the most part these girls aren't who they are because this is the path they've chosen but because in some way they are pushed into it by their parents or because they feel it's what they have to do to be accepted or to be a cut above looser. 
 Hanna 
 Was the overweight one of the group, she began eating more than normal after her parents' divorce because she didn't know how to deal with anything. Now three years later she much thinner and has re-invented herself into Ms. Popular and Sleek making fun of everyone she considers a looser. She hasn't seen nor spoken to her father in the three year since her parents' divorce and what she views as her father's subsequent replacement of her with his girlfriends perfect daughter, she thinks her father left her for a better more beautiful family (daughter specifically). Now she finally has everything she ever wanted including the boy she's been in love with since before Ali went missing. Or does she? 
 Hanna doesn't seem to ever see her mother and when her mother is at home she's working and on her phone. But she has given Hanna everything and anything that money can buy. Hanna has a number of secrets, one of which is she's actually bulimic. That's how she lost weight, binging and throwing up, but of course she's convinced that she has control over this. Also although she can afford to buy anything she wants...she steals anyway. Why? Because it gives she a thrill. 
 Hanna is looking for someone to accept her and love her, she feels imperfect because of the way she used to look and is determined to do everything in her power to make sure she stays beautiful and popular. The one positive thing about Hanna is that when she didn't like the way she looked she took it into her own hands to change it, but in the process changes her personality as well. Becoming someone she doesn't like, a bully, yet she doesn't even seem to see it. All she sees is that she is now the perfect physical package, yet at the same time she is still so very insecure. She even has a new best friend who has also re-invented herself right along with Hanna, that's how they become friends in the first place, she seems to encourage Hanna to do everything she probably shouldn't be doing. But could Mona really be called a friend, as she doesn't seem all that supportive on other levels and only seems to want to be friends with Hanna because they have been able to snub others together, the same people that used to probably snub them. Also their friendship basically seems to hinge on Hanna maintaining the perfect image and going alone with what Mona wants. 
 Aria 
 Like all teens she is trying to fit in, but in a more conventional way. She tries different looks and different interests to find her place. Only when her family moves away, after Ali goes missing, for three years to live in Iceland does she finally find herself. In that time she is guarding a horrible secret her father has been keeping. A secret that can destroy her family, but up until they move back everything seems picture perfect. Aria seems the more balanced of the four. 
 Spencer 
 She is the super achiever of the group, she's a top grade student, plays sport and is the head of more school groups than I can count. Ali was the only one of her friends who she competed against but with Ali gone she is top of her friends not that she seems to have any. For all her brains and smarts and the fact that she is a joiner Spencer seems to be completely alone. 
 Even where her family is concerned. 
 She seems to be in constant competition against her sister Melissa who is older than what she is and it should no longer be the case, yet everything Spencer does she measures against her sister's achievements. Which classes her sister took, what grades she got on her papers, was her sister the head of this group, what did she accomplish while she was. Her main goal in life seems to be to outdo her sister. But this isn't just from Spencer's side. Her sister Melissa also seems bent on never allowing Spencer to shine. She constantly finds ways to remind Spencer how much better she was at school. At first I thought it was all only in Spencer's mind but through the first book, whenever Spenser mentions an achievement of the day Melissa has to point out something she did better than Spencer in the past and "Oh I also did this great thing today-kiss my feet mom and dad". 
 Talk about walking in your sisters shadow (as far as Spencer is concerned). 
 But Spencer's parents encourage their children to compete against one another, they even have a game they play call "Star". Where each person names an achievement of the day and the person who's done better than everyone else is the star of the day. I'm all for encouraging you kids to do the best they can but that is kind of ridiculous. The minute Spencer messes-up, she is shunned by her whole family. No one speaks to her or even acknowledges her existence. Yes I get that messing around with her sister's boyfriend (not the first time) was really messed up, but at least Spencer tried to keep it quiet not wanting to hurt Melissa (and it only happened once and also she did try a to avoid the guy). But for some reason her parents won't even give Spencer a chance to tell her side of the story. Even through she apologizes profusely, they don't seem to care nor see that there might be more going on, which pushes Spencer to keep seeing her sisters ex and even starts to fall in love with him. Melissa meanwhile, after making it clear she wants nothing to do with her ex, and also knowing that Spencer is falling in love with him sees him on a continuous basis and then after he breaks it off with Spencer Melissa brags to her that she's been seeing him all along but now she doesn't think it will work. In other words, now that Spencer is in love with him and Melissa has made sure to cheat with him with the express purpose of rubbing it in Spencer's face and then dumping him (now that is really sick). 
 It is also very clear that the only reason her parents want their daughters to do well is so that they can tell others about how great their children are. 
 Emily 
 What can I say about Emily, to me she is the saddest one out of the lot. Nothing she seems to do is in anyway for herself. She's an amazing swimmer, but only because every one of her siblings has been and because her parents want her to be. She is a parent's dream child. Doing everything that's asked of her even dating a boy that her parents approve of, because he's on the boys swimming team. 
 The minute she expresses a desire that swimming might not be what she wants, her mother acts as if she's just found out her daughter in using hard drugs. I mean really. 
 Even worse! She might be friends with a black girl and who wants that kind of association. 
 Alison 
 The person we never really meet, except through the eyes of her old friends, yet she is still at the center of everyone's world. 
 In a way it's sad when they remember her, how she brought them together and made each of them feel unique and special. She always seemed to be right there when they needed her and she was the center of all secrets not just the center of the circle. 
 But as the novel continues we begin to learn that maybe Ali wasn't as perfect and nice as the initial picture each of the girls gives. There seems to be something darker beneath the surface. 
 A 
 We never meet A either or hear anything from A's point of view, but A is just as much a developing character as the others, maybe even more so. as A is in some ways more ahead of the other characters. A has goals and drive and knows exactly what it is that he or she wants. Whereas the other girls are still growing and learning, the fact that A is also set on such a path of destruction is in itself disturbing. Cause let's remember these girls are still mostly only 16, they are still experimenting and trying to figure out who they are. And let's face it not one of them as a clue. All of them is living only to please their parents and to please their peers. But A...A is manipulative and somehow their actions seem, yes childish but also more mature at some points because it is very clear that A is carefully positioning them. But for what is the question. 
 At first A only hints at the past, which all though it's horrible there is no actual proof, since the one person who knew is still missing and probably dead. But when A begins to talk about secrets the girls have shared with no one, not even Hanna's so called best friend Mona knows everything that's going on in Hanna's life it even set me on edge because suddenly A seems to be everywhere all at once. 
 One thing that I found annoy, besides the fact that everyone one of these kids don't seems to lack not a single thing (no wonder they're so messed-up) is that all they seem to do is drink. Hell not only do they drink but they drink right alone with their parents at supper, come home totally sloshed and not one of these people seem to bat an eyelash. The reasonable parents seem to not existing in this world! 
 I mean does Hanna get in trouble when she's caught steeling....? Hell no! Mother dearest covers for her and even buys her other things to make up for the loss of returned the stolen items, then disappears off to work. WTF! Some perspective people!  
 A is not going away, A definitely loves playing with them. So who is A? My money is till on Alison. 
 Definitely a fun read!

I've had this on my to-read list for a long time and finally got around to reading it. I don't know what I was waiting for--I loved it!!! This story is based on the twelve dancing princesses, one of my favorite fairy tales, and I loved the twists and unique way that the story was told.

It's easy to be dismissive of rich white people problems. Having just finished Cristina Henriquez's excellent "The Book of Unknown Americans," featuring a protagonist who is vulnerable in every way that poverty, race, and disability can make her, it was hard to have sympathy for Lockhart's Cadence. By the end of the book, though, she seemed less untouchable. Her tragedy is not enacted systemically, or implicitly sanctioned by a state that views her as second-class. But it is a tragedy. And strangely enough, the book ended up in much the same place as "Unknown Americans," with characters struggling to forgive themselves. Harder to forgive is some of the writing quirks and adolescent drama (maybe that's unfair to complain about in a YA novel?), and--come on, amnesia? Still, I think high schoolers will enjoy the twisty plot and possibly even the "it's rough all over, Ponyboy" ethos. Echoes of fairy tales and King Lear resonated enjoyably.

It was heartbreaking to read Beatrice journal when Giovanni left her for five years... And I get that she was angry at him when he showed up. I even felt real bad for her then boyfriend Mano... But I also feel as frustrated as Giovanni when she keeps clinging to Giovanni yet repeating the fact that he left her, ugh... At some point I was screaming for her to "get over it!" Hell, her best friend, Dez, gets it more than she does... and she just learned that vamps exists. 
 Giovanni's reason for leaving Beatrice was admirable by letting her chose her path, to grow... but there was also something wrong with that logic when you show up after five years later and pursue her and not leaving till she be with him again. 
 Anyway, it's obvious where the story was heading.... 
 I also didn't get why Beatrice would be that stupid to go out and ditch her bodyguard knowing someone evil is out to get her... Nope, I didn't get that at all... To be captured and rescued again... Was it to show that she can kick ass now since she's been practicing? Let me borrow her words exactly, "stupid, stupid, stupid." Right! 
 Then, everybody, meaning all higher up vamps, seems to want Beatrice for her father... or something about Beatrice that is a natural with the vamp politics, it feels like she is being build up to be something bigger than what she is. I have no problem about making one stronger, something more, I love that... but for me to get into it, it's got to be supported and he/she has to be somehow different from everyone. Sadly, so far, I don't see that here in Beatrice case besides the push of words coming from the Giovanni and his circle. 
 In this sequel, not much was resolved... not Lorenzo, the villain, or where her father is and what Lorenzo wants from him... But at least there were hints near the end. I do wonder, powerful and smarter as they are supposed to be than Lorenzo, yet they couldn't get him. Hmmm... 
 I love the turning point of the story, when Beatrice had finally seen the light and realized what she wants. Finally! 
 If I were just rating this for writing alone, I'd say 5 Stars... Despite the problems I have with the story, it did engage my attention and I find their interactions quite interesting.

Somewhat of a chore to read, this almost proved to be pointless for me to finish. Walking trees that kill people aren't the most entertaining or realistic sci-fi trope ever created. Large parts of this are well-written (particularly for a 50s sci-fi novel), but others are almost laughably ridiculous. 
 Wyndham also suffers from an archaic view of women; his female characters are mostly dim bulbs or shrews. Females are even referred to as roaches at one point and their role is chiefly considered to be baby producers. 
 One of the few redemptive aspects of this whole thing is that it does provide an incidental cautionary tale about the current GMO craze and the potentially adverse side effects...even though this was published 64 years ago. I guess that the more things change...

 My eyes were already open to the terrible injustice of the death penalty. This goes further, detailing how our country creates an environment for mass incarceration, treatment of children in the judicial system, and the unbelievable existence of for-profit prisons.

Yeah. To start off, I don't know why Sally Green went in that direction with the ending. Was it for the shock factor? It was shocking. Was it for the sake of tragedy? It was tragic. I just don't understand the reasoning behind that decision. If I did, if it were clear to me in some way, then I might excuse it somehow and accept it. But I don't quite understand the reasoning behind killing Gabriel and writing the most miserable last couple of chapters for a trilogy, followed by the protagonist turning himself into a tree, because he's done living as a person, at the young age of 22.  Why end a book like that ever? 
 Also, I may be in the minority here, but I seriously don't get the hate for Annalise's character. I really don't. She's a pretty decent character that got a lot of hate solely - let's admit it - for the fact that she was cockblock. She stayed decent until the very end too. She did what she did to Marcus because her own family was being shot down in front of her. She didn't exactly have a great time risking her life for Nathan before or after what she did. She didn't have to do any of it because she had all the privilege that white witches get and yet, she chose to stand by Nathan. I admit she was a mildly annoying character on the whole, but I didn't understand the hate. Nathan is no walk in the park with all the brutal killing he's done, so he can cool it on the hate and judging. I'm glad she got her happy ending. 
 This is the part where I'm going to confess that the ending got spoiled for me (damn you Tumblr!). So I knew Gabriel bites it, and as I read on, it became sadder and sadder knowing what happens in the end when I would read the dialogue between the two characters and the life they had planned for after the war.  And here's the thing, I was accepting in some ways because I'd had the time to prep before I reached the end of the book (YEAH WE'RE TALKING ABOUT THE ENDING AGAIN!) but then it happens and the last chapters of the trilogy that followed were so damn depressing. Was this truly what was to become of Nathan in the end? Really? 
 And can we please talk about how Green glossed over the whole he-has-a-son bit and turned him into something, quite frankly, crueler than Marcus? Did he really not want to see his son ever? Even though there's no premonition that his son is going to kill him like the prior (perhaps almost legitimate) problem. (Also, the fact that the author plugged in a son at the end was eternally confusing. Why dump that in all of a sudden and do nothing about it?) That bothered me. 
 I might have enjoyed this book had the author not blundered the ending so badly. I would have accepted what she had done if she had tried to offer a little more solace or comfort to her readers at the end of a trilogy.

This is my 2nd time of reading this book while I write this review. 
 I flew through this book as quickly as I did the first time I read it. Sage is just an incredibly likable character and I instantly want to know how this story resolves, even if I already knew the major plot points when re-reading it. He is just so clever and witty. 
 Sage is an orphan boy who is picked up by a rich nobleman to be trained along with 3 other boys to play the role of the lost prince of Carthya. Carthya's royal family, the king, queen, and elder prince, were all murdered by what is suspected to be poisoned. This nobleman, Connor, is one of the few who know before the general public does, and he hopes to instill a false prince on the throne to prevent a civil war among the nation over who will rule the kingdom next. Kiersten White writes political intrigue as if it is only second to breathing. And I Darken is a toxic concoction that you'll drink down till the last drop and leave you craving more. This isn't a fairy tale in which the sultan gets the girl or the boy gets the sultan. It's a dangerous game played out among Radu and Lada as they shift their allies and enemies like chess pieces into position to claim what is rightfully theirs. For Radu, it's acceptance and to gain the love of his good friend. For Lada, it's to reclaim the glory that is owed to her homeland of Wallachia, and to break the shackles on her of what a man thinks a woman ought to be. As Lada's and Radu's carefully crafted plans come into play, things get savage. The costs are high and many times it's the siblings who find themselves covered in blood.

 "And when you get married, the most important thing isn't being in love. It's making sure you marry your best friend.  "Tied" is a well-timed comedy that is one good-time moment after another.

Alas. Grace of Kings was written to breathe Chinese mythology into the modern epic fantasy. A worthy cause. But for me, I found this book to be a mythology with no grandeur, and an epic with no gravity. 
 It also suffered from constant speedbumps, painstakingly recorded for your amusement and edification at the end of this review. But here's the overview: 
 It's a story of rebellion against a callous empire. And it's a story about power - who has it; how to get it; how to keep it; and at what price it will come. The two central characters are Kuni, a commoner with his ear to the people, and Mata, a ferocious warrior groomed from childhood for pure vengeance. 
 But we stray from these characters frequently - the book is structured as more of a mosaic, with smaller tales interspersed at every turn. It's an ambitious structure, which gives the book an unusual feel and tone. And it's one of several devices aimed to make the book feel halfway a fable, or folklore, or myth. 
 The problem is that myth is built on tremendous resonance - and for me, Grace of Kings has none. Indeed, it's downright discordant - full of snags and bumps that make no sense at all, except as arbitrary decrees of author fiat and artifice. 
 So it is, for example, that Kuni and Mata meet, and immediately we are told that they become the fastest of brothers. But they never actually do anything very brotherlike. They never even seem to get along (and indeed, they have every reason not to). The only way in which their brotherhood is displayed is that occasionally, one or the other (or both) will announce how close and brotherly they are. So when, in a later act, tensions begin to rise between the two, the book seems to treat this as a cataclysmic tragedy. Whereas I the reader say, "Ummmm, yeah." 
 In truth, the entire characterization of our two protagonists suffers the same flaw. We're told that Kuni is daring, compassionate, and inspiring - but reading what he actually says and does, he mostly seems like an over-romantic loafabout who happens to be infallible when convenient for the author. And we're told that Mata is admired and respected by all - but from the text, it's very hard to see what anybody sees in him. Here's a character who apparently likes Mata very much: She did like Mata, liked his awkward, stiff demeanor; his sincere, unadorned speech; his open face that could not hide how he felt. She even saw his faults in a forgiving light: his hot temper, his fragile pride, his overweening sense of honor. Now, read that and tell me true - does any of that actually sound attractive? Awkward and stiff and a hot temper he can't hide? What a catch! 
 It is as though, knowing he is writing grand myth, the author feels free from the constraints of logic and literature, and expect us to unquestionably accept anything he pronounces. This lets him stage grand battles and foul betrayals with great economy; the problem is, they feel hollow and forced. This problem repeats itself in so many ways, shapes and forms: in characterization; in plot twists; in battle sequences. I jotted down some reactions as I read, so you can see how many speed bumps and WTF moments I ran up against (scroll down to the status updates). The reader is continually expected to accept conclusions that just don't follow from the build-up. 
 The cruelest cut of all is that this should be true at the thematic level as well. Liu's writing is heavily concerned with moral, ideological, and political issues - but by waiving any commitment to plausible cause and effect, any statement he tries to make rings hollow. 
 Liu is trying to cover complex territory and shades of gray. It's a novel about rebellion against a cruel oppressor, but it isn't a story of mere bravery and glory. It's about how power corrupts; about how noble causes can be brought low by individual opportunism or fracticiousness; about how a ruler who ignores the well-being of his people must come to regret abusing their trust. But a ruler can't be saintly and pure either; there come times when truly horrendous acts are necessary. 
 Liu does a very good job of setting up these themes and tensions. Indeed, any hundred pages of Liu's should convince any sane reader that responsible leadership is an out-and-out impossibility. The only one who doesn't seem convinced is Liu himself - who showers Kuni with success, victory, and moral vindication, no matter how far-fetched or unearned this result may be. Kuni doesn't make mistakes (although sometimes other people make mistakes for him). When something morally questionable needs to be done, it's other people making the suggestion and other people making the call that, yes, this atrocity is really necessary. If he's ever at any risk of that whole business of being corrupted by power -- you know, that central thing the book's about -- then Kuni just shrugs it off and decides to not be corrupted by power instead. Easy! 
 It's back to the same problem: Liu's writing in broad strokes, and he is telling us that Kuni is heroic, capable, and good, without showing us that he's actually so. And instead of showing us somebody coping the the impossible conflicts of leadership, he just tells us that Kuni copes with them; every last blessed one of them. So Grace of Kings presents itself as navigating through the murky waters of power and war. But in fact, all we see is Kuni blithely overcoming hardship after hardship, because the deck's stacked solidly in his favor. The book lays out a formidable minefield, and then dances its protagonist right through it. Some may find that inspiring; I can't see it as anything more than false hope and wishful thinking. 
 Should I Read This Book? 
 Grace of Kings has gained quite a bit of acclaim already; obviously, this review is only my own opinion, and you might enjoy it a lot more than I did. 
 I would say you're likely to enjoy this book if you're familiar with Chinese culture and mythology; if you're a fan of a wide range of Liu's short fiction; if you enjoy epic power struggles on the national level, more than the personal; or if you enjoy trying out unusual writing styles. On the other hand, I would be very leery of comparisons to Game of Thrones or other familiar epic fantasy; this is a very different sort of beast, which you're likely to find deeply unsatisfying in that capacity. 
 What I will say is: If you're debating, read the preview at Amazon. It's an excellent representation of the book's tone and style. If you love it, great. If that doesn't wow you, then rest assured, it is not going to get better. 
 Further Reading 
 If you aren't sick of me already, you can see the reactions I jotted down while reading. Scroll down below the review, to the status updates. There's no better description of my reading experience than seeing exactly what I experienced while reading. And in this case I frequently get ranty, which is probably amusing. 
 Below, under the spoiler tag, I wrote a kind of case study about Kikomi - one of the characters and arcs in the book I found most infuriating. It's kind of a companion piece to this review, because I take a specific, limited chunk of the story and explain why it didn't work for me. Like, really really really didn't work for me. 
 ---- 
 A Few Words About Kikomi 
  
 Kikomi is presented to us as a tragic figure: because she is the princess of Amu, and a beautiful one, her nation has cast her as their symbol of perfection and beauty, and made into a living ornament. And she has one more defining trait: an immense loyalty to her people; a desire to serve and protect them - at whatever cost to her self. Truly, she is a noble soul, cruelly wronged. And her chapters had me spitting nails. 
 It was a cliche for a beautiful woman to complain about being cursed with beauty, Kikomi knew, but just because it was a cliche didn't mean it wasn't true, for her.It's not the use of the "I'm only valued for my beauty" cliche I'm objecting to. It's that it was used so very, very poorly. What we have here is that simultaneously, the entirety of Amu thinks Kikomi is doing something very very important, and at the same time, Kikomi thinks that she is doing nothing at all. 
 There are a million ways to explain why Kikomi sees her role so entirely differently than every single other person in her nation (the nation which, I remind you, holds her undying love and loyalty). Unfortunately, the novel doesn't bother to suggest any. It's taken entirely for granted that a whole nation is really invested in keeping Kikomi miserable for absolutely no reason. The closest we get is an attempt to explain the purpose of Kikomi's ornamental role:"You're a symbol of the revival of Amu," her granduncle, King Ponadomu, said. "Of all the Tiro states, we have always been known for our dedication to the essence of civilization, of grace and refinement. Being beautiful is the most important thing you can do for the nation, Kikomi. No one else can remind the people of our ideals, our self-image, and our goddess as well as you."That's the rationale. 
 Is it a good rationale? A bad rationale? Kikomi never responds to it. Let me repeat that, because it might not be entirely clear: Princess Kikomi has no reaction whatsoever to the justification her people provide for why her life needs to be miserable and pointless. 
 This is the very definition of hollowness. 
 Grace of Kings does not bother building up enough background and culture to actually justify the value it claims Amu places on Kikomi's beauty. It just tells us "It's really really important to them." 
 It doesn't bother building up Kikomi's character, to explain why she's so different then the entire culture surrounding her. It just tells us "She's really really miserable." 
 This is not a real society; this is not a real person. This is not even real sexism and oppression - which are deep-rooted, self-renewing, and provide tangible value and privilege to its beneficiaries. No; this is the Idiot Plot of gender politics - Idiot Sexism, where an entire society unites to make one woman miserable for no reason besides that the plot needs it. 
 Kikomi's story continues beyond this starting point, but not well, I'm afraid. A goddess comes and makes some speeches on women's power which falls squarely into the "As You Know, Bob" category. Then she tells Kikomi what to do next, because heaven forfend Kikomi should come up with an action plan herself; it's not like we just spent a whole chapter explaining how capable she'd probably if she only had the opportunity. Then that doesn't work and somebody else gets Kikomi under his thumb, and now he gets to tell her what to do. Then she goes along with that well and obediently, getting herself in position for a month or more. Then, in the instant between murdering a man and being discovered, she comes to the sudden epiphany that she's been played all along. Good timing there, Princess! 
 This has been a long rant on one very specific element, but I took the time to delve into it because it exemplifies my experience of the entire book. The book is deeply invested in Kikomi as a tragic character; in discussing sexism and women's position in society; and also in a plotline of intrigue and seduction. But it just doesn't get any of them off the ground. They're too superficial, too easy, too damned convenient to have any weight at all. 
 Ambition is a fine thing, and it shouldn't be forgotten that this is Liu's first novel. But I don't remember the last time I read a book that failed so completely at its own basic goals.

Old fuck you's, horsing around and a million forms of hate. 
 I was kind of scared going into this book, since I'd previously read a few reviews that contained some really negative opinions or worries concerning the (in some cases bad) impact this book had in the past. 
 So I started it anyway, and I can without a doubt say I was hooked after the first two pages. Salinger's writing feels like butter and it's surprisingly easy to digest. I felt like I was listening to a friend while drinking coffee and the story flew right in front of my eyes, and before knowing it, it was over. 
 I definitely see why some people didn't enjoy this novel. It basically has no plot and it's literally about this angsty teenager (spoiler ?) getting, not for the first time, kicked out of school and not knowing what in the world he's gonna do next. Still, I was hooked with Holden's storytelling and his extremely funny remarks and opinions. I'm his age and I could definitely relate to some of the things he was feeling, which made the reading experience much more enjoyable. 
 Excepting the language and the CLEARLY 1940's-1950's way of speaking and writing, I couldn't believe I wasn't reading a novel published in the 2010's. I imagine that, like every other classic's story, Holden's has captivated readers for more than half a century. I can definitely say I was.

 This was so much better than I expected it to be. There are constant power plays, scoundrels, formidable captains, backstabbing slaves. Instead of the lame issues most YA heroines have, Yarvi truly does have a crippled hand with only two fingers. He cannot grip much of anything, and his arm is weak as a result too. And, being born into royalty, Yarvi is met with unrelenting scorn from everyone in his life, from his own family to the guards that watch over him. So when his father and brother die and suddenly leave him as the new king, no one's all that happy about it--least of all him. 
 Yarvi's uncle betrays him and throws him into the sea to drown. Yarvi's situation gets worse after getting caught by slavers and being forced to be an oarsmen for a crackpot drunkard captain. But along the way, he makes some lasting friendships too. 
 What makes this such a success is the fight that Yarvi has with everyone. He begins as a coward, a boy with no motivation to become better than himself other than what others already expect from him. Plus, it's never too hard to believe. Yarvi has a hand that doesn't work, so he is not a master swordsman. His accomplishments come from fighting up close with someone and stabbing in the back, because that is the only way he can get ahead. It felt much more realistic but didn't take away from the fantastical appeal of the setting or the characters. 
 The novel is fast-paced but never felt rushed. The moments that counted got their due time and it made for wonderful pacing. It was hard not to keep reading this straight through. 
 There was even a big reveal that I didn't see coming! A big fat giant curve ball that came out of left field and scrambled all the laid plans of conquering! I certainly did not see that coming and I AM SO EXCITED ABOUT IT. 
 BUT. The BEST PART was the reveal of the bad guy in the end. I did not see that coming either, and I was thrumming with excitement while reading the final chapters. I got all giddy and had to reread some parts because I was starting to skim as a result of wanting to see EVERYTHING as quickly as possible. Yarvi's mental fortitude is no clearer than in those last couple chapters, and I cheered at his decisions. He was a wonderfully developed character, the sinister plan was well developed, everything was well developed. I literally have no bad things to say about this novel.

I'm not a history buff by any stretch of the imagination (I could not tell you one single thing about the real lives of the inspiration for these characters), but it just always bugs me when fake words and situations are given to real people. I also thought the whole fantasy element of people turning into animals (Edians) was just weird to have in historical fiction. But then I kept seeing glowing review after glowing review and decided to finally see what the fuss was about. And now I understand! 
 I have never read anything by any of these authors before, but if the rest of their writing is as clever as this I am definitely checking them out. I laughed so much during this book! Out loud even, which almost never happens. Each chapter is given to Edward's, Jane's, and Gifford's point of view and the narrators of the story would occasionally interrupt with some (often humorous) insight, explanation, or random comment. Though I did enjoy the Edward and Gifford's chapters a little more than Jane's for the most part, I was never sad when it came time to shift POVs. 
 I loved the friendships and the romances. Gifford and Jane were so easy to ship and their interactions were always so humorous and/or sweet. I liked the friendship between Jane and Edward and how much they cared about each other.  The only thing that kind of brought the book down for me was that the pacing got a little slow at times. Though I enjoyed the characters so much that it didn't really matter what they were doing, I did wish the plot would advance a little more quickly on several occasions.

I definitely plan on checking out more from these authors (I did see on Good Reads that though this book is a standalone, they are planning on collaborating on more books about other famous Janes). I wanted to like this book because of the reams of good things I'd read about Pamuk's writing, and because I respect his integrity and courage as a person. How many are willing to be thrown into a Turkish jail in defense of free speech? That said, I found the novel hard going. Margaret Atwood in her review of this book for the Times coined a term for a genre she calls the Male Labyrinth Novel (which I think could also include Ishiguro's "When We Were Orphans") in which an exiled, rootless, wandering protagonist prowls bleak city streets having encounters with various untrustworthy characters. The novel takes place in an uneasy climate of political instability; no one can state anything without prevarication for fear of spies (whether they be for the state, or for Islamicists), and the prevarications seem to extend even to the emotional states of the main characters. Every feeling is qualified by an undercurrent of its opposite. The interpretation and sincerity of every action is suspect. I found the indeterminacy exhausting. The slow pace of the novel was also a problem for me. For a while, I acclimated to it, and it was lulling to take my time, but eventually, I was restless to finish the book and leave it behind. The last criticism is of the writing. I just don't understand how everyone loves it. I found it very clunky. Could it be a translation issue? But I find it hard to believe all these encomiums are coming from people who read it in the original Turkish. 
 On the upside, the novel explores a lot of interesting issues about identity in a diaspora, about the struggle for the Middle East, and Turks in particular, to reach a working relationship with modernity, and I particularly enjoyed the doubling of many of the characters (Ka and Pamuk, Ipek and Kadife, Necip and Fazil), but then I always like those kinds of explorations. The novel could grow on me now that I've finished the actual struggle of reading it, but I dread to approach the other Pamuk on my bookshelf.

Geraldine Brooks is so great at finding all the perfect notes to make me love her books. I love historical fiction but often find it lacking in its writing and depth, but her books include both while still being highly readable. I ADORED this. It raises important questions on truth vs. lies, idealism vs. reality, dreams vs. practicality.  I loved the shift to Marmee's perspective midway through the novel to allow the reader to see the flaws in March's thinking and to consider the ultimate question of the novel of whether it was all really worth it.  I don't know that I've ever read a Civil War era novel that gives such a strong picture of the brutality of slavery, the War, and its aftermath. I did think the love triangle aspect was a little overdone and frustrating, but the rest of it was so strong that I didn't really care. A perfect companion for adult lovers of Little Women.

I wasn't so sure about this book, it sounded really out there and it was written for the young adult genre.  Because of a fish whose flesh has healing abilities, Rudy is forced to move with his family out to a desolate island near which the fish are found. Rudy is a typical troublemaker sort of teen boy prior to the move. His main pastimes have been smoking, drinking, sleeping around and sketching. On the island though he feels like he is in purgatory, there is only one other girl on the island anywhere close to his age and she won't leave her house. Nevertheless, he meets homebody Diana, who makes him wonder what he even knows about love. Rudy starts drawing again and meeting up with Diana, but his life mainly revolves around his brother's health. One day he may be permitted to leave to attend college but until then everything else in his life is put on hold for the sake of his brother. He loves his brother and wants to do what he can to aide in the battle against the cystic fibrosis which threatens his life. Rudy has to get up early to get the best fish from the fisherman and the rest of his time is spent in tedium and boredom. 
 All that changes when Rudy saves Teeth from a brutal attack by the fishermen and finds out that the miracle fish have a steep cost. Teeth is a half fish, half boy (merman) of sorts who has a sad story and an even sadder existence. They become fast friends. Rudy can't remember the last time he felt so connected to someone, but being friends with Teeth is more than a little bit complicated. Teeth brings adventure into Rudy's life by begging Rudy to assist him in releasing the netted magic fish and waging a war on the fisherman who remove them from the waters. He soon learns that Teeth has terrible secrets. Violent secrets. Secrets that will force Rudy to choose between his own happiness and his brother's life. Teeth sees the special fish as his siblings and tries to protect them from the fishermen. When Rudy realizes this he is torn between acquiring fish to aide in his brother's recovery and his friendship/attraction to Teeth and the defense of the fish. 
 Moskowitz assumes that readers are intelligent and doesn't necessarily spell everything out for you. The book is very atmospheric and the spare descriptions are both beautiful and horrible. This is an interesting read about family, love, friendship, magic, loneliness, and what humans will do when they are desperate. The events that take place are never really described in detail but what the reader is left to assume is happening is very disturbing. At times this makes the story kind of ambiguous. As a reader you pretty much know what's going on but you kind of hope you are wrong. 
 The book is engaging and so different from everything else out there. It is gritty and raw with ambiguities that leave the readers to fill in some of the holes that we wouldn't want filled by the author. Aside from the fishes' healing abilities and the unnatural form of Teeth, the magic in the story is very subtle. The book does not fit in a pretty little box. There's a lot of thought-provoking parts to the story where the question is raised about what is right. For example when is it right to sacrifice something to save something else? It ties things up in a realistic, if not fully satisfying, way.

The Sleeper and the Spindle is a retelling of sorts. Part Sleeping Beauty, part Snow White, 100% Neil Gaiman dark fantasy filled with twists. Our Queen is reluctant to get married, but on her wedding day her Dwarf friends arrive with a wedding present and some bad news: The sleeping sickness from the kingdom on the other side of the mountains is spreading into the Queen's kingdom. And not slowly either. Setting aside her plans, the Queen and her dwarven friends embark on a journey to stop the sickness. Rumors tell of witches and dark magic putting the princess to sleep over 60 years ago. But they are just rumors, and the Queen cannot let her kingdom be threatened. 
 As with many of Gaiman's tales, our story in intriguing from the start and slow to develop. As it to be expected, albiet unpredictable, Gaiman takes everything stereotypical the reader might know about traditional fairy tales and twists them slightly. There are a handful of fascinating gradual reveals. There are some hilarious moments of common sense being applied to problem solving in fairy tales (  I mean, he has a point. Why didn't any of the previous heroes who arrived at Sleeping Beauty castle set fire to the roses? They just decided to climb over them? Silliness, in retrospect.  ) As with all fairy tales, this one is built upon lust for beauty, power, youth, and freedom. But all threaded together into a unique spool of yarn. 
 With a few twists, Gaiman eliminated almost all fairy tale troupes in The Sleeper and the Spindle. In doing so, and featuring the women he did, Gaiman provided a swift feminist kick to tradition. A beautiful story, I would recommend it to anyone who loves fairy tales, surprise twists, and dark fantasy.

 Finally a shiny new and original story from Nora Roberts. When you've read nearly everything an author has written you sometimes can't help but be reminded of other story lines by said author {Dark Witch I'm looking at you!} so I wasn't expecting too much from The Collector. 
 As soon as I saw it on my kindle on release day I sat down to read it and was once again back in love with Ms Roberts. The Collector is everything I've come to expect from Ms Roberts single yearly releases. A delightful mix of contemporary romance and romantic suspense that pulls you in and takes you on the journey with both the characters, this time Lila and Ashton. 
 Lila is a professional house sitter and loves going from one person's home to another, meeting her clients, their houses and occasionally their pets. She gets to travel and see parts of the world which she may not have been able to see. Lila is also a novelist writing the second book in her YA werewolf series. Which I found amusing and wondered if Ms Roberts would ever publish her own version of it. Rather unlikely but still... 
 Lila has a habit of taking a pair of binoculars with her everywhere she goes and likes looking out of her clients windows to see what other people are doing, until one evening when Lila is house sitting for a new couple and out of their bedroom window see's a young woman pushed out of her window to her death. 
 Ultimately bringing Lila and Ashton together for a friendship and relationship that neither of them expected or wanted. 
 I loved Lila and Ashton they were both brilliant characters with such fire, passion and strong beliefs. Ashton is a very famous artist who comes from a family with money and has lots of interesting connections and while he wants information from Lila about what she saw the night his brother died he also finds her fascinating and is determined to paint her. Which starts the interesting relationship between Lila and Ashton that takes them on a dangerous adventure on the search to what happened to Ashton's brother and what he was up to before he died. 
 I seriously highly recommend The Collector. It is an amazing read and possible one of the best books Ms Roberts has written recently. I might possibly be buying the paperback copy too to add to my collection.

Yet Eli was the bad person at the end of the novel. Also Mitch of course. He really does remind me of Hagrid.

 On the good side, I liked that Barrie isn't a damsel waiting to be saved by a guy when she gets into trouble. I couldn't figure out why he was so into her when she's constantly furious with him. Despite what YA books like to portray, this doesn't work in real life. Portraying male/female relationships like this does a disservice to teenage girls in understanding how healthy relationships work. 
 Anyway, this was basically amateur hour. One-dimensional stock characters. Completely implausible scenarios (usually involving the burned-beyond-recognition dead mother). A mythology felt beyond forced. The abilities to find lost things and to tell what people want are just so random. Believable mythologies should feel like the story follows their lead, rather than that they were created to fit the story, you know? This felt so cobbled together. 
 When I read the reviews raving about the book, most of them point to the gorgeous Southern setting. I agree with this: the setting is nicely drawn, and definitely felt more like the Lowcountry than some other South Carolina-based YA I've read. But...I don't know...a family named Beaufort? I live in Beaufort, SC. I just kept thinking that the author had gotten a guidebook about the Lowcountry and picked out details that appealed to her. 
 I want so badly to find an awesome YA book that takes full advantage of the crazy amounts of atmosphere in the Lowcountry. Beautiful Creatures was a huge disappointment. This one does a better job with the setting, but the rest of it was so whackadoodle that I wanted to quit reading after 50 pages. There are promising elements, but as a complete novel, it doesn't work at all.

I really liked this book, but I found some of the translation awkward (but I nitpick). 
 The overall plot was great (and the hangman is an interesting character that I wish had been more developed), but the ending fell kind of flat. I will be reading the sequel, though. 
 Another note: could anyone elaborate on why the book is called The Hangman's Daughter?

I am a sucker for these books. I was riding the Gillian Flynn fan train loooong before Gone Girl was a thing, and I'll happily hitch my wagon to whoever the next big one is for psychological thrillers. I haven't read Paris' previous book yet so I can't compare, but I definitely enjoyed this. The unreliable first person narrator is getting a little old for sure, but I think here it works better than a lot of other cases because there's a strong reason for her unreliability. 
 You'll probably guess who the baddie is here if you've read enough thrillers. There's not a lot new on that front, and the pieces to the puzzle are revealed fairly quickly. And while Cass was extremely annoying during her downward spiral, I love her actions in the last fifth of the book. She was fully redeemed in my eyes once that happened. 
 Unrelated question: Did you change your last name to Paris because you lived most of your life in France, miss B. A. Paris?
This one just didn't work for me. Still a great series though.

I was so excited when I found out there was a spin-off series. Let me first say I was in love with Vampire Academy, so reading this was a little hard for me simply because I missed Rose, Dimitri, Lissa and Christan. I like Sydney, but sometimes I found her a little boring, but slowly I am warming up to her. I've always loved Adrian. Jill reminds me a lot of Lissa, as in they are both pretty annoying. I did find this book a little slow and boring, maybe because their wasn't much romance and I was pretty much waiting for Adrian&Sydney to kiss the whole time. It was nice to see Abe and Rose return at the beginning and I simply can't wait to see who else returns in The Golden Lily. I also did have a bad feeling about Kieth and Lee from the start so it didn't surprise me that they were trouble. I can't wait to see what happens in The Golden Lily, hopefully more action and romance!

This one is a stunner. My initial reaction was four and a half stars, but I changed my mind. Yes, this is the source novel for the ScarJo movie, but other than a very small part of the plot, the two works have very little in common. 
 The novel is as lyrically stunning, prose wise, as the film is visually stunning and is vastly superior. The plot in the novel is a stunningly powerful allegory about meat eating, class differences, and sexual exploitation. There are elements of a thriller, science fiction, and horror here as well. 
 The writing is lyrical and beautiful, without feeling artificial. The protagonist is endlessly fascinating and is filled with so many contradictions that you'll be continuously torn about your feelings for her. This one is in no way mainstream or conventional, but if you enjoy that kind of thing, you'll like this one.

I went into this with high hopes, because I've read other Marie Lu books & loved them, but this one just didn't wow me. 
  A virus swept the land. Those who survived were left with strange markings and even stranger powers. Adelina is one such Young Elite (as they are called). But she is also labelled a malfetto, a scourge on society, because of her strange powers. 
 But the thing is, Adelina cannot access her powers. She doesn't know why, but nothing happens, even when tested by her Father in terrible situations. 
 Then one night, as Adelina tries to run away from her father's arranged marriage, her powers overwhelm her and she kills her father. She then runs into some other Young Elites who try to help her hone her powers to be more useful and less volatile. 
 As time passes, Adelina cannot control her desire to do bad things with her power - the fury and fear is to heady a feeling. 
 This causes many problems for Adelina, who is eventually banished from the Daggers, the very Young Elites who took her in and tried to train her. 
 Woven in between Adelina's battles with herself, are the battles she must face with the other Elites, against Teren and the Inquisitors - those who are trying to eliminate the malfetto from the general population.  
 Overall, the story did grow. I found the story to be quite confusing at times, but it did unravel itself enough to make sense. 
 I found the main character, Adelina, to be quite unlikeable, mainly because she seemed to be an antagonist, fighting other antagonists - there didn't really seem to be a good presence in the book at all. 
 Perhaps the next book in the series would bring more of Adelina's story to light, and I might learn to like her more, but this book just didn't do it for me.

This book was one big confusing mess. I still am completely baffled by Drew. It felt like there was a cliffhanger, but there wasn't. And there was very little chemistry between Tanner and Berry. 
 Basically 'Veronica Mars' + 'Alias' + 'Pride and Prejudice' does not = a good book. It just got too convoluted, like it was trying to be all twisty and complex. 
 At least the writing flowed well, which is more than I can say for most books these days. Maybe keep it a little more focused next time.

Best one in the series for me. The plot felt solidly cohesive and progressed logically, Verity is as charming as ever, and there was SO MUCH DANCING!! 
 Plus there were mice, and Grandma Alice (!), and more female friendships (have I ever mentioned how much I love that Verity has friends?) 
 Just great.

Ugh Rick Riordan. You took the things I love most and put them all into one big series. You took Roman and Greek mythology, added the greatest power couple of all time, and every new book adds a new Roman or Greek god. Percy and Annabeth are still the greatest parts of these stories, and I absolutely love how much we get to see them grow and change. Especially Percy--going from a clueless twelve year old who runs into every situation gung-ho to a sixteen year old with more measured decisions. 
 The same could really be said for a lot of the characters in this book, and I think this book in particular was meant to be the ultimate in character building. We see Frank Zhang mature into his own by killing a herd of poisonous cows. We learn some really important stuff about Nico, what finally is causing him to act so strangely Nico is gay. And had(has?) a crush on Percy. And since he grew up in the 1940s before being stuck in the Lotus Hotel, needless to say he's internalized everything and withdrawn from anyone who could possibly guess. It is when he confronts Cupid (Eros) with Jason that he finally has to come to terms with it, which in turn leads to Jason being much more understanding of Nico's moods.  We learn that Hazel and Piper both have some pretty freakin' awesome powers, which I loved because so far we hadn't really seen too much from Piper that was actually helpful. We finally learn why Coach Hedge is acting funky  His wife Mellie is pregnant! Yay!  and Bob the Titan makes a comeback. 
 Percy and Annabeth's trek through Tartarus was fantastic. They're such a strong couple, really I think the best in any YA book. It's easy to see why every other demigod that comes into contact with them is in awe of them. They're truly a power couple in every sense of the word, and I think provide a pretty damn good model for kids to follow, unlike many other YA romances. 
 But anyway, they had to face some pretty terrifying foes in the underworld. I think the zits full of monsters was disconcerting and that coupled with having to face a physical embodiment of Tartarus is just plain terrifying. But they were steadfast and always taking care of each other. 
 One thing I will say too is that I love that we are revisiting old characters, and that Percy is finally starting to feel guilty about not following through. First he realized he never made any effort with Bob. Then Calypso makes an appearance with Leo, and we learn that the gods never followed through with releasing her from her prison island Ogygia, and Percy never bothered to follow up with her afterwards. And I like that because it means that maybe it will lead to him actually making an effort to be a friend to all of the people that have helped him over the years. His greatest downfall is that he never thought twice about those who helped him, so I hope this will change his tune. 
 But really, Percy and Annabeth are still the shit. Rick Riordan is amazing at making me care for a million different characters. I can't wait for Blood of Olympus.

This is an intimidating book. Weighty in terms of themes, the prestigious prizes it has won, and the clever structuring and style that reflects the planets and the phases of the moon, it is also literally an extremely large book. It's also a book that seems to have divided opinions considerably, so I was very interested to see what I would make of it. 
 The story begins with the arrival of Walter Moody in Hokitika, New Zealand, in 1866. He walks in on a meeting of twelve men at the Crown Hotel, and is soon pulled into their discussion of a series of events, and of the sinister man who seems to be behind it all somehow: Francis Carver. 
 This section of the novel immediately drew me in; mysterious events, a group of such different characters all driven together by fate, a historical setting and a fascinating look into a New Zealand Gold Rush town - all great elements! The events themselves are related in a slightly odd way; each person describes what they experienced to Moody. This isn't related in direct speech from the person telling their tale, but described in third person as a summary of the events they have just told to Moody. Within these stories, other characters might tell their own story, sometimes also related in third person rather than direct speech. This can become quite confusing, particularly if listening to the audiobook, as it is harder to flick back to find out whose point of view we are seeing events from, and because events are often told in the narrator's voice rather than a recognisable character's voice. This isn't a fault with the audiobook, but is a result of the slightly odd way that the story is related in the beginning section. There are also moments where the reader appears to have been given more information than Moody has been told - for example, would a man describing to another man something that happened to him really break off mid story to deeply analyse another person's character? 
 After the meeting of the men at the Crown Hotel, the story continues and slowly little things begin to be revealed as the chain of events is unravelled. It becomes clear that every detail mentioned in the story is significant, that everything ties in to the greater story that's being told. This is extremely well planned and executed, and I really enjoyed seeing all the different threads pulling together. This doesn't happen all at once, at the end of the book, but steadily and surely throughout the story. It's carefully and brilliantly done. 
 The sheer amount of characters in this book is a little confusing to begin with. I had a hard time keeping track of who was who, something that is a bigger problem in the audiobook because you can't flip to the front for the cast of characters. Thankfully, the narrator is very skilled at giving each character a distinct voice, so though I couldn't always remember at first what a specific person's background and profession was, I always knew exactly who was speaking. The large cast of characters becomes a strength later on in the story once the reader has wrapped their head around who is who, much like in something like Game of Thrones, where the interactions and connections between different people, the little co-incidences, and being able to see a situation from all sides, really brings the whole thing to life. Unfortunately, some characters were more rounded out than others, and some who were explored deeply at the beginning were almost forgotten later. In the end, perhaps there simply were too many people for one book to deal with. 
 The main characters are each connected to a celestial body, astrology being an important theme running through the novel. This was clever, but I do wish the author had let the reader assess each character for themselves through the characters' actions, rather than suddenly breaking the story each time a new person was introduced in order to describe their disposition, hopes and dreams and character traits in extensive detail. 
 The structure of the novel was another aspect that reflected the movements of the heavens, in this case the phases of the moon. The early chapters start off very long, becoming shorter and shorter in proportion to the waning of the moon until the final chapters are mere slivers of the beginning sections. This structure is alluded to on the front cover of the book. I really liked this and thought it was a clever touch, but there were some points where the story perhaps suffered a bit from the need to stick to this structure. Most notably this was in the middle, where the story began to drag a bit, for me, and at the very end, where the chapters were so short the introductory sentences at the beginning of each one had to sum up all the events, telling us rather than showing us what happened. 
 However, what I did love about this approach was the strong fatalistic feeling that this connection with the heavens gave to the story. There are also many references to the paranormal - ghosts, seances, astrology, visions, weird connections between people. Even the name 'Crown Hotel' has associations with Dracula. I loved these aspects, and I particularly liked how many of the stranger happenings were explained logically, but not in a way that entirely convinced, or that wrapped up everything. For example, the strange connection between two characters was still a little mysterious, and I don't think Moody's vision at the beginning was ever really explained. This leaves the reader with the feeling that there are still mysteries in the world, and forces that move us beyond our control. 
 The Luminaries is an interesting book, different in many ways from things I've read before. I appreciated the clever structure reflecting the themes and ideas in the story, as well as the possible supernatural elements and the feeling of fate guiding the characters' interactions. I do think the book was too long and that the story would have benefited from some cuts, especially in the middle section, and in some places the book was perhaps a little too clever for its own good. But overall this is a fascinating and impressive read in which everything is connected and all events pull together into a satisfying ending. The narrator reads the audiobook extremely well and I really enjoyed listening to it!

I love Laini Taylor's writing so much I want to cry. It's so beautiful! I love how her characters, locations and storytelling are so detailed, so vibrant, so vivid, so alive. I just want to read everything she's ever written and just lose myself in the worlds she creates. 
 I'm holding off on giving this a five star because, as much as I loved this, I honestly believe the series is going to get even better and there were a few minor things that I wasn't such a fan of. I wish there had been more build up instead of the instalove we got. Seriously, they fight, and then suddenly they're both in love with each other. Having read on, it started to make sense, there was reasoning behind the instalove, but then, there still wouldn't have been as much build up (not a lot of difference between a month and a day). And I especially dislike it when it happens in book one of a series. Luckily having read the whole thing, I don't think it's going to be as much of an issue.

I absolutely know why this book gets so many 5 stars. Colleen knows how to write. For me personally, it was more of a 3, which on GR means "I liked it", because I'm not a fan of really depressing books. So I balanced it out at a 4. I made a point of knowing nothing before I read the book & I would have done better if I'd had a heads up. The book makes a point (one I got before reading it but if I hadn't, it may have struck me more intensely) and is very touching once I read Colleen's notes at the end. That was the point that brought a tear to my eye. Powerful stuff for an author. 
 Spoilers ahead... the main point of the book has been discussed so I'll mention the thing that turned my stomach and was hard to read just because it was the part I could relate to: Ryle's mental illness. He's described as blacking out and having no knowledge that he acts violently. If he'd just acted horrible when riled, I could have written him off. Yes, no matter what, Lily should have left him. But as someone who has suffered from intense clinical depression & anxiety and knows the horror of having your emotions not be your own and out of your control (not anger. I don't even know if that's a real thing. God, I hope not.), Ryle's situation was gut-wrenching. His life was ruined from 6 yrs old and he is branded, horrifyingly accurately, as unfit for love or being able to be close to someone. That rang way too close to how it feels to be in the pits of clinical depression where you feel to your core that you are nothing but a disaster waiting to happen to anyone you dare love. With depression, I'm wrong, but for Ryle... the horror of it being right turns my stomach. It's a book that I personally should have passed on. (Thought I should clarify in case anyone reads into this: I don't want trigger warnings. I love to read blind and will continue to do so.)

"Because it wasn't okay- it was never going to be okay. I was stuck in this life I didn't remember, squeezed into the shell of this girl- in this Samantha Jo Franco- and the more I learned about her, the more I was starting to hate her." 
 Samantha was a mean girl along with her best friend Cassie. Except since the accident and Samantha losing most of her memories, she starts to relearn who she was and how she treated people. She sees how truly awful she was and wants to try and make amends for what she had done. Except her old friends and boyfriend don't really like this new her and want the old one back. 
 As for her family. Well her brother likes the new her for the most part. But her parents don't really like this new Samantha, sure they kind of like it, but they also miss something things that the old Samantha did, mostly her ex-boyfriend's family. 
 "I didn't want to remember the terrible things I'd said and done, but I suppose it didn't matter. Even if I couldn't remember who I was, everyone else would never forget. No matter how badly I wanted to ignore the person I used to be, I couldn't escape a past I didn't remember." 
 What really happened to Cassie was a surprise to me. I never would have guessed that on my own, but after we were told it was easy to see how the signs were there the whole time. 
 Samantha's new romance I liked for the most part, but at times it just seemed a little weird as well considering how awful Samantha had been to him. 
 "You deserve someone who can give you the world, someone who can stand on his own. Do you understand me?" 
 What I liked the most though was Samantha's brother and the sibling relationship they had. Even though she had treated him like dirt for quite awhile he was still there for her when no one else was. And when a certain person was trying to make her believe that she really was going crazy. Her brother was there and made sure she was always okay. Which was a good thing considering how absent her mother was throughout the whole thing. 
 "Things weren't perfect. They were far, far from it, but they were getting there, and I wasn't look back. Not when there were so many good things in the future." 
 I'm glad I gave Armentrout a second chance with this book after I didn't enjoy her Lux series. If she writes more books like this one I can't wait to read them.
