 There were many impressive things about this book. One, the world of fae/fairy and goblins though repeatedly told and rehashed at this point in YA literature Tyger Tyger still remains kind of fresh and enjoyable. Two, the interwoven details of religion. I was skeptical but as soon as I opened the book, I was intrigued and immediately drawn into the book. It's not everyday you read about a girl's sweater being used as toilet paper by an ape after the ape drops a load and this actually was done out of spite too. The characters themselves were likable. 
 Interesting enough, I greatly enjoyed one of the back up characters: Abby. She's dim-witted, girly, and entertaining. She mixes psychic with psychotic... calls herself psychotic when she meant psychic, but at the core she cares about Teagan, our protagonist, and Teagan returns that feeling. Abby also seems to have mob connections so another point. The only character that made me sour was the social worker, Ms. Skinner, who tries her best to ruin the lives of the Wylltsons (Teagan's family).  This more of a rant than spoiler. Just a side rant. Ms. Skinner isn't fit to be a social worker, especially since she threaten Teagan to take Teagan and her brother, Aiden, from their parents because they were being uncooperative. Also, personal feelings about Child Services just ills me (A day or two ago I came across an article about a man who emotionally lost it, killed his wife and himself because he was accused of beating his infant child (who they took away), only months later it's revealed the child had a rare bone disease that cause the fractures, etc.) <- not the only story I'm familiar with the wrong doings of child services... breaking and destroying too many wrong families and yet does close to nothing for the children who really needs it. Now, I know it's not always the case, but there are enough cases. I'm not bashing social workers either... my best friend is a social worker, she comes home crying and stressed but at the end of the day she feels like she helped someone and feels good about it and I think its great for her and I think she's great at what she does.  
 What I really liked about Tyger Tyger was the influence of religion. It was smoothly done and not heavy-handed or a slap in the face. It was rightly and easily detailed in, fitting perfectly with the overall lore and arc of the story. Now, to clarify it's not religious in the sense of church going, televangelist (not that there's anything wrong televangelist) but in the context that it uses God, Angels, and church to evoke a fresh take on Goblins/Fae. Here in this book, there was a hint of distinction that the goblins are not fae/fairies but through details and description they are fae/fairies (when compared to other novels). There is yet to be an explanation of what the fair folk (fae) are like... only the hint that maybe they're the same only "nice/good" and goblins are evil fae. 
 The relationship between Teagan and the love interest Finn I'm split down the middle. It seemed Finn took an immediate liking to Teagan (love at first sight) while Teagan is resistant. While it wasn't quite love at first sight (which I dislike) it almost is (from Finn's perspective). Their relationship was thinly built and so when they agree to what kind of relationship they have I'm like... I'm not sure I buy this though I guess Hamilton has two more books to explore it. The chemistry was lacking because they spend most of their time running and hiding (which is believable and rightly so), but there were no small tender moments or moments of confessions through actions, rather enough of these moments to cement their relationship for me. There were just doubt and thoughts... which isn't enough for me because, lets face it, a good lasting relationship requires verbal communication. 
 I also had a hard time accepting the age of Aiden. He's supposedly five but acts much more older than a five year old. At times, I feel like he's ten and there is even one or two instances he sounds like a young teen (13 or so). Mind you, I work with children a lot and there are some very intelligent five years I have come across... but at five when you're faced with goblins and such... I question the stride Aiden takes the creatures and their situation. Some of the smart comments I can accept, I can see that as "oh that's really smart and way above a five year's mental growth" but for Aiden it's okay, but there are also many moments I question the things Aiden does or says. 
 Overall, this book is an enjoyable enough read with an interesting spin of the world of goblins. Slight mishaps (or lack of) with characterizations aren't enough to cause issues. The pacing of the story is excellent and moves forward quickly without spending time on irrelevant things. Hamilton gets to the point of a scene quickly and moves on. 
 Verdict: A "Maybe I should Buy" list. Library Check out. I'll keep tabs on next books.

 Heaberlin effortlessly weaves together past and present into one suspenseful tale of a woman trying to outrun her monster. Ignore the Gillian Flynn comparison. Julia Heaberlin's Black-Eyed Susans is so good it doesn't need it. 
 Black-Eyed Susans is not your usual serial killer story. Details to what exactly happened to Tessa when she was taken at sixteen are kept vague. The horrors the other girls in the grave may have faced are also not expounded upon. There is no grand speech from the killer explaining what made him/her the way he/she is. The story is really more about Tessa's journey to recovery, which after almost twenty years, is still not quite finished. 
 Tessa is the lone survivor of the Black-Eyed Susan killer. She testified against the man who is now on death row with very little time left. When Tessa finds the out of season black-eyed susans planted outside her bedroom window she believes it's the work of the killer, her monster. And it isn't the first time it's happened. She joins the team working to free the man she helped convict before it's too late. In doing so she is forced to confront secrets she's kept and memories she's repressed. 
 Tessa was a likable heroine. Other than being super protective of her teenage daughter and that the other "Susans" talk to her in her head, she's not as crazy as you might think she would be. She's paranoid (maybe even rightfully so), but she's functioning and has made a good life for herself and Charlie, her daughter. Adding to the paranoia brought on by the flowers she finds outside her window, she starts receiving gifts from her childhood friend Lydia, who she hasn't seen since the trial ended about twenty years ago. Lydia and her family disappeared into the night and no one had heard from them since. 
 The story is told in alternating chapters of Past and Present. I'm a big fan of multiple timelines and it's done excellently here. There were several chapters that ended in cliffhanger moments and the next chapter you were in a different timeline. It definitely kept me turning the pages, feeling unable to stop because the story was continually suspenseful in at least one timeline at any given time. After the first two parts of the story, the third is told in Tessa's Present and Lydia's Past, and one chapter from The Monster which was also very effective story telling. 
 This is a very character-driven novel, which I loved. I feel like we really got to know Tessa, even though she was not always the most reliable narrator. I liked all of the side characters, her daughter Charlie, their neighbor (and comic relief) Effie, the lawyer and love interest Bill, Charlie's father Lucas, and the forensic scientist Jo. I also felt the side characters from the Past, Lydia and the therapist that is helping prepare Tessa for trial, are very well done. 
 There's not much more I can say that wouldn't involve spoilers. Overall, I really enjoyed Black-Eyed Susans. It was a well paced, character-driven, suspenseful novel that I couldn't stop reading. And during the few times I wasn't reading - for silly things like work - I was thinking about reading it. I would definitely recommend it to fans of Suspense and character-driven novels.

 As for character development, Meira develops even more in this book, and really comes into her powers and accepts herself and her role in the war. Other characters also follow this trend. I am glad that Meira decided to be honest in this book regarding her feelings and how to win the war. I think I'm just really tired of miscommunication in books, and characters trying to take everything on themselves, which usually causes more problems. Additionally, since this is a finale and the stakes are high, I found that the emotions in this book were more raw and intense than ever, and I loved that. I felt for these characters. Every time I pick up a book, I expect to be taken on a ride. Sometimes it's a short drive into the city for dinner, consisting of laughs and entertaining conversations, leaving me full and content by the time I reach home again. Other times it's a fast-paced roller coaster, ups and downs twisting my stomach in knots, exciting me until the very last page. My favorites are road trips, the ones that take forever and a day to get through, but every adventure is new and you get to know the characters on a more profound level. 
 With Prep, what started off as a promising book---a protagonist with room to grow, a realistically structured setting, the timeless coming-of-age plot---quickly became one of the most boring, ridiculous things I have ever read. I wanted very much to like Lee Fiora, because I related to her shyness, her seeming invisibility, and her self-deprecation. I waited patiently for her to learn from her mistakes and was sorely disappointed when Lee stayed exactly the same through four years of high school. As a time of self-discovery and growth, it is not only uninteresting for Lee to remain unchanged through one of life's most crucial periods, it is impossible. 
 As if the protagonist being a stagnant, unlikable mess weren't enough reason to give this book a mere one star (I wouldn't even give it that, had I a choice), the plot mirrors its protagonist, setting up what could be a wonderful story about finding oneself, but ultimately going nowhere. Think about taking a very long and slow drive around the block; about fifty laps of seeing the same neighbor mow his lawn, the same houses, cars, and weather, before you pull back into your driveway disappointed, frustrated, tired, and just as hungry as when you left. After turning the last page, my exact words were "That's it?" 
 I wasted a week of my life on a book that did nothing save leave me with the bitter taste of a girl, similar to myself, who gets used by her crush for a game of sexual conquest, ruins every potential relationship she might have, ultimately ends up alone and unsuccessful, and doesn't learn a thing throughout the entire process.  
 I read to find romance, inspiration, fantasy, and escape. Sometimes my forays into a good book are rewarded with tears, sometimes with giddiness, but always with the satisfaction of having gone somewhere outside of what reality can offer and having learned something new and exciting. 
 Prep offered me a pathetic woman with nothing to show for herself but an ungrateful, cynical attitude. If I've learned anything, it's that after two hours of passing my own driveway, I should pack it up and choose a different ride.

Last year I loved Julie Buxbaum's Tell Me Three Things and I was really hoping to love What to Say Next just as much. At first, I didn't think I would. I even put this one down to read something out before coming back to it. I'm so glad I kept reading, though, because I did end up really enjoying it. 
 I LOVE DAVID DRUCKER. I love him! While I wasn't sold on the story from the very beginning, I was sold on David pretty much instantly. He's such a different character than I've read before. He's on the Autism spectrum and while I'm not exactly qualified to comment on how realistic a portrayal it was, it did seem pretty realistic to me. There were several times he reminded me a little of Sheldon from The Big Bang Theory. He was sweet and funny and so, so honest. I just adored him. He went through some heartbreaking moments in this book and I loved seeing him end up stronger because of it. I also really loved his relationship with his sister. 
 It took a little longer to warm up to Kit. She's grieving the recent death of her father and while I think it could be cathartic for readers who are going through similar circumstances, it was a little redundant. I kind of feel awful saying that because I know there are stages of grief that everybody goes through at different rates and if it was me I would probably be much the same, but at the same time it made her kind of unlikable for awhile. (I also thought this particular storyline was a little too similar to one in Buxbaum's last book.) However, as she learned to deal with things in a more emotionally healthy way she became a lot more likable. And her friendship with David made me like her even more. My biggest problem with her storyline has to deal with her father's accident. I felt like there was supposed to be a bit of a mystery surrounding it, but I thought it was obvious and was a little annoyed that it wasn't "revealed" until close to the end. It brought with it an extra bit of drama I didn't feel was really necessary. 
 The story is told in dual 1st person POVs. At first I didn't think it worked and wished we only had David's POV. I felt like David and Kit's stories didn't really go together. It almost felt like reading two different books with a couple of shared scenes. Once David and Kit started to spend more time together and be a bigger part of each other's lives, though, I started to really appreciate the style. Also, Buxbaum nailed their individual voices. There was never a time when I didn't know which character I was reading. I also absolutely loved being in David's head. 
 Overall, What to Say Next started out a little rough for me, but I ended up really loving it. I loved the growing relationship between David and Kit and watching David learn how to better interact with those around him. David Drucker has become one of my favorite characters of all time. I definitely recommend this one.

First impressions: With regard to how I came to read this book, the phrase "borrowed from a friend" is not entirely accurate. Let's call a spade a spade - I was book bullied into reading this.  Lasting impressions: This book could actually happen. Which is definitely equal parts scary and awesome (as a reading experience, not as life). 
 Conflicting impressions: Alex may have needed to know how to kill and skin animals. I didn't. Too real for me. 
 Overall impressions: Have you heard of the supervolcano underneath Yellowstone? You haven't? You should Google it. It's terrifying. I first learned of it through another fiction writer, James Rollins, and it is not outside the realm of possibility that it could blow in my lifetime. That kind of real, impending natural disaster is ripe for the picking when it comes to good stories. 
 Mike Mullin does not disappoint. Our young protagonist, Alex, is home alone when the volcano erupts and his neighborhood is quickly decimated by falling ash. Determined to try and escape the deteriorating conditions, Alex heads east across Iowa trying to reach his family across the Mississippi in Illinois. He straps on a pair of cross country skis and heads out. 
 This version of post-disaster American life is dark, frightening, and full of danger. It quickly becomes dog-eat-dog, and Alex runs into his fair share of unsavory characters out only for themselves. He does all he can to survive, relying on his own skill, luck, and occasionally the kindness of strangers. Just when you think he's found a bit of peace, something else goes wrong and he's forced to move on. It's gut-wrenching. 
 It would be unfair to give away too much. Will Alex find his family? Will he figure out how to survive in this new and dangerous landscape? What will happen to the U.S. in the aftermath of this horrific eruption? We get a great story full of action and terror, and the promise of more with the reveal at the end. I can't wait for the next installation in this series!

Quite The Novel Idea ~ Words from the Clouds 
 4 REASONS YOU SHOULD READ THE SIX OF CROWS DUOLOGY 
 The Writing 
 Leigh Bardugo's writing has always been amazing. Right from the start. And while the Grisha trilogy was written brilliantly... somehow she got even better this time around. Both Six of Crows and Crooked Kingdom have writing so good it should be envied and admired by all. And it probably is. Leigh is still one of my favorite fantasy authors and she always will be. The way she built the world, somehow making it the same as the world we knew in the Grisha trilogy, but also very distinct and unique at the same time, is brilliant. Everything is, really. From the narrative to the different POV's to the delicious banter between the characters. Everything is just fantastic and it's writing so good I want to eat it with a spoon. 
 Long story short... I want to be able to write like this. Very much so. 
 The Story 
 How do I even start with this? The story is a masterpiece. Both the stories from each book individually and the overall story. The details in it, the feels, the epic finale, the heists and cons,... All of it was so SO good and it was never ever boring. Crooking Kingdom is over 500 pages long but it never felt slow and it never dragged on. The pacing was perfect and the stakes were high and everything was evenly balanced between sad and happy, peace and action, calm and tense,... THE TWISTS. Oh my god the twists. AND THE FEELS. They destroyed my poor sensitive heart. 
 And while the story is perfect the way it is, I still want more. I want more of this world. More heists and cons. I want to stay in Ketterdam for a while longer. But it's over for now. And I will miss it dearly. 
 Story-telling like this is something everyone should strive for if they call themselves a writer. 
 The Characters 
 While the story and the writing are brilliant in every way... what makes these books shine is the characters. All of them, but mainly our main six. Kaz, Inej, Nina, Matthias, Wylan and Jesper. All of them. I love them SO much. They're SO amazingly well-developed and they grow throughout the book but it's never unrealistic, but they're so real and amazing that it hurts that they're fiction. Their pasts are so well thought out and all given equal time to unfold. Kaz is an evil genius in every way and he's villainous and can be cruel but he's also so precious and vulnerable at the same time. Inej is a badass who, admittedly, I didn't like much in the first book. But I warmed up to her more in the second book. Nina is the best of ever. She's so fun and sassy and sensual and she LOVES food and I love her. Mathias was the one that I had my doubts about in the beginning, but halfway through the first book I loved him. He is so stubborn and strong and grumpy and just adorable really. Wylan is precious and adorable and smart and I feel like I want to protect him at all costs. And Jesper is honestly my favorite of the group. He is a sharpshooter that loves gambling a bit too much and he's funny and awesome. 
 The banter and chemistry between these six is golden. Even over a hundred pages of them hanging out and talking would still be the most entertaining thing ever. Seriously. 
 Squad goals. 
 The Ships 
 Because we have to talk about the ships. We live for the ships. I loved all of the ships and I shipped them so hard it's insane. They all sailed and I loved that and of course my favorite ship is Wylan/Jesper. WHO IS SURPRISED HONESTLY??? I can't talk much about this though without spoiling so I'll just say that all of the romances were handled perfectly and I adore them. 
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
 I could wail about these books for a long time but this should be enough to convince you. RIGHT? If not... honestly what are you doing with your life? Go read these books and come tell me you were wrong for doubting me. Now I'm gonna go sit in a corner and cry because this series is over.

 Walpole's idea was to say that he translated an Italian text The Castle of Otranto that went all the way back to the crusades when in fact he didn't. He was quite successful in his hoax but alas a hoax is always reviled and so was Walpole. However this is the book that sparked the desire for gothic romance. Now I know who to blame! 
 The Castle of Ortanto is not a standard gothic novel, for starters there is the element of supernatural in this book and a sense of the ridiculous. Which personally I thought made it a perfect short story for Halloween. 
 The start of this story the only son of Manfred, Conrad who is fifteen and sickly gets crushed to death by a giant helmet falling from the sky on him just before he is about to attend his wedding. His father Manfred who's only heir is his daughter Matilda, but can't inherit because she's a girl decides that he has to get rid of his wife, he decides the only decent way to do this is to send her away to a nunnery, and he will marry his son's intended Isabella instead and continue on his family legacy (creepy old man!). 
 The Castle of Otranto continues to get even more bizarre as the story continues with floating limbs, people being locked up, falling portraits, murder and a brief romance, all of this just packed into just 115 pages! It's a punch that's totally worth it. 
 To be honest this is one of the strangest books I have ever read. Especially when you consider it was written in 1798 and is not what I would have expected of the time but that's what makes this a really good read. When I first finished reading this book, in 2011 might I add, I threw this book against a wall in complete exasperation because a) I wasn't sure how to take this book and b) because I was so surprised by what I had read. Even though The Castle of Otranto is technically a 'classic' I certainly would not call it that but I can say now on my third read that I appreciate it more than the first time I read it. It has a rather dry sense of humour to it and takes everything you would expect in a book written in the 16th Century or from gothic novels and twists it into a really interesting read. 
 I would highly recommend The Castle of Otranto for any classic and gothic horror fans but also those who want to try something little different too.

I love goosebumps when I was a kid and this was one of my favorites. 
 'Say Cheese and Die!' was the fourth book in the Goosebumps awesome book series. 
 The story starts with Greg finding an old camera at a spooky house owned by Mr. Spidey (a strange old-man with spider-like appearance). Greg's very amuse with the idea of having a camera so he began by taking a picture of his friend Michael who is leaning on the stair railing. Suddenly, the railing gives way and Michael falls. Michael obviously got hurt upon the uncanny landing. Greg surprisingly discovers that the picture does not show Michael standing by the stair railing but instead FALLING. Caught dumbfounded, Greg and his friends continued to investigate and discover the unearthly events the "evil" camera had caused to go along with them. 
 Years after years, I found out that there's a sequel to it (forty-fourth book): Say Cheese and Die - Again!, and Say Cheese - And Die Screaming!

WHAT I LIKED 
 -Annie's relationship with her dad. Though they had some fights, he was always present and always supportive. He wasn't perfect, but he was realistic and a good parent. 
 -Annie's sense of humor and the banter between her and her friend, Lenny, and also with Brody. 
 -The behind the scenes look at the baseball industry was an interesting plot line that I haven't seen in YA before. 
 -The character development. I really liked all of the main characters - Annie, Brody, Jim, Savannah, Lenny and they all go grow throughout the book. 
 -The romance is cute. There could have been a bit of an ick factor with the one character being an "adult" major league player and the other being a high school student, but really they're 19 and 17 and about the same level of maturity, so it wasn't really bad. 
 -The ending was sweet and gave good closure for all the characters. 
 WHAT I DIDN'T LIKE 
 -This little gem that made me definitely feel too old to be reading YA, "He's still handsome, even at thirty-six years old." It's the "even" that gets me haha. 
 -Another YA book that's a little too graphic, with a somewhat irresponsible view of sex. 
 -There was a lot of emphasis put on how Annie needed to not cause any "scandals" because she's the pitching coach's daughter. Admittedly I don't really pay attention to baseball, but I couldn't even name a pitching coach, let alone care what their kids do. That part didn't really seem realistic at all. 
 -The relationship between Annie's parents could have been explored a little bit more. 
 Overall, Whatever Life Throws at You was a sweet, enjoyable read with strong character development. While parts were a little too mature for what I think YA should be, it's probably one of the better YA contemporaries I've read. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5) 3.5 Stars

I am a hoarder of pleasure. If you looked at my house, you wouldn't know it because I don't really keep a lot of things, but what I do have I like to savor, and I always save the best for later. When I was a kid, I saved my chocolates at Easter and Christmas so long that my brother and sister started begging me to share. When I eat a meal, I always leave some of my favorite food until the end. And with books, I store up potential treasure-troves rather than reading them right away. I suppose I'm like a dragon with its hoard, happy to think about what's in store and afraid of using it up. 
 But there are a few anticipated times every year when I let myself indulge in some of the saved-up treats. Times when I know I'll have an entire day I can bum around without guilt and just read myself into oblivion. Thanksgiving break is one of them, and yesterday (Wednesday), after a couple false starts, I settled on reading The Girl of Fire and Thorns. 
 This was a real treat. It was easy to get into, the high fantasy world atmosphere was the kind I love to sink into, and the pace was just right for a day when I didn't have to stop reading. It had action and intrigue, and Elisa was a girl who really grew and changed throughout the book. I thought I knew where it was going with the romance a couple times, and was surprised at what actually happened. So it's not totally cliche - something to make me happy anytime I read a novel with a romance aspect. Now I'm not sure what's going to happen in the sequel, which I've already moved onto. 
 I've seen some other reviews that mention some flaws, like a lack of depth in knowing the characters and the relationships between them. I agree, and it's one reason I'm not giving 5 stars. I feel like there was potential for me to be more emotionally involved. 
 Another tiny thing that holds me back from a 5 star rating relates to how Elisa uses the stone in her navel, especially during the last fight. Elisa finally figures out what to do with the stones, attaches the amulet to the one in her navel, and then it spins around blasting everything.  This scene was just a little too comical to imagine and took me out of the seriousness of the moment. Really, this was not a good mental image for a life-or-death battle. 
 Still, this had just about everything I enjoy in a fantasy while not being so serious and complex that it took me 200 pages to get into it.

This one is going down as one of my favourite fantasy trilogies. 
 Without a doubt! (This review contains some spoilers of book 1 and 2) 
 Part of it is very typical Robin Hobb (after 6 books I'm allowed to say that right?) she makes characters so incredible real they become existing people. I've said it before, but it's just really true: they become people for you to love or loathe. But it's also remarkable how mean she is to them all: she sends them through hell, leaves them there without food or drinks, and then kindly asks them to walk back barefoot. Mean, mean! 
 There is however one thing she does in this trilogy she didn't do in the previous one; for this one she took a trick of the fantasy writers tool box: multiple point of view characters with storylines that are all coming together. Not one 'catalyst' but a whole family of them. 
 I thought the general world building was very well done. The serpents, dragons, elderlings, pirates... enough mystery to keep you on your toes until the very last chapter. 
 Safe to say that i loved this trilogy. It just has all the elements right: Well developed characters, check. Marvelous world building, check. Solid writing, check. Enough tension to keep you going, check. A few unpredictable twists, check! And so on. 
 I want to end this review with Paragon. While I'm typing this, I have Mumford and Sons playing in the background (a CD obviously, if they would be live in my living room I wouldn't be typing!), and this song reminds me of him. 
 Now I'll be bold, as well as strong 
 Use my head alongside my heart

 That tethered mind free from the lies memories 
 In my mind, I see Paragon, waiting all those years on the beach for someone who will push him back into the winds. Someone to restore him to former glory. And at last, the waiting is over, Paragon is sailing again and I loved every second of it!

Two stars. 1 star was added because the author did a reasonably good job of making me believe I was in a boy's head, and I liked the writing style. 
 What I can't get over is how completely and utterly STUPID everyone is here. Every single one of them. 
 You know the story. Ryden is a 17 year old single father, left that way as a result of his girlfriend Meg dying. She had cancer, they had sex. She got oops pregnant. She decides she'd rather die to make sure she has a legacy in the form of a baby. To start with, this is already a highly-contentious topic. Should she have aborted the baby to save her own life? 
 I won't even get into that debate, because that's not where the crux of the story is. The emphasis is on Ryden trying to live life while suddenly having a newborn to take care of. And let me tell you, he fails hard. I think the author did a great job of characterizing him. He's the top boy in the school--mister popular, gorgeous, "sex on legs" (a quote from one of the female characters in the book), and the school soccer all-star. For all intents and purposes, he is King, and his actions show that. His first thought is always for himself, he's stubborn, he's sullen when he doesn't get his way, and he thinks his choices are always 100% the best ones. 
 He's a total idiot. 
 Let's just go through the steps, shall we? Meg. Meg has cancer. Meg and Ryden have unprotected sex, because he thinks she being on birth control means there's no other chances of babies. That's the first issue. The second comes when Meg makes a completely fucking stupid decision to keep the baby, and make Ryden the father. Ryden, who did not ask to be the father. Now granted, it takes two to tango. But Meg KNEW the chances of her surviving the pregnancy were nil, and she still cornered Ryden into fatherhood. The third issue: Ryden has no real reason for keeping the baby. Now, I understand that may sound rash and horrible and like I should burn in hell. Here's the thing: his family is poor. They do not have vast wealth lying around in a vault at Gringotts. Meg's very wealthy parents refuse to even acknowledge the child, which is an issue all on its own. So instead of giving the child the best possible hope of succeeding with adoption, he keeps the baby he's not equipped for because she's a part of Meg. Awwww 
 Gag me. 
 It was incredibly selfish and he takes everyone down with him. He starts asking his grandparents for money because he can't afford the baby on his part time job at Whole Foods. His mom has to work constantly in order to feed them all. His mom's life is put on hold so she can help him. 
 Wait, you ask. What about Ryden's life? Is his put on hold, too? 
 No, my dear friends. It's not. He pawns the baby off on everyone and anyone so he can flirt with the new girl at his part time job, so he can go to soccer practice, so he can be alone. You are a father, you immature brat. You are not the most important person in the room anymore. 
 So yeah, I hated Ryden. Pretty much from the get-go. Just because he's more adept at wiping baby butts at the end of the novel doesn't make him any more of a good father. He only finally made good decisions after they were forced on him. I don't see the character growth in that. 
 But worse than Ryden, SO MUCH WORSE: MEG. Through Ryden's little obsessive journal hunting, when he should have been taking care of his baby but was instead spending a week looking through a storage unit, he comes across a little secret. 
 Meg, in her infinite wisdom, got pregnant on purpose. She knew she was dying, and she wanted to leave a legacy of herself. She intentionally got pregnant, kept the baby while her body was dying, and then left her new boyfriend with a child he never wanted or asked for. She was absolutely despicable to me, cancer or not. She willingly uprooted everyone's lives for her own selfish whim, a whim that she wouldn't even have to deal with the consequences for. Why not, right? It's not like she's going to have to deal with any of it! Joke's on you, Ryden, HA HA HA! 
 I absolutely hate Meg. For someone who is painted as being intelligent, she is a complete fucking dunderhead, and a thousand times more selfish than Ryden. 
 Those two, together, are giving baby Hope the very least they could give her. Now, baby Hope has a dead mom she'll never know. She has a father who, if we follow the same characterization as the novel, will only ever think of himself and will probably take out some of his bitterness at Meg on Hope instead. Hope is in a family that does not have the means to take care of her. Her grandparents refuse to even acknowledge her existence, let alone be invested in her life. Which is all the more hurtful when she's old enough to know that they could help give her a good life. 
 The idiocy here knows no bounds. I hated every single one of these characters. Which is why I give that one additional star--the author did a great job of crafting them into believable, stupid, SELFISH people.

I picked this book up, not because I had even the smallest expectation of enjoying it, but because I kept seeing copies of it at the airport when I was on my way to the annual Association of Zoos and Aquariums conference, and I was curious. I was shy a book to read on the plane, and the first 24 or so chapters were free on my Kindle. (This isn't quite as impressive as it sounds, given that the chapters run about 1,000 words each.) 
 Plus, I reasoned, even if it was awful, it'd be interesting to see how Patterson deals with anthrozoological issues. I figured it'd be interesting on at least a anthropological or sociological level. I looked forward to analyzing its fears and arguing with it. (Notice all the excuses I'm offering. That's because I deeply regret the poor decisions I made that resulted in me reading this book.) 
 Instead of an academic interest, though, as soon as I began reading a sickening sense of horror crept over. This book is worse than The Da Vinci Code. This book is worse than Twilight. This is, in fact, the worst book I've ever read. 
 I'm not sure which is the worst facet of this festering heap of detestableness, but I could break it down into a few headings of horrible: 
 1. The writing style. It's just awful. The chapters average about three or four pages. The sentences are all short and choppy and written in such an action-adventure cliche style that it comes off as a parody of itself. In fact, Dave Barry writing a parody of a Dan Brown novel has better prose than this. He actually used the phrase "rosy-fingered dawn," which I thought was illegal. He also threw in all sorts of things meant to be cute such as, when a grizzly is attacking his SUV in DC, "I assumed he wasn't from AAA." Ha ha. Very clever. At this point, I was rooting for the bear. 
 2. The stupidity of all the characters, without exception. The gist of the story is that the protagonist Jackson Oz is a "scientist" (more on this later) who believes that animals are going nuts and attacking humans. And yet he thinks nothing of keeping a chimpanzee in his apartment. Chimps are dangerous even if you're not confidently expecting the animal world to run amok. 
 3. The sexism. The first (and actually only) sex scene in the whole book is so flagrantly written to play up Oz's rampant masculinity and dominance that it was unintentionally hilarious. Later, when Oz meets his obligatory Sexy Science Babe, every single time she's mentioned he reminds us how gorgeous she is, how very pretty and delicate and small, how totally unlike every other scientist woman he's ever met. Blargh. Not only that, but her whole role is to admire, cheer-lead, support, fall in love, and need comforting and defending. 
 4. The "science." Patterson read, at maximum, two Wikipedia pages as research, and that was it. I would be surprised if he even got all the way through both of them. He may be able to spell hydrocarbon and grasp some extremely basic (third-grade-level) concepts of pollution, but clearly not chemical dissipation, bio-accumulation, or any other chemical, biological, or ecological process. He's just throwing around the words to sound important. And don't get me started on the acronyms. Also, no, Oz is not a "scientist." He got an undergrad in science. That's not the same thing. He's a hack. 
 5. The fact that, at a critical point in the plot, Patterson skips five years for no apparent reason except that he apparently got bored. 
 6. The totally unnecessary violence and sickening detail on animal deaths. I'm not even going to go into this. Seldom has a book given me the actual physical urge to regurgitate. 
 7. The ending. Or lack thereof. In a better, braver, deeper book, Patterson's choice for an ending might be brave or bittersweet or thought-provoking. Here it's an admission of defeat. If you're going to come up with some big thorny problem, you owe it to Science Fiction to at least try to come up with a solution or at least a message. "I dunno, we're screwed" doesn't cut it. Plus, do you expect me to believe they're not burning fossil fuels to stay warm up there in their ivory tower beyond the Arctic Circle?  
 This is a book that had to be downed quickly, much like a very unpleasant shot of hard liquor you're drinking for some unimaginable reason. I saw someone had it shelved as "burn so as not to inflict upon other library patrons." I thought she was exaggerating, but now I whole-heartedly back that decision up. This book has absolutely no redeeming qualities. 
 Deep down (Very deep down. Thousands of miles.) this book has two good points: 
 1. Humans are more distanced from animals than at any other time in history or pre-history and this is not a good thing. 
 2. We're affecting the environment in unknowable and dangerous ways. 
 But that's it. This is an execrable excuse for a book. It shouldn't even get a star. No one at all should read it, even as an example of everything you shouldn't do as a writer. Or an editor. Or a publisher. Or a human.
Meh. Opposite sides of a post-colonial continent, but this reminded me of The Stranger if The Stranger were about humans instead of robots.

This means that as soon as a beat in one thread is resolved, there is something you have to know about one of the other threads. Consequently, I spent far too much time reading this book when I should have been at my job. 
 The book ends with a particularly shocking twist, and something that I think is a genuinely new subversion of the genre. I can't work out whether I like it, or think it's legitimate -- I think I reserve judgement until I've finished the last one.

Sigh. Another example of a great debut and a sequel slump. Hamilton's a strong writer and she has a great voice, but at the very least, this book needed another editing pass. There was a lot of repetition that should have been cut--which would have solved another problem: this book is too long with too little momentum. 
 I had a number of issues with the plot, which can be boiled down to three main points: 
 1. Most of Amani's problems were solved either via deus ex machina or by running away. 
 2. Amani is impulsive and action-oriented. Yet she spends most of the book whiling away her time in a harem, judging other women. It was downright painful to watch her attempts at subterfuge and political machinations, and not in a good character growth sort of way. It was the wrong plot for Amani. 
 3. This whole point is a massive spoiler because it's the crux of the book, but it's also why so much felt off. Leyla's double-cross of Amani, Rahim, and the entire rebellion came as a huge surprise to me, and I imagine, to many readers. But not for the reasons it should have. It was a surprise because there was nothing in Leyla's character to suggest why she would act the way she did. Her motivations are never explained: Why is her brother so devoted to her? Why is she loyal to her father over her brother? Why is she loyal to her father at all? What danger is her brother trying to save her from? Why would she choose to harm Uzma, Mouhna, and Ayet after they taunt Amani when Amani is her enemy? So many things did not add up.  
 And, to top it off, the conclusion contained one of my least favorite tropes: the villain explains the plot to the protagonist. Never mind that they're in the middle of a stressful, time-sensitive situation and gloating could give your enemy the precious few minutes they need to regroup. By all means, tell us why and how you did what you did.

I never planned on reading this. But my 11-year old daughter is a huge fan of The Hunger Games and Katniss Everdeen. She went through the trilogy like starving tributes gobbling up food scraps, and has been bugging me for an archery set repeatedly (the answer is no, of course, since we live in Tokyo). Most of the kids in her class love it. Then I saw the movie, and I thought, "Wait, this is a pretty cool story with a kick-ass heroine and a believable dystopian scenario." And I noticed that many of my friends on GR, who are pretty serious sf-fantasy readers, gave this high ratings and glowing reviews. 
 So I gave in and read it over 2 days. Just seeing my daughter enjoying it so much brought back memories of my early reading days. The story is exciting, brutal and pulls no punches, despite being aimed at the YA market. And I think that's why it has met with such success. Frankly, kids these days are pretty savvy about their entertainment (well, there is Twilight but let's just ignore that for now), and they like a gripping survival tale that depicts a dystopian world that is still believable. And with the plethora of reality TV shows (Survivor in particular) and mixed-martial arts bloodfests (MMA), it's not hard to extrapolate to a future like Hunger Games. 
 Bottom line: A compulsively-readable, tightly-paced story with likable, realistic teen protagonists facing harrowing conditions in a grim dystopian future.

When I first heard about this book I knew immediately that I would want to own it. It sounds just like my cup of tea-- a regency era steampunk space traveling adventure with a girl disguising herself as a boy. 
 I think this novel is very well crafted. There is a lot going on across the entire book, but it is sectioned off nicely by chapters. I was never overwhelmed with the world, the science, the characters, the plot, or any other elements because they're introduced gradually overtime. It was also really refreshing to reach an end point of a chapter and feel satisfied to pause my reading if I wanted to continue later. This also means that the plot itself was laid out well. It had a wonderful flow that causes one event to lead to the next. 
 I also really enjoy the blend of the sci-fi, fantasy world. It's fantasy because atmosphere exists between Earth and Mars, making it possible to travel between Earth and Mars by airship. The sci-fi, other than the airspaceship and automata technology, comes in at Mars where we find out that Martians do exist and have a well-developed culture and society. Arabella even has a Martian nanny to teach her Martian ways. I definitely would like to learn more about the Martians and possibly any other lifeforms that exist within this universe. 
 One thing I was not completely sold on by this novel is the romance. I love a good romance as a side-plot of a series, but I do not completely understand where Arabella's and the Captain's  feelings come from. I was not really anticipating/on the edge of my seat waiting for the characters' to admit their feelings like I usually am. The novel has a lot of other great things going for it and this doesn't take much away, but it is the main reason why I didn't give it a 5 star rating. 
 I think it's a great start to a series and I will definitely pick up a copy of the next book.

Once in a while you'll pick up a book and it'll knock you for a six. Or 5 in this case. We have all heard stories of the horrific acts experienced during the holocaust, but I found I have never heard a story such as this. Narrated by Death, through the eyes and heart of a young german girl. Poetry of song, lyrically engaging with many subtle surprises. Incredibly well written, warmth found in description. 
 The girl simply didn't care any more. For a long time, she sat and saw. She had seen her brother die with one eye open, one still in a dream. She had said goodbye to her mother and imagined her lonely wait for a train back home to oblivion. A woman of wire had laid herself down, her scream travelling down the street till it fell sideways like a rolling coin starved of momentum. A young man was hung by a rope made of Stalingrad snow. She had watched a bomber pilot die in a metal case. She had seen a Jewish man who had twice given her the most beautiful pages of her life marched to a concentration camp. 
 "The Standover Man", and "The Word Shaker", lovingly written by a desperate man, a gift of hope in the heart of defeat, 'Make them come back alive,' she repeated. 'Please, Lord, please. All of them'. Even the wrinkles around her eyes were joining hands. 
 The tightening of my chest closing the final page, thinking that death shouldn't be feared, after all...... 
 I've seen so many young men over the years who think they're running at other men. They are not. They're running at me. 
 I loved the thought process of death, and his non bias way of caring for the souls he carried. 
 Having personally seen the concentration camps, and the jewish heritage museums, this book was an element that reminded us, that it wasn't just one race that suffered but many.....

Veronica has been asked by the Neptune grand to investigate at incident at the hotel. A woman was beaten, raped and left for dead. The last place she was seen was in the new rooftop bar, waiting for her boyfriend; a married man she doesn't want to name. She has suffered some memory loss but does remember seeing a staff member who was an illegal immigrant and has recently been sent back across the border. The hotel may owe her damages and they want to exonerate their staff member, as well as learn the truth. 
 After asking some questions, Veronica wants to know the truth as well, and she has a lot of tools in her arsenal. 
 Mac is still working for mars Investigation, Keith is back as well and supporting Weevil in his case against Celeste Kane (who shot him) and Sheriff Lamb (the department planted evidence on him). He also has a civil case against the Sheriff's department supported by the statements of dozens of others who were also fitted up. 
 Meanwhile, the Sheriff is up for re-election. Keith isn't running but a woman from his past is. Deputy Leo is now working at a different Police force and helps Veronica out when he can. 
 Wallace is still coaching basketball and Logan is home on leave. But Veronica is spread pretty thin trying to work on the rape case; something that is always an issue for her on a personal level. 
 *** 
 The thing about these books that works so well is that they have a cast of thousands from three series of the television show, innumerable events where a viewer might have wondered what happened to character X after that scene, and a thousand locations to use. So, they mention someone or a location and it strikes that note of resonance. Veronica pretends to be a guidance counsellor? Ding. The victim goes to Hearst college? Ding. Wallace sees an underage sportsman buying alcohol at the sac and pack? Ding. Mac spends hours working with computer footage? Ding. Logan buys a puppy... wait... what? 
 Resonance. That's the word. 
 So when readers discover that the rape victim is none other than Grace Manning (the child Veronica and Duncan found locked in the wardrobe at Meg's house), it works. I always wondered what happened to that kid.  
 A couple of story lines felt unfinished: the woman from Keith's past, the return of Leo and the death of Deputy Sacks are still hanging. 
 It also makes sense that Veronica would use tools that are basically illegal - heck, she always pushed the line, or leapt right over it. It also makes sense to me that the Navy would give Logan the sense of order that has been missing from his life up till now. It's just a strain that their relationship doesn't need; the long service times are strain enough. 
 But one thing felt odd to me. I guess she had already ID'd her prime suspect, but the book title is the net user-name of the rapist. So, once I knew that, any suspense was gone. I suppose it then became more of a procedural thing - catching him and proving it - which is a Mars thing. The bad guy is often a known entity, but still...

"...reading The Perks of Being a Wallflower. It's a very peculiar-esque book, in a very Charlie-esque way." ~Me 
 The Perks of Being a Wallflower was such a quick read. Chbosky sucked me into this book and I'm not sure I expected it. I've been eyeballing the book since I was in high school. What finally made me pick it up? Probably the fact that it was being made into a movie coupled with the fact the book kept staring me down at work (yes, I work in a bookstore, and oh, what wonderful books I encounter there). So, I bought it. Like I said, I'd been eyeballing it an I figured, why not? 
 What made me unable to put it down? Good god, there are quite a few things, but they primarily fall into one category: the epistolary format of the book. Chbosky could have chosen to tell Charlie's story via first person narration or third. Frankly, it just wouldn't have produced the same results. There is such a brutal honesty that Charlie pours into his "friend" who "listens and understands and didn't try to sleep with that person at the party even though [s/he] could have." Through his letters, Charlie is able to freely let his thoughts flow. That is the whole advantage to writing to a "friend" he doesn't know--he can be as candid as he'd like to be, which seems essential to who Charlie is. Charlie, at his heart, is a good person; he tends to over-think things and put others needs and wants before his own. I am confident that Charlie has always been this way, and that these natural character traits have been dramatized by the events of his childhood: Essentially, the fact that Charlie was molested by his favorite aunt defined the way he reacted to certain events (ie. watching a girl being forced to have sex in his bedroom, his sister getting hit from her boyfriend and then witnessing them having sex only days after, etc).  In these scenarios, it is hard for Charlie to respond to any of these situations because he was unable to respond to them himself, and I get the impression that if he were able to respond, he wouldn't feel as if he knew how to do it. I think what his English teacher, Bill, had said struck a cord with Charlie, "We accept the love we think we deserve." Charlie never forced his way into any relationship, but received openly the love his family/friends gave him and he accepted--only occasionally over-thinking it. Charlie's character was very dynamic; his honesty and innocence sucked me into his life, and I always wanted to know more. 
 I realize that this book has become another piece of pop-culture with the production of the film, and I also realize that there were quite of few people who sort of bashed Charlie and the way he told his story of growing up. Charlie, like us, is different. Maybe he is a little bit more different than the rest of us, but I think that if you can see past his differences, you can pick out the similarities. There are probably more similarities between Charlie and ourselves than there are differences. My biggest similarity? I think it centers around one of Charlie's favorite sentiments: the concept of being "infinite". 
 "And in that moment, I swear we were infinite." 
 There is something philosophical to me about Charlie. He thinks about life, realizes things that I don't know [if] many of us realize. A prime example is when Charlie is looking at his parent's pictures. Charlie gets that not only were they happy in the picture, but in that moment they were happy beyond what the camera showed. He understood that by taking the photo, the happiness of the people in the photo would always be infinite because it was being remembered. I suppose I can identify with Charlie's thought process, so maybe he doesn't seem so hard for me to understand. Whatever the case maybe, it was a pleasure to read Charlie's letters. He told me his story, it was relevant, and I got it. Charlie's story is anything but typical, but then, if it were, it wouldn't cause such a stir. So, the only question that really matters is what will you make of Charlie? 
 (For anyone who has read it, there are questions at the back of the book. I don't think I am ready to be done with Charlie yet...Anyone else not ready to be done with Charlie?) 
 My rating: 4.5 stars out of 5. It may actually be a 5, but I'm not sure yet...I'm still mulling over Charlie and his letters.

It's been awhile since I read a book that made me feel this way. You know how some books just have interesting plot and twist, with character you fell head over heels with and wish they exist somewhere - yet you don't really seem to get any out it? Not really? Yeah. This is different because it's not just a normal fiction story. 
 I mean it's not anywhere close to normal because Before I Fall is about this girl Sam who keeps reliving the same day, again and again for 7 days. 
 When Sam relives her days, she started to see what she did, other than getting popular. Things she had been doing. 
 It was no big deal. 
 Until she had to relive it. 
 Until she started to see beyond 'the moment', more of the consequences. 
 Some she can't even place how they started, but they did, and she, classified as popular, had the 'duty' to continue those deeds. 
 She was a 'dork', she got laughed at, songs made for her, about her. She started to develop this "better you than me" behaviour. 
 (It didn't give her a free pass to be mean, bully even people. But it helps understanding a character knowing where they came from.) 
 Then, she gained popularity and put the being laughed days behind her and had this "you're a dork, you can try to make an effort not to be. But you're., so you deserve what you get. I'm popular. So I get privileges you don't" 
 In High School, or just anywhere there's people who concern with 'social groups', most people would wanna be with Lindsay, Elody, Ally and Sam. Just to fit in, just to be not on the getting shit for nothing side. 
 I think the thing that makes this book so hard to read is because it kinda shows how even when you get out of high school, the ugliness we're capable of, don't just end and for most of us, it just gets worse. 
 And Lauren Oliver don't hesitate to shove into your face. Whether you were or are Sam or on the receiving end of what people or groups Sam belonged to do. Both side can relate to it, and those (like me) who belong nowhere can relate to both side. 
 You know, over the course of the book, Sam did change for the better. I mean from denial, to impulse and recklessness, to finally accepting for what kind of human she is. On the very same day for seven days, and she knows more and changed to the better side. She defied those needed defying, concern herself with things that make her 'uncool', making up lost times or amends. 
 (From day to day, she did different things, some of them I just wish she would do it on another day, on the last day. But there's only so many hours a day. ) 
  
 But in the end she still dies. It broke my heart. I cried. I cried bullets of tears at Mcd earlier. 
 She knows there's no escaping it. It's too late for Kent and her. It's too late for a much better her. It's too late to make more good impact on people's life. 
 But she lived the last day, last of her lasts (knowing all the while she'll be only one dying in the accident), making most of it, breaking it off with that fucking jerk, showing Kent how they would be if she lived, realising all the things they won't never be able, realising all the things she won't see her sister doing. Best of all, the impacts that might just change a few people's life for better.  
 That's when I realised that certain moments go on forever. Even after they're over they still go on, even after you're dead and buried, those moments are lasting still, backward and forward, on into infinity. They are everything and everywhere at once. 
 (I also wanna say I understand sorry doesn't cut it for too many things in this world.)

MFA books tend to default to present tense for no good reason, and this one, like many others, runs into a couple awkward grammatical spots because of it. Also, a minor weak link in the plot:  We have to suspend a lot of disbelief when Nathan doesn't tell the police about Jack right away. The only reason he does this is to serve to draw out the plot further.

I enjoyed the "modern" feel of this novel, with a believable integration of such issues as drug abuse and feminist nationalism. The mystery does have real tension, which is a weakness of some of the other novels. A good mixture of clues given and information to be discovered. I like Dene a lot more than her future paramour. A star knocked off for the rather dramatic catching of the killer.

It's been years since I've read a book less than 250 pages, so I wasn't really expecting much. The synopsis promised so much, I didn't think it could all fit in such a little book. 
 Boy was I wrong. It took only two pages to get me hooked and two chapters to fall in love with Paige. The side characters were just as easy to like, even the unlikable ones. This story may have been shorter than 99% of the books I read, but it had more content than probably half of them. Even though I figured out what truly happened to Paige by page 44, I still loved reading this book.

I had a very hard time reading this book from the very beginning. Something about the writing kept pulling me out of the story. I couldn't connect with the main character at all, and I had a hard time liking most of the supporting characters, especially Mama. I've read books with overbearing mothers who only care about getting their daughters married to a rich man, but it was a little much in this book. There was absolutely nothing redeeming about that character and I wanted to punch her in every scene she was in. 
 I actually was going to put this down when I got to the 25% mark, but then I just happened to skip a large chunk and found myself interested in what I was reading. I caught on almost instantly and was able to keep reading from the point I'd skipped to without having to go back at all. Honestly, I don't see that as a good sign at all. I think part of that was due to the fact that I had predicted most of what was happening and why. 
 I skimmed the last few pages of the book. The only reason I finished it was because I like endings and I had read enough that I felt like I needed an ending. It was a good ending and I like the main character a lot more than I did when I first started reading, but I'm not going to continue the series. The story line is very interesting and I would like to read more, but I just couldn't get behind the writing style and I don't think I want to suffer through two more books of it. But if this is made into a movie, I'll gladly pay 10 dollars to watch it.

Dante, a Breed vampire warrior, is gravely injured one night after discovering a disturbing new addition to the war against the Rogues, vampires that have given over to bloodlust and kill without restraint. He finds his way to the office of veterinary doctor Tess Culver, where he thinks he's found the perfect solution to his blood loss in the beautiful woman. Intending to only take what he needs and see her mind wiped of the incident, Dante's plans go horribly wrong afterwards, when he learns a horrifying fact about the good doctor. He wishes after that he'd never taken her blood, but once he has, he can't wipe her sweet taste from his mind. Driven by more than just Tess, Dante's visions of the future soon lead him to believe she is part of his destiny, whether he wants her to be or not. In turn, Dante's embrace awakens in Tess desires she never knew she possessed and special, secret talents of her own begin to make sense after the strange warrior's appearance in her life. As she becomes further involved with the mysterious man, she soon find herself in the middle of a war, and a passion she cannot resist.

 Grandma Harken is old but she isn't stupid and she's pretty darn annoyed when something steals her tomatoes. Tomatoes are hard to grow in the desert; they need to be staked, watered and nursed to ripen. She guards hers jealously. 
 The same people in town who muttered about black magic swore that she was using unholy powers on her tomatoes. This was a little more plausible than general black magic, because obviously if you had unholy powers, you'd want to use them on your tomatoes. 
 Exactly... but she discovers it is a mockingbird shifter that is stealing them, and not for herself. It's a long time since Grandma has done much more than keep her own nose clean, but she wants to help this girl who is clearly bound in a magic way. She has a tongue bolt of silver and she can't say, or is literally unable to say, who sent her. All she can manage is that he likes tomatoes. He. 
 Grandma sets off to follow the flight of the girl home but reaches a point where the train tracks fold between worlds. 
 The trains run in three worlds. We will not speak of the fourth. 
 *** 
 This is a magic world where the power of trains, and the entrenched belief of the people who rely on them, has made them into gods. They are capricious gods who chose to deliver the mail because messages matter but can be erratic about when the trains run, where their tracks go and what they choose to go around. A grandson is the train god priest and she asks him if there is a place where the trains don't go. He tells her there is a bend in the track; trains don't like sharp bends. Theirs is a world of gentle curves and inclines. 
 I read a joke tweet recently that prophecies were wasted on the young, with their lack of knowledge of the world and their busy schedules. It suggested they'd be better off given to grandmas. And lo, then I read this story. *grins* 
 It make sense that the magic world attracts lost magic beings. The bad guy is a long way from home. The power of three, as always. And an enterprising coyote. 
 I had to look up what a cholla was; it's a kind of cactus with a woody latticed structure. Bones made of it would be super fragile. 
 That girl is going to need Grandma Harken but I reckon she'll be around for a while longer yet.

Oh My Liar is a complete mind bend, This book By K.L. Slater took me completely by surprise and what I thought I knew was turned topsy-turvy in this totally addictive tale. 
 From the moment I picked up Liar, I was sold, This story grips you from the start and I found it impossible to rest until I uncovered the mystery that was Amber. 
 Who is Amber? 
 What is her purpose? 
 What does she want? 
 And why the animosity towards Judy Bens Mother? 
 The plot thickens and I was rubbing my hands together in glee as this is totally my type of story. 
 And I can honestly say I so wasn't disappointed, Liar manages to layer the mystique superbly. 
 Bringing the story to a dramatic unexpected finale that I really didn't see coming at all. 
 No spoilers here Just the need to convey that this story is totally worth a read. 
 This is one of them books that you really can't say too much about the plot without giving away what in my opinion is a pure genius conclusion. 
 So my opinion on the main characters here, We have Ben widowed for two years and ripe for the picking. I found him a loveable mummy's boy and an easy target for Amber's schemes. 
 Amber herself is an enigma, it's clear she has her own agenda that we the reader are kept totally in the dark about. 
 Judy Bens mother, well she likes to be completely involved in her sons and grandsons lives she seems a strong determined lady. 
 Henry Bens dad and Judy's hubby, well he really got on my wick, he needs to get off his butt and help Judy more and as for the other things we discover about him well reading Liar, I'm just going to say it put me right off him. 
 The two little boys are cute Noah and Josh I would have liked a bit more interaction from these two. I felt we didn't quite get to determine their individual personalities. I think it would have been nice to sit down and get to know the boys properly. 
 So, in conclusion, this was a very delightful read, Liar was well written and brilliantly constructed. 
 It was easy to follow and kept my interest till the finish, and as an added bonus it even managed to shock and surprise me, so job well done K.L. Slater. 
 Thank you to NetGalley and the publisher for providing me with an advance reader copy Of Liar By K.L Slater.

There's something subversively satisfying about reading a take on history that brings it down a few pegs in our collective memory. The Good Lord Bird treats John Brown and other historical figures irreverently (Frederick Douglass is skewered especially well), but also expresses great respect and admiration for Brown's cause and efforts. I found the ending wonderfully moving, and got that same feeling I have whenever I watch The American Experience, a deep sense of the immense impact that these people had on our history and who we are today. 
 The book's dialect is done incredibly well and makes the tone lighter and more realistic than it would be if it had been written in the third person. James McBride's ability to stay in that dialect, and still make it readable, was impressive. This is well deserving of its National Book Award.

Not sure if it's relevant to you, but this is a review written by a Japanese person. So if you want my thoughts on the authenticity of it and such, read on! 
 I had high but nervous hopes for this book, based on its premise and GR reviews. As I said in the paragraph above, I am Japanese, so the idea of a YA fiction paranormal romance based on Japanese mythology and set in Japan instantly appealed to me. I was apprehensive because of the numerous negative reviews here on Goodreads. I was also very nervous because I knew that the lead girl was a white American girl, so I knew there would be potential for cultural ignorance or other offensive possibilities. 
 In the end, I felt this book was just okay. Nothing about it felt particularly special or stood out from everything else I've read, except the Japanese elements, which I rarely see in YA fiction. The romance was okay, there were some cute/romantic scenes but nothing that made me absolutely die or anything. I'm not sure if it's because I'm Japanese, but I had a hard time sympathizing with the MC, a Wai Ren (gaijin, or foreigner) who whined non-stop about being forced to live in Japan with her aunt. I didn't get why the lead guy, Yuu Tomohiro, was so attracted to her, aside from the fact that she was American or whatever. The insta-love was rampant! And though they made it out to be a joke, Katie really did straight up stalk him. 
 Now for authenticity, a major concern of mine starting this book. I was so scared this was going to be some totally inaccurate, "weaboo" piece. It was authentic enough, I suppose. The author spent so. much. time. explaining everything my eyes started to glaze over every time (though I guess you could blame that on the fact that the explanations were, for me, very unnecessary). I wasn't really crazy about the way she interspersed Japanese into the English, making characters say a whole sentence in English then add "ne" at the end. Very awkward, even though Japanese people do say that. It was definitely weird reading everyone speaking English when technically they would be speaking Japanese. Spent a good amount of time trying to picture everything they said in Japanese instead. I did find it rather unbelievable that the MC, Katie, would have such a high level, slang-filled understanding of the language after just a few months. Honestly, the language barrier was barely included. 
 I will admit, the way the author portrayed modern Japanese culture was pretty accurate. From taking off shoes at the genkan (genkan, or front entry area), to wearing slippers, to having students clean the school. I could tell these things had been thoroughly researched. In fact, it all made me a bit Japan-sick (as in wanting to return to Japan) and rather hungry (the author kept bringing up curry, my favorite dish, as well as other Japanese dishes I know and love). I liked how the author included things like Qi Xi Ji ri (Tanabata/Star Festival), which I excitedly recognized. So I'm glad at least I got to enjoy those elements. Thanks to my extensive time spent in Japan, I was easily able to envision the scenes in the book, from the train station to the high school, but I'm not sure how this would go for a non-Japanese person. As for the translations, it was all pretty much fine except for one part where Tomohiro was confessing that he liked Katie, where he said [An haJun noShi gaHao ki] (ore wa kimi no koto ga suki) which the author said meant "I love you" when it actually means "I like you".  Pretty big difference there, in my opinion. 
 The mythology was okay. I felt the book left it a bit unexplored, though this will probably be resolved in future books. It wasn't as captivating or intriguing as I expected based upon other supernatural YA I've read. I liked Tomohiro well enough. He was your classic YA fiction romantic male lead and was attractive, if a bit angsty. The love triangle between him, Katie, and Jun was, like everything else, okay. I liked Jun decently enough but I saw his plot twist coming a mile away. It wasn't even remotely mysterious. And the whole, "wow so beautiful" while supposedly talking about something else but really staring at the girl cliche thing was so cheesy I think I could use it to make nachos.  
 I guess I will read the next book in the series if I have time. To be honest though, if this book wasn't about Japan I would be less inclined to do so.

** spoiler alert ** 
 So I've been reading this book steadily the last few weeks during my breaks at work. It's left an impression on me, one that is mostly positive. While I do have my gripes about it, they are few. 
 However, the largest issue with this book is its organization. I understand what the author was trying to do. Each chapter jumps to a different character, a different set of events. They don't seem to connect to each other at all. Of course, in the end, they all blend quite nicely and suddenly the random assortment makes sense. The thing is, it wasn't quite so effective in this case. I found myself distracted by the editing and therefore not as invested in the novel as I would have been otherwise. I think maybe on a second reading, I would be able to disregard the jumps since I know the storyline. But as a first-time reader of this book, I was hopelessly confused as to how these random characters fit together. 
 The book starts with the sudden appearance of an entirely black and white circus appearing on the outskirts of town, seemingly out of nowhere. It then jumps to a small girl named Celia being dropped off with a man named Hector, who turns out to be her estranged father who wasn't even aware she was born. It turns out little Celia is very gifted with producing magic--in the literal sense. Others see only illusions, but what she does is real and true alterations of her surroundings. It jumps to Hector meeting a man always dressed in gray, and they make a deal about some kind of game. Miss Celia and a young orphaned boy seem to be the centerpieces of this game. 
 To do a real play-by-play of this novel it would take quite a bit of explaining, considering there are so many important characters that have some kind of involvement in the storyline. To be honest it is a bit convoluted, but the real draw for this book isn't the plot or the main characters falling in love with each other. 
 Instead, the thing that truly grabs the attention is the game between Celia and her opponent, Marco. Without directly competing, they use the Night Circus as an arena to show off their magical skills. It's like walking into a dream every time the tents are described. Each one depicts something different: some kind of theme or activity that is only in that one tent. With such a variety of tents (all black and white) and only small signs to indicate what's inside each one, it's near impossible to know what's in all of them. And with two very real magicians behind the scenes always adding more, it quite literally IS impossible. 
 The imagination behind the different tents is incredible. To be able to enter a tent and see an entire living, breathing nature scene made of ice is whimsical. To find a small tent that is filled with tiny bottles filled with scents that can tell a story of lost times is nostalgic. I'm impressed that the author managed to make me nostalgic for something I've never known. And frankly, I don't think there are many people who would turn down an opportunity to go into a room completely filled with climb-able clouds. 
 I felt a longing to go somewhere that isn't real. For those of us who get deeply immersed in a book, this isn't unusual. But I can't describe the ache it creates when you know it can't be. And you move on to another book that may or may not have the same effect. 
 Overall, this book is a step into a more magical realm of our own world. While the characters and the plot get convoluted at times, the descriptions of the circus alone are enough to make this a worthwhile read. I find myself wishing I could visit the Candle Tree.

3.5 stars. Two things made me not give this book a higher rating: 
 1. Language. There wasn't a ton of swearing, but I cannot stand seeing profanity in books, and especially the certain words that were used. 
 2. The ending. UGH, the ending!!! WHY????? I feel like this whole book was leading up to something, and then just copped out in the end for an ambiguous ending where we're left totally wondering, "what the heck just happened here?!"  Spoiler: I breathlessly read the last 200 pages of this book, feeling like things were heading to a disastrous end, and hoping the author would pull some amazing ending that would leave the characters at least SOMEWHAT happy, and miraculously end it in a somewhat decent way. But no...it seems to me that the main character completely betrayed her changing-for-the-better life and just ran off and took the easy way out, joining the mermaids. And, FOR WHAT?! To be unceremoniously dumped on a beach a month later, consigned to a torturous slow death in a mental institution?! Wow, way to wreck what was, until the last ten pages, an awesome book! I could not stand the ending to this book! Also, why were we left with so many completely unanswered questions?! What happened to Nessa? Did Calie see her in the mermaid world? Whose is that voice in the ocean, calling to all these women? What's the mystery with the Morgan family, and is there a way to break this "curse"? I totally thought that all the talk about choosing your own destiny and all of that was going to lead up to Callie making some amazing choice, breaking this spell or curse or whatever it was, and freeing the rest of the descendants from this awful fate.  
 This author has some really beautiful, lyrical writing that really made me feel like I was there, taking torturous breaths with Callie, feeling what she felt and seeing what she saw. But oh that ending...just ruined it for me. PLEASE let there be a sequel, so I don't have to imagine the characters ending like that!

My first experience of Neil Gaiman was Neverwhere, a bizarre, spiralling urban fantasy that left me swinging between whether he was a genius or a madman. Either way, several months on it is still on my mind so he must be doing something right! I decided to try something else. 
 While I knew this book was aimed at a YA audience it was aimed a little younger than I expected, so I have taken that into account. However, I was impressed that even when discussing complex topics it never seems to talk down to the reader. 
 The idea of the living growing up in a graveyard, given access to its inhabitants, and an access that is almost like supernatural powers of their own, is fascinating. Especially when the "youngest" of these inhabitants died 200 years before and they are your only source of knowledge. This certainly was fed into the protagonist's attitude and speech at times, but I would have liked to see it get him into trouble and confusion a bit when meeting the current living world. 
 The hinting at various supernatural creatures, who are different from both the classical interpretation, and the current YA romance one was refreshing and an interesting source of thought. 
 Overall a very good fantasy, I would have liked more from some storylines which felt they concluded too early or suddenly though. 
 My verdict on Gaiman: a genius with just the right level of crazy
