"My Unexpected Forever" - Heidi McLaughlin 
 RECOMMENDED! This rockstar book rocked my world. I got to see the wild side, as well as the sweet side of the rock band's drummer, and I loved it. "My Unexpected Forever" is about learning to find the balance between following your heart and your mind, even when they don't always agree. Heidi McLaughlin tells a tale about two people's second chance in life and love. 
 I don't think Heidi McLaughlin could ever write a bad book. She rocks! I seriously love The Beaumont series. Book one and the novella prior to this book, just plain rocked. I've been anxiously awaiting the arrival of book two, and I'm so excited I finally have it. I knew right away I was going to love it, because I was already interested in Harrison at the end of book one. I wasn't disappointed at all, and tried to read in every spare second I could find. This was one of those 'just one more chapter' kind of reads. I never wanted to put it down, but life's responsibilities kept getting in the way ;) - I finished it within one and a half days...but if you counted the actual time spent reading this book, it'd be just a matter of hours. 
 Harrison is such a sweetheart and a bada$s rockstar at the same time. He is a dream come true for many women...including me. I would love to have Harrison on my arm. The idea of a great guy like that existing, who's a great father and single? Yes, please. I'm a single mother so that sounds great to me! 
 I love the way that Heidi McLaughlin writes. She is a great storyteller and her characters have so much emotion. They're like real people. "My Unexpected Forever" had some heavy topics, such as moving on after your spouse's death. There really is no right and wrong way to move on (or not) after someone you love dies. I like how the author handled this topic though. She showed that is was tough for Katelyn to move on, and she was afraid to do so. But, she also showed that Katelyn is human and her feelings towards Harrison were real, even if she fought them as hard as she could. 
 I loved that Josie and Liam were a big part of "My Unexpected Forever." They were the main characters of book one, and I was happy to see them again. I liked that the kids all had a large role in this story, too. It's not often that you read a romance novel where kids are already a part of their lives. Usually you find kids coming into the picture in a '5 years later' epilogue. As a young, single mom...I liked how Heidi McLaughlin added the kids. It made you feel like you could still have this great romance even if you had kids. 
 Again, I would absolutely recommend this book. "My Unexpected Forever" by Heidi McLaughlin is a 5 STAR read, that fans of the Contemporary Romance New Adult genre would like. And, if you like hot, tattooed, rockstars? Then yes, you will love this book. 
 RECOMMENDED! 
 Reading Order: "My Forever Girl" - "My Everything" - "My Unexpected Forever" (all 5 stars!) 
 Pre-order "My Unexpected Forever" on Amazon: http://www.amazon.com/dp/B00EOVJWR8 
 Happy Reading! 
 Brianna Lee Book Reviews

The Kill Order: Loads of Lunatics 
 So I liked the idea of The Kill Order. I feel like the Maze Runner series overall lacked some clarity in certain aspects. Thus, I wholeheartedly welcomed an entire prequel devoted to explaining the Flare and its origins. 
 But. 
 I was severely let down. 
 Never have I ever so vehemently disliked an installment from a series that I, on a whole, quite liked. I cared about the Gladers. I loathed WICKED. I invested time and effort and love into the Maze Runner series, and you may disagree, but it was well worth it in my opinion. 
 Likewise, I invested time and effort into The Kill Order, and I came up with...nothing. Nada. Zilch. 
 The characters felt flat, the action sequences far too long, and the whole plot seemed to revolve around evading hordes of savages, driven to barbarism and insanity by the Flare. I have nothing against crazy people. But when you have too many crazy people doing too many crazy stunts, well, that makes me a little crazy. 
 There was plenty of punching and kicking, but not much else. 
 Furthermore, the whole "justification" and "reasoning" behind the release of the Flare really irritated me. I didn't buy it. Not one bit. And one could argue that it shouldn't bother me the PFC's motives don't really matter when what's done is done and that those of us who have read the rest of the series already know the outcome of that incredibly poor decision, which is a valid argument. But still. Really?  They decided to mess around with biological weapons and wipe out a good portion of the population with a highly contagious virus all in the name of preventing human extinction? And they thought that they could control the epidemic?  I mean, really? The rationale behind that decision was dubious at best. 
 I never did truly latch onto the story and begin to care. My interest and attention kept rolling off the pages, like water droplets on wax paper. 
 But there were a few redeemable qualities in The Kill Order, the first being the technology in the story. Hijacking the Berg was the best decision the characters made in this book, and Transvices are things of nightmares. Then there was the epilogue.  THOMAS.  It was like getting a little wave from an old friend. And finally, Alec. "The bear." He saved Mark's hide countless time and each time he, my fondness for that soldier grew. He may be old, but he was leagues better than any of the other characters.  And thus, his ending (it's implied at least) made me very very disappointed.  
 I tried, guys. I truly did try. I tried to love this book, but I just couldn't. I don't despise it, but I don't necessarily like it either. 
 The Kill Order, loaded with lunatics, lacking in everything else.

Quite The Novel Idea ~ Words from the Clouds 
 In 2015 I read a very special book. A book told through letters between two boys that would probably never be able to meet. A book that some of my friends did not enjoy that much because it was marketed as Contemporary while it's actually closer to Speculative Fiction or very very soft Sci-Fi. I went into it expecting Contemporary. However, what I got was so much more. And I just went with it. I suspended my disbelief and all that jazz. Because the story just had me hooked. The characters were in my heart. And they have been since I finished that book in May 2015. I've been waiting for its follow-up, Nowhere Near You, ever since. Safe to say I had a lot of expectations, which can be dangerous, but in this case... it wasn't. Because Nowhere Near You met every single one of my expectations and went far past them. Safe to say I loved this book just as much as that first one. 
 Nowhere Near You continues the story of Ollie and Moritz through their letters to each other. And while the letter format doesn't always work for me, it somehow works perfectly with this book and its predecessor. While other books don't give enough developement to their characters and the story because of the format, this book actually succeeds big time on both parts. The writing is so gripping and it just hooks me instantly from the first page. Ollie's and Moritz's voice are so unique and distinct, which is SUCH a hard thing to accomplish even without the format this is written in. So major props to Leah Thomas for this. I worship at your feet. And I will beg you for another book with these characters until I have one. Who needs knees anyway? 
 As for the actual story... Well, what do you want me to say? I love it. I went through all the feels about a hundred times and it was flinging me back and forth and I loved every second of it. It could've have easily been boring given how long it is, but it never was to me. If anything, I craved more at the end of it. So much more. Nowhere Near You continued Ollie & Moritz's story perfectly and introduced new characters for me to love and ended so amazingly that I just... I want more. I will always want more. My heart is so full right now and I can barely contain all the feelings I'm having right now. Can you tell? 
 Now what can I say about the characters that I haven't said in my review of the first book? I still love them just as much. No, more actually. Ollie and Moritz keep going and being brave and strong and they lean on each other even when they're nowhere near each other. Their friendship is beautiful and it's everything. I cannot possibly describe how much I love these two. It's impossible really. They have my heart, these two. Speaking of hearts... There are a few new characters introduced in this book and I don't want to spoil anything but I do want to mention that I loved them. Arthur, Bridget and Brian in particular. So much love for you three. But also Molly and Klaus and the returning characters from the first book. I love you all and I want more time with all of you. 
 Honestly, I could talk about this book for ages but that would just be boring to you after a while so instead you should go read this book instead. If you haven't read the other one, Because You'll Never Meet Me, then please start with that one. And then get your hands on Nowhere Near You. Pretty please?

Cather and Wren (Catherine), twins, started college together. Cath decided on an English Major, while Wren wanted to be a Marketing major, and work in advertising like their father. In High School the two sisters did everything together, even write fan fiction about the uber popular Simon Snow Book Series. Fanfixx was their domain; Magicath and Wrenegade were their aliases for writing fan fiction, Simon and Baz love stories. Magicath has 20,000+ fans! Cath went on alone to write her story "Carry On Simon" It's to be her version of the 8th and last novel of the series. She wants it done before the famous Gemma T Leslie (GTL), releases her last novel of Simon. Cath's version is basically a love story between Simon and Baz. 
 Cath and Wren's mother left when they were little and never came back. Their father, who is technically a "Mad Man" in more than one way. He has bi-polar and is very manic at times. He raised the twins on his own in Omaha, Nebraska. 
 Cath was dating Abel for 3 years in high school, but he went to college at MoTech. Wren always said "He's an end table", someone to dump on and be comfortable with. It wasn't really a relationship, so when he called to break up because he found Katie.. well it wasn't a real big deal and now Cath could celebrate being truly single! 
 It just so happens that Cath's roommate is Reagan, who has a tag-along ex (Levi) that always hangs out in their dorm (Pound Hall 913). Reagan and Levi (both from Arnold), try to get Cath out of the dorm and experience life. Cath was too afraid to ask anyone where the dining area was, she lived on protein bars for two weeks before Reagan asked if she had an eating disorder. Levi even stole some Blueberry Bliss to help out. This is when Cath became her special pity project. 
 Cath also liked to stay in the dorm because she was trying to finish 'Carry On Simon', but in class with Professor Piper she thinks to herself... 
 Why do I write? 
 "To be somewhere else" 
 "To get free of ourselves" 
 "To stop being anything or anywhere at all" 
 and "To disappear". Now we can see Cath really has some anxiety issues, and is troubled inside. She believes her twin has abandoned her on her quest to be independent and experiment with the drinking/party life with her roommate Courtney. 
 Cath slowly comes out of her shell and has adventures of her own, especially in the boy department. She met Levi in her dorm, an Agriculture Major, and she meets Nick in her Intro to Writing 3rd level course with Professor Piper. Professor Piper doesn't believe in Fan Fiction, she thinks it plagerism. She tells Cath to write her own story after Cath turned in a story about Simon and Baz. 
 Will Cath forever be in love with Simon and Baz? Or will she fall for Nick or Levi? Will she be able to write a story that is not Fan Fiction?? Will Cath and Wren start talking again? 
 I think that Simon Snow is a parallel of Harry Potter, and also the quotes interspersed throughout the book tie in to what Cath is going through emotionally and physically. 
 "Simon Snow is an 11 yr old orphan from Lancashire recruited to attend Watsford School of Magicks, to become a Magician. As he grows he joins the Mages fighting against the Insidious Humdrum, an evil being trying to rid the world of magic" Characters Include: 
 Penelope~red hair in pony tails with old fashioned glasses (the smart friend like Hermione) 
 Simon Snow~ Main Character Caramel Brown hair, roommates with Baz (Harry Potter) 
 Tyrannus Basilton Pitch aka Baz~ Slicked back Black hair, cool grey eyes 
 Apparently the Crucible cast Baz and Simon to be roommates and they are to watch out for each other like brothers. 
 Baz seems like a cross between Draco and Ron. 
 Agatha is the pretty girl so she must be Ginny who gets married to Harry. 
 The Insiduous Humdrum is Simon, so it is Harry and Voldemort tied together. 
 Quote from Chapter 23 Book 7 of the Simon Snow Series 
 "You're the most powerful magician in a 100 ages. The Humdrums face is Simons own boyhood face, looking dull and tired. Nothing glinted in his blue eyes... Do you think that much power comes without sacrifice? Did you think you could become you without leaving me behind? 
 This quote sounds like a girl version of Levi to Cath 
 "Every smile from Agatha was like waking up to a perfect sunny day. Agatha knew it and she smiled at everyone who crossed her path." 
 Another Quote on page 275, Chapter 34 about Agatha not being able to choose between Simon or Baz, is like when Cath doesn't know to choose Nick or Levi as they both make mistakes and both have good qualities... but I won't tell you which one wins...:) 
 I enjoyed this book, it was a fun read. It was just hard for me to put together all four of the stories going on in the book. I had to read just the Simon Snow book quotes from GTL and then just Carry On quotes, and other fan fics by Cath to really understand how it all folds into one another. The four stories are Simon Snow Series by GTL, Fan Fic by MagiCath, Cath's real story and the story by Rainbow Rowell.
It broken my heart. A little. And it put it back together (even if the end was a bit abrupt, READ IT.).

Entertaining. But in this format, without Rowlings writing style, it's basically fan fiction, and it reads like fan fiction. The characters were 1dimensional but the overall plot was intriguing. A good play, a pathetic book.

 But this is also the second book in the Howl's Moving Castle series. Let's just say if you're expecting to see a lot of the characters from the first Howl book, you'll be disappointed. I know, I know, Calicifer and Howl are *with* Abdullah for a good portion of the book as carpet and genie, and of course Sophie as Midnight, but none of them really displayed their known personalites in full in their transformed-enchanted states, so I don't think that really counts.  Now if the gradual inclusion of the Howl characters had been done in an organic way or with the "ah-ha!" satisfaction of a puzzle clicking together, I think it could have worked, but it feels abrupt and kind of grafted on. Abdullah's amusing quest would have worked on its own, Howl-less ie, you could make Howl and friends be just another wizard of the kingdom and that wizard's friends, and the castle could just be a creation of the djinns and it would not change the plot substantially at ALL . 
 If you like Jones, it's still very charming and worth reading, but with the above caveats (I was warned by friends of this, which helped a lot). I've heard the third book does not have this issue, so I'm looking forward to it.

3.5 stars for story bumped down to 2.5 stars for "bad" writing/editing 
 I was conflicted about how to rate this book. 
 After the first hundred pages I was ready to give up. All the smiling was starting to make me frown. Seriously. Characters smile when they're happy, when they're sad, when they're angry, and even when they're tired. And sometimes...they smile twice in the same passage. See spoiler for examples  
 'I'm not sure I did tell you,' she said, smiling at the memory. 'We met in the park - I was out walking, and there was a sudden downpour.' She smiled. 
 I gathered up the next batch of completed letters and smiled as I pulled on my coat to go and post them. I would hunt again tomorrow, and the very thought lifted my spirits. I smiled. I couldn't help myself. 
  
 I'm sorry, but that's way too much smiling for me. Still, it wasn't just the out-of-control smiling that turned me off. The smiling might not have bothered me so much if not for all the pale faces and gloomy, foggy days (yeah, I know it's 19th London and two serial killers are on the loose and all, but still). 
 Add to that a plethora of typos (way too many for a professional publication) and the author's repeated and somewhat awkward use of the phrase "here and there*" and I thought I'd reached my breaking point, the point where I admit I've wasted my money and my time then lick my literary wounds and move on to something more readable. 
 *In the author's defense, maybe the phrase "here and there" was a commonly used phrase during the late 1800's. If so, I've never come across it. But every time I encountered it in this manuscript I immediately formed an image of Dr. Seuss' 'Sam I am' from Green Eggs and Ham. 
 Then right when I was about to give up, I got sucked into the story. After all, it's a paranormal take on the Thames Torso murders which overlapped the famous Jack-the-Ripper murders. This is the kind of book that seems written just for me. Plus the cover art is quite intriguing and the quality of the book and pages...all top rate. (I'm someone who still enjoys holding a book and this met all my tactile expectations.) 
 In the end, I'm not sure whether the writing improved or I was just more invested in the story, but I no longer found myself repeatedly stopping to brood over the "bad writing". With the exception of a few typos, I was enjoying myself. 
 Amid all the smiling, pale faces, and gloomy, foggy days/nights there's some good stuff here. For example, though it took a while, I eventually felt invested in the protagonist Dr. Bond and read the last 100 pages in two extended sessions. There was even a handful of Sherlock Holmes-esque moments and a satisfying ending. Still, when I read a book, I expect a minimal level of professional editing that seemed absent here. 
 Will I read another book by this author? Well, seeing as when I ordered this book, I also ordered another based on the description, yes, I will. 
 Bottom line - I didn't hate this book, but feel strongly that it could have been so much better. I liked the premise and some of the writing was quite good, still some of it wasn't, and why my rating dropped from 3.5 stars down to 2.5.

I remember hearing about this book when I was a child after my mother read it and brought up the concept of multiple personalities. As an adult, I got it in a box of books but never got around to reading it until it was requested by someone through my paperbackswap.com account. Needless to say, this book has been on my shelf for a long time. I read this book concurrently with another one (review also posted by me on Goodreads) written to disprove it. Knowing that there are so many arguments against this being a true story, I looked at it as a novel and a testament to the many facets that the modern woman has to maintain. As such, there were some gripping moments but one of the major weaknesses of the novel was its pace. 
 The beginning of the novel throws the reader right into the action and confusion as Sybil wakes up from one of her "blackouts" in the middle of a strange street during a snowstorm. The novel keeps this steady pace for the first part, but then, after the author introduces us to many of Sybil's child-like multiple personalities and describes Sybil's childhood, the pace slows to a crawl. During Sybil's formative years she was subjected to mental traumas and physical tortures that most people don't even want to imagine. It is explained that Sybil's psyche dealt with these traumas by creating walled off personalities who were forced to face them. The abuse is so malicious and despicable it is hard to even read about it. It makes us wonder what the hell was up with her parents. During the middle of the book, Schreiber describes Sybil's parents' backgrounds and religious beliefs. While this is necessary for the total picture, it is still very tedious and could cause the reader to become uninterested and stop reading the book. The pace accelerates once again during the third part of the book, but towards the end in the final chapters of the book the plot goes by faster and faster. Not as a page turner but more like a skeleton described in very clinical term which will never be fleshed out. On some occasions years will go by on a single page. It seems as though the author wants to end the book as quickly as possible so she stops explaining how Sybil's treatment is working and just tells the reader that it is working. 
 I followed up my reading of the two books by borrowing the four hour made-for-tv-movie starring Sally Field from the library. The biggest difference between the book and the movie was that a neighbor/love interest was created for Sybil.

 Reading The 5th Wave by Rick Yancey is like watching an action movie crossed with one of those sci-fi movies that follows the lives of several Americans meant to be absolutely typical and relatable, like the football jock and the teen girl with a crush on the most popular guy at her high school. 
 Once The 5th Wave really gets going, it's un-put-downable, but it doesn't have the quality of character development I look for in a favorite book. I had trouble relating to most of its characters, particularly Cassie (the typical blonde teen girl with the crush) and Zombie (the jock whose interests are "cars, football, and girls"). These characters have big, bold personalities it's easy to like; I just felt like I already knew most of them from other books and movies. That said, I did really enjoy reading the sections told from Sammy's perspective, as that felt the most authentic and relatable, and Evan's short section near the beginning was fairly good, too. Unfortunately, the reader sees through Cassie and Zombie's eyes for most of the book. 
 The so-so characterization is okay for this kind of book because it's mainly driven by plot and the post-apocalyptic situation, not by character development. Nevertheless, there were some scenes focusing purely on character that made me roll my eyes because the dialogue was cheesy or else zone out a bit because I just didn't care. As an example, here is a mild spoiler (that you should see coming a mile away) about a romantic moment in the book: When Cassie and Evan kiss for the first time, it's set off in its own paragraph, like it's some big surprise, but the lead-up to it is quite obvious. Then they continue to grow closer, yet almost all I know about Evan as Cassie falls head over heels for him is that (1) he looks like a "teenage version of the Brawny paper towel guy" (p. 159) and (2) he's weirdly obsessed with Cassie--lurking outside her door all the time and sneakily reading her diary--and tells her repeatedly that she's his only reason for living now. (It's like a more wholesome version of Edward Cullen.) I don't see what sets her apart in his eyes. She can be funny and spunky, and Evan says she's pretty, with blonde ringlets and a young-looking face, but my impression of her was still fairly ordinary. Their relationship felt mostly physical to me. Not a compelling reason to betray one's own species  and risk one's life. 
 The first hundred pages or so were a bit slow, despite some gun battles and explosions, because it took me so long to warm to the characters and because, I admit, I was nitpicking the writing a bit, like Cassie's statement on page 9, "If you can't trust anyone, then you can trust no one." Duh? 
 But once I started to care about them (which was around the time Yancey writes from Sammy's perspective for the first time, on the school bus), I grew more and more engrossed in the book, and I ended up staying awake until way past when I'd meant to go to bed, just to read to the end. I found myself feeling some affection for the characters for their appealing tenacity, ingenuity, and humor. I was left with a few questions, some of which will probably be answered in Book 2, but I don't think Yancey ever plans to address why Evan lived his life as a human farmboy yet has soft hands . Despite a few unanswered questions, I closed the book feeling fairly happy with the ending (with one glaring exception:  did Evan really die? really? He can't be dead. I won't believe it unless I see a body. ). 
 The 5th Wave might not be one of my favorite books, but it is entertaining, fast-paced, and touched by tender and thought-provoking moments. I also enjoyed its frequent, unexpected little jolts of humor. 
 I'll end as usual with a few favorite quotes to give you a feel for the writing style and humor.*

 'You need to get out,' she said. 'They'll hit the cities first.' 
 'You're probably right,' I said. 'They'd never dream of taking out the Magic Kingdom.'

 But. The ending justified it, at least enough that I added one more star to the review. I liked that it actually had a reason for everything, instead of just being a bad plot.  Rachel being in a coma and dreaming all of it isn't necessarily the most original idea, but it's the first time I have seen it in a YA novel. It was clever, and justified all the sappy moments and the seemingly perfect environment. And I liked that the final scene was her plugs being pulled in the hospital room while she's riding off into the sunset with Jimmy. Her dying and joining Jimmy in the afterlife was well demonstrated in the writing.  
 Kudos.

Oh dear, dear J. K. Rowling, 
 Even though I was disappointed by your last attempt at prose, I must say that your second attempt is better. Not by much, mind you, but better nonetheless. You are much more practiced in the way of the mystery, considering that most of the Harry Potter Series was exactly that. Your strong suit in writing is your ability to foreshadow events, provide us with clues so we as the reader cannot let go of your book; we clutch it till our hands bleed and our eyes blur. So thank you for an enjoyable story overall. 
 However, I do have some problems with your writing style. You tend to over describe the scene in which your characters inhabit, so much so that I find myself wondering why you tell us these things in the first place. I think you would really benefit from limiting the amount of pages, let us say no more than 350. This would cut down on the amount of pointless clutter that seems to fill most of the novel. Harry Potter also suffered from this problem but we didn't care; we wanted you to keep writing and we feared the end. But for mysteries such as this one, it becomes an exhausting marathon that we did not choose to run. 
 All in all I must say that I will not read your next attempt at adult literature. I suppose it is of little consequence to you, because millions will still read whatever you write anyway. If you do decide to return to children's lit I may join your fans again, because I do love your imaginative storytelling. 
 Sincerely, 
 Barbara

Months after the first murder, in the small town of Lake Eden, Minnesota, a bake off happens in town and everyone is getting ready for it. When a judge has to call in sick, they have a substitute who is none other than Coach Boyd Watson. After the first night of the bake off, Boyd is found in his garage dead. Hannah Swenson, the Cookie Lady, who owns her own bakery, knows something isn't right, especially with town reporter Lucy, is having new car and clothes even though she doesn't make much from her job. Hannah knows Lucy is getting money from somewhere and its not exactly the legal way. With the Dessert Bake-Off in full swing, and list of suspects, its going to take some time for Hannah to figure out who the killer is.  I didn't really like the motive for this. Mason killed Boyd because he was going to suspend his son off the team for using steroids which was given to him by his father. And he killed Lucy because she had a picture of him and was going to show it to people.  
 I had initially thought it was Danielle, Boyd's wife, for obvious reasons if you have read the first book. I am still interested to see how she is taking this and what she is going to be doing in the third book. I didn't feel she had much closure and how she felt about the death of her husband.

This was what made the book worthwhile reading for me, and kept me interested to keep reading to the end. There is not a lot of action in the book, nor mystery or intrigue, but it offers an emotional journey into delayed grief, family dynamics, relationships and personal growth. Unfortunately the character of Melanie, who featured strongly in the beginning of the book, nearly dropped off the scene towards the end, though in my opinion she had a lot more to offer and would have given another perspective to the emotional load involved in her mother's death and the hidden family secret. All in all a fairly enjoyable read if you don't expect too much in terms of mystery or action.

4 Stars & lots of Feelz

It is full of heartfelt emotion, lots of feelz, eye opening situations, some hot as hell moments, and great support characters who you fall in love with as well. Caleb and Josh are two MC who you just want to get their happily ever afters and as a reader become emotionally involved in their plight to freedom, love, and happiness. 
 So, why is this rated 4 stars instead of 5? Well, I had a bit of trouble grasping how a commune such as Paradise Ranch could exist without someone knowing what was going on there, one of the castoffs, or a nosey neighbor, or a freaking forest ranger. Someone would have wondered about this self-sustaining commune that basically allowed women to be treated as birthing/sex machines, isolated and kicked out the smart ones, and forced their rhetoric and divine beliefs on each member, as law. I just couldn't fully buy into that aspect. In Posey Roberts Naked Organics series that was also about a commune at least they had a "cover" of being an organic farm and interacted with the community by selling their products at a farmer's market. So, there was that aspect of the story that bugged me. Then, I hated that NONE of these people stood up for themselves and pressed charges, especially Miriam, and all the others before her who ran away or were kicked out, like Josh. They just left. They allowed the situation to continue and left others to the fate they escaped. So, yeah...those were my main issues with the plot that caused this to be a 4 star story versus a 5 star story, for me. 
 On the other hand, this is a beautiful bestfriend to lovers romance. Josh and Caleb will grab your attention and never let go. Watching them figure out it was okay to love one another was pretty emotional. Then as they worked to overcome fear of rejection and possible hate from others, those fears and feelings were well portrayed. 
 The audio book was well done and brought life to the story. I enjoyed it on my way back and forth to work, finding myself captivated by Caleb & Joshes story. 
 I would recommend this story to anyone who loves a friend's to lovers romance, with a side of forbidden, and a strong HFN ending.. 4 Goodbye Paradise Stars!!

I'm going to do a review of the full series in general on the first book in the series, its just easier that way because it didn't take me all that long to finish the series, about a week (-+) I think. 
 I love a fairy tale re-telling, the problem is there aren't that many good re-tellings out there, I've been disappointed time and again. Show White and Cinderella redo's are very popular and either there is to much sap or so much action it just isn't appealing to me. 
 Picking up this series I didn't have all that high hopes for anything really remarkable, I cringed thinking it was going to just okay since it was based in the real world happening in everyday life... 
 After the first chapter, though it was worse than what I initially thought: bleh kill me NOW, stab my eyes out with a red pen. 
 Why?! 
 The grammatical and language errors made my eyes burn, not to mention the words that just didn't fit with what she wanted to say or the idea that was trying to be conveyed, things just didn't...."gel". 
 And right through to the second book she seemed to forget key things that she's mentioned earlier and the way Mina, our clumsy, unsure annoying protagonist reached her conclusions just didn't make sense. There was nothing that lead up to how she managed to figure things out. For example : when she figures out Jared is Fae...how she reached that conclusion before he stated doing magic I have no idea. Because the words used clearly indicates that she had already reached that conclusion. 
 There is a great lack of world building, if that had been stronger toward the middle of the first book the novel would have been a lot stronger. And Mina was just completely annoying throughout both books, there isn't a single page where is isn't complaining about her lot in life, she was a total whiner baby! 
 Here's this girl who literally has all this power at her finger tips and she's in constant tears because the boy she likes doesn't really know what he wants... Blah blah blah. Started wondering if maybe Mina was suffering from depression and becoming a little crazy. 
 But the twist at the end of the second book was definitely a turning point for the series. 
 After that the last three books became really good, and the language problems weren't as bad. The concept was something very different, and each time Mina had to overcome something it wasn't a re-telling, it just had elements from the original tales. For me who always wondered if there had been some grain of truth to the Grimm stories; like a serial killer who ate children, it was just enjoyable. 
 Also the good guy wasn't always annoyingly good and the love triangle you initially think it's about is definitively not the triangle you should be looking at. My initial problems with the crazy Brody and Mina episodes of crazy possessive/infatuation started to make sense later in the series. The author actually cleared up a lot of things that didn't make sense at all by book four and five. The loss Mina experiences during the course of the other books is something you do feel with her and for her because time has been taken to build the relationships between the characters, which is one of the things that has been done quite well. 
 In the end I was glad that I'd pressed through with this series because by the end it really wasn't all the bad. So although the first two books only got about and iffy two stars the rest of the series I'd give a 3 1/2 stars, for surprising me. This is a fun series that just takes some getting into.

The Plot Thickens in Torch 
 Torch by Jocelynn Drake and Rinda Elliot is book three in the Unbreakable Bonds series. These books, while they are technically "standalone" in that each story has an ending, they are NOT standalones meaning you can't pick up book three and start the series there...you will be so lost with the details. This book focuses on Rowe - his story is heartbreaking and his world was shattered in book 2 of the series when his wife was killed in a car wreck. Now, the authors are bringing Rowe back to life and putting him and his broken pieces back together with the help of Lucas, Snow, Ian, Andrei, Jude and his old friend Noah Keegan. 
 There is a lot that happens in this story. First, we watch Rowe as he struggles with grief and moving on with his life. Does he dare give his heart away again...what if something happens to the person, will he survive another loss? This is what Rowe struggles with throughout a large part of the story and it is brought on by the arrival of his old Army buddy Noah Keegan and the resurfacing of his attraction to the man. The authors did a great job of revealing Rowe's history and his sexuality - he is what I would describe as demisexual, he falls in love with the person - male or female. 
 "Rowe was into this and he wasn't an idiot. It had everything to do with the man. Not just any man would make him feel this way." 
 Noah Keegan is a man that we don't really get a huge backstory on as he is introduced to us. He is someone that Rowe has known since his Army days, his best-friend outside of his family of friends, and someone that has been in love with Rowe for years. He happily stepped aside and never told Rowe his feelings when Rowe met and married Mel...but now, he is back and he isn't denying his attraction and feelings any longer. 
 "Noah couldn't think, didn't want to think. He was so damn tired of fighting this when all he wanted was Rowe." 
 These two are hot. Hot. HOT! Rowe takes to being with a man like he has been doing it his whole life. No shyness or hesitant touches. 
 "I'm working on instinct here, but I'm all in." The wicked grin he got in return sent butterflies into his belly. 
 "Instinct is how we all do this at first." Noah ran his hands down Rowe's chest, scraping his short nails through the T-shirt. 
 "It takes practice to learn how to do it right. Practice with the same person." He kissed him. "Over." He kissed him again. "And over." 
 "Lots of practice," Rowe breathed before he spun Noah around, hooked his foot behind his knee, and sent him to his back on the bed. 
 Yeah, the sexual attraction between Rowe and Noah isn't the issue these two have to get past, it's the fear of the "what if..." and guilt that is eating Rowe alive that Noah is up against. 
 The "what if" game follows each of the guys in this story until finally...during Thanksgiving dinner, Ian sets them all straight! 
 "Enough! We're done playing the fucking blame game. Andrei, you feel guilty for getting kidnapped and pushing Lucas into being reckless. Lucas is drowning in guilt, because he thinks what he did led to all this recent hell, including Mel's death. Rowe has undoubtedly twisted the events in his head to feel guilty about Mel. Snow probably feels guilty for attacking Gratton all those year ago." 
 "Nope," Snow interjected and just flashed him a wicked grin. "Just guilty about not killing him the first time we met him." 
 "Whatever," Ian said with a roll of his eyes. "You want to get technical? This is my fault. If Snow, Lucas, and Rowe had never met me years ago, had never tried to help me, then Jagger would never have entered your world. But you know what? Fuck it! I love my life. And I love my family. And this entire shitstorm comes down to one man: Boris Jagger." 
 Ian suddenly swung around to face Snow, poking him in the chest. "You want to get Lucas back here? You call him and tell him I'm going after Jagger. We are done with this bullshit and we are bringing Jagger down for what he's done to this family and other families." 
 Beyond the romance the plot around who is trying to kill this group of men and why gets pretty thick in this book. We learn of some new connections, some covert-ops in progress, and there are of course several attempts to kill our guys throughout the story. Trust me you will be flippin' through the pages as fast as you can to see what happens next! 
 In addition to Rowe, we get glimpses into each of the characters lives. 
 Lucas & Andrei - it takes another catastrophe for Lucas to finally admit his feelings. While Andrei knew he loved him..Lucas has been a stubborn man in actually saying the words. 
 "I love you so fucking much. I should have told you that every day for the past year. God knows I've thought it a hundred times each and every one of those days, but I was too much of a coward to say it. Not anymore. You will never doubt how important you are to me." 
 Snow & Jude - they are settling into couplehood and all seems well on the surface. Who knows if our authors have something brewing for them... 
 Ian & Hollis - There is actually a little progression in this book and I am sure we will get much more back story in the upcoming story, Devour 
 Overall, 5 amazing stars - now to see what our guys go up against in Devour and of course hopefully watch them all settle into happily ever after!

Picked up an ARC from the Sourcebooks booth at BEA. Thanks! 
 I did not know this was part of a series. (That seems to be an ongoing trend with me.) I liked the description and the cover and had absolutely no idea that there are four books that come before it. That said, this isn't a series the way HP is a series, in that you need to read the other books to understand what the heck is going on, so don't let that knowledge deter you from picking up Breathe, Annie, Breathe. 
 Annie is still reeling from the death of her long-time boyfriend, Kyle. She has started training for a marathon to honor his memory, as he wanted to run one and never got the chance. But it's during her training that she meets Jeremiah, and for the first time since Kyle died, she actually feels. Unfortunately, one of the feelings she feels is guilt that she is moving on, and with Jeremiah's penchant for getting injured, she worries about the possibility of falling for someone else only to lose him as well. 
 Funnily enough, I finished this book on National Running Day. I thought it a fitting tribute. 
 I have never trained for a marathon. In fact, I don't run. But I felt for what Annie was going through, with her messed up stomach and her bum knee and her leg cramps, and it seems that the health issues associated with running long distances were the perfect not-really-a-metaphor for dealing with the death of a loved one. It sucks, and it hurts, but the only way to get past it is to push through the pain. 
 I liked Annie's story and was eager to read it. Knowing that she would eventually both a) finish the marathon and b) allow herself to move on did not diminish the giddiness when it actually happened. (I will confess that I spent a good portion of the book worried that something awful would happen to Jeremiah -- there was too much emphasis on how dangerous his activities were, and how much she hated that he participated in them -- so I was pleasantly surprised that nothing did.) 
 At times I found the dialogue a little too ridiculous, but I've learned that it's not always easy to write really good dialogue, and so I generally forgive it unless it's truly atrocious (which this was not). I liked Jeremiah as a character but I found him a bit too unbelievable -- he talks about how the rush he felt when he first met her was bigger than any of the ones he felt while doing his extreme sports, and I cannot stand when books use "love at first sight" as a way to jump start a relationship. But then maybe I've just never felt that rush and am being bitter and cynical about it. 
 I don't know anything about the other books in the series, so I can't speak to the cameos that apparently made other people giggle and squee. 
 Overall, I enjoyed the book and may consider going back to read the others in the series...once I fight my way through the massive stack of books I got from BEA.

This book and I had issues. I first of this book in my Reading Videogames class, where I with my casual gamer knowledge attempted to learn more about videogames and other games. I've been requesting this book since about the beginning of the semester (around Feb?) Apparently, it came in like 2 or 3 times and the e-mails telling me when it arrived never came, or I didn't check my eReader in time... 
 Such frustration. The semester ends in one week and I've finally FINALLY finished this book. 
 Phew~ Now that that is out of the way on to the review!! 
 Brief Summary: 
 Why live in reality when you can live in virtual reality? In the year 2044 reality sucks and most people spend as much time as they can as their avatars inside the VR game/program OASIS. There is pretty much nothing you can't do in OASIS. The creator of OASIS passes away and in his will he says that the person to find the hidden egg within OASIS will inherit his mass fortune and ownership of the company. This starts a mad hunt and a revival of 1980s culture since he was obsessed with his childhood. Wade Watts is determined to find the egg and rise up out of his poor life. Unfortunately, he has no money to travel within the game, therefore unable to actually search for the egg. 
 After years of no clues of progress by anyone, Wade (Perzival) stumbles upon a clue and starts the hunt up once again. It isn't just normal people he is competing against either, a vicious money and power hungry company (IOI) will do anything in order to have the egg. Anything. 
 -------------------------------------- 
 This book was a wild ride. There is just so. much. here! There is so much information needed to understand the riddles given to aid people in their quests to find the egg so, I felt like I just had to hang on and enjoy the ride. 
 I do not know 80s pop culture all that much. I recognize names and places, most of the games really, but not to the extent of the characters. --I sometimes found this to be a downside of the book because the author had to explain out the games, the movies, pretty much everything so that the readers could understand. It adds to the book but, I also thought it took me out of the book. 
 But the world of this book was really so cool. I mean... it sucks big time but, OASIS and the way the author set everything up was so awesome. OASIS is an utopia with no limits. Yet, this makes the story a dystopia because as the book mentions, the real world sucks and is more obvious because of OASIS. Sometimes while reading I would forget that Wade wasn't really in OASIS. 
 The characters were interesting. It is one of those cases where 'beauty is on the inside.' Personality is much more important than looks. And it really shines here. Also there is character growth. Wade goes from being a nobody -to- a celebrity. He has to deal with this change and he isn't perfect. He has to learn from his mistakes and mature. 
 Since the characters are geeks, some with anxiety issues and afraid of the outdoors there are lots of issues that are brought up and addressed. Trust is lost and earned and in OASIS one of the biggest pieces of showing trust is knowing the other person's face and name. 
 --One little thing I had a problem with was that Wade developed a fear of the outside (Doesn't affect story much so I don't think it is a spoiler). But, he gets over it really quickly with no mention ever again... I wanted a little more on this. 
 LOVED the diversity of the characters and mention of variety of shows and games -- not just American ones. So, seeing Gundam and Ultraman mentioned was super cool to me. 
 Really enjoyed this book and I'm glad I finally got to it. I might read the author's next book Armada but, it seemed most people in class didn't like it so, I might pass. 
 If you like 80s references, shows, classic arcade games as well as futuristic aspects --this is a book I think you should read. 
 If you like adventures and/or quirky characters -- probably a book you should try out.

However, in the middle of the book, things started to pick up when Ma and Jack planned their escape and everything was smooth sailing for me.  Short summary: This is a story about 5 year old Jack, and his Ma. He's lived all his life in a tiny, one story bedroom (More like a shed, makeshift into a room).  Not a long novel, but one which I expect to think about for a while. Yeong-hye has some bloody, disturbing dreams and decides she just can't eat meat anymore. It doesn't seem earth-shattering, but from there her situation spirals into complete catastrophe. Divorce, estrangement from her family, and institutionalization in a mental hospital all follow her seemingly innocuous decision. And each of these developments locates itself on Yeong-hye's body as she's assaulted, violated, seduced, restrained, and eventually force-fed. Is this a comment on Korean society's strictly homogenous and hierarchical organization? Is it a criticism of how we've divorced ourselves from the natural world to which Yeong-hye yearns to return? Is it a comment on how we treat the mentally ill and whether they have the right to seek a different state of being, even if it leads to their deaths? Or is it an existential horror novel with all of these rolled in, along with darker, abstract concerns about subversion, submission, and violence that implicates us all? I felt it was an update on Bartleby the Scrivener, who asks again in a different voice if she could be allowed to not work, to not eat, to not live.

 I read some mixed reviews about Criminal before starting this book, but I have to say that it's my favorite Karin Slaughter book yet! 
 The story is told in alternating views and timelines, but all revolves around the same case (or cases involving the same villain). One timeline focuses on Amanda Wagner, Will's boss at GBI, in the seventies when she was just starting out. When women were employed by the force, but not treated like cops. When Amanda and fellow female cop Evelyn (Faith's mother - before she was Faith's mother) realize a murdered woman was wrongly identified, they start their own investigation. 
 I really enjoyed the chapters from Amanda's past. She's been such a frustrating, inscrutable character thus far in the series and it was great to see her origins story. We get to see her influences, her emotions (yes, she actually has them), her growth, and most importantly, her connection to Will Trent. 
 In the current timeline, Will is finally happy, settling into his relationship with Sara (despite that pesky detail that he's technically still married to Angie). However, the happiness is short lived when news is announced that a young girl has been abducted and his father has been paroled from prison. 
 From both timelines we get a lot of background on Will - on his parents, on his childhood, on his career with the GBI. Everything that's been lacking for me in Will's backstory was satisfied in this book. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Criminal. There were times the story got a little bogged down with too much detail (especially in the forensic explanations) and I still find it off-putting that Sara and Will fully committed to their relationship before Will even tried to divorce Angie, but those were really the only parts of the book I didn't like. The story was fast-paced, the mystery was interesting - especially how it connected to the present - and the character backstory and growth was very satisfying.

When I saw this book on a must read before the movie comes out list, I snatched it up and I am so glad that I did. I don't give a lot of five star reviews. I have described the opening scene of the novel to my husband and my book group (it wasn't our selection but I recommended the book to the members for their personal reading) hoping that it's intensity would emphasize what is so great about the two layers of the book - the horrors of starving in a war torn country and the quest to stop a serial murderer in a country that is supposed to be a crime-free utopia due to communism. 
 It really captures the bleakness of Russia (USSR) in the 30's and then in the 50s before Stalin dies. This book explores the psychological aspects of the politically minded very well. It's matter of fact tone sits well with the plot, and the (not often) action within is worthy of a Bourne-like movie. It's an excellent look into the communist's frame of mind, and the way people have to behave and act for their very survival.  The story follows one man's hunt to catch a serial killer of children. In typical thriller fashion, different chapters reveal what is happening with the protagonist, the killer, and occasionally victims or other side characters. Most chapters end with a cliffhanger before checking in with another character in the next. 
 Where Child 44 differs from the usual thrillers is in its setting - the story takes place in a Soviet Union ruled by Stalin. Clearly the author did quite a bit of research into that era, and he does a good job of showing the horrors and difficulties of life during that time. Much of the novel is spent developing the characters and setting - the murder investigations don't really rev up until the second half of the book. 
 "There is no crime." Stalin's Soviet Union strives to be a paradise for its workers, providing for all of their needs. One of its fundamental pillars is that its citizens live free from the fear of ordinary crime and criminals. But in this society, millions do live in fear . . . of the State. Death is a whisper away. The mere suspicion of ideological disloyalty - owning a book from the decadent West, the wrong word at the wrong time - sends millions of innocents into the Gulags or to their executions. Defending the system from its citizens is the MGB, the State Security Force. And no MGB officer is more courageous, conscientious, or idealistic than Leo Demidov. 
 A war hero with a beautiful wife, Leo lives in relative luxury in Moscow, even providing a decent apartment for his parents. His only ambition has been to serve his country. For this greater good, he has arrested and interrogated. 
 Then the impossible happens. A different kind of criminal-a murderer-is on the loose, killing at will. At first he tells the victim's family that no crime has happened but when the bodies start stacking up, Leo knows he must investigate even though the higher-ups would rather cover up. 
 Soon, Leo finds himself demoted and denounced by his enemies, his world turned upside down, and every belief he's ever held shattered. The only way to save his life and the lives of his family is to uncover this criminal. But in a society that is officially paradise, it's a crime against the State to suggest that a murderer - much less a serial killer - is in their midst. Exiled from his home, with only his wife, Raisa, remaining (sometimes reluctantly) at his side, Leo must confront the vast resources and reach of the MBG to find and stop a criminal that the State won't admit even exists. 
 Although the dialog is sometimes over-earnest and the who-dunnit aspect of the story is not edge-of-your-seat exciting, this book is still worth a read because of the dark but fascinating world and time it draws the reader into. This book should appeal to mystery/thriller fans, as well as those who enjoy historical fiction or even a dystopian story.

Nitpicking I know and most people wouldn't miss it but it just stood out to me. It did have other common fantasy tropes galore: 
 1.	Applied Phlebotinum (Pixiedust effect)- magical wizardwood makes talking Liveship. 2. Teenage Brat - Malta. 3. The Evil Empire - Jamailia/Chalced. 4. Dark past - Kennit, Paragon, Brashen. 5. Living Legends - Liveships, Kennit the Pirate King 6. Machiavelli effect - Kyle was the wrong choice for captain. 7.  Made a slave. Wintrow  8. Sex-change- Althea pretending to be Athel

I just think her becoming a boy was unnecessary in a universe where we have repeatedly seen women sailing on ships, a disguise yes, a sex change no. Overall I decent read that picked up at the end, I think the next one will be better.

Oh god. I'm going to say a lot of things because I just finished this and I don't know if any of them will be coherent. I think, I think this is somewhere between 3.5 and 3.75 stars. But maybe I'll save it at three, because there is just... there is so much. And I don't know what or how to think. 
 My short review is: This is the best novel Handler has written (as Handler) since The Basic Eight. I love Adverbs, but I don't quite count that as a novel; if you know me, you'll know that I was NOT ENAMOURED with Why We Broke Up and I DNF the incest book that I pretend doesn't exist (because god, why, why, why was that written. why did that need to be written). The prose remains Handlerian--Handler is a stylist, I get it, he has a huge crush on Nabokov (and why shouldn't he)--but at the same time, it's toned down. One of the reasons I couldn't stand WWBU was because of how pretentious it felt, except for the giant paragraph at the end where Min says everything she isn't. I know him well enough to spot the hallmarks of his style ("I thought," he said, "that I said that"; not a direct quote but he does have a habit of putting his dialogue tags in strange places in the dialogue, so you've got to wait for it), but at the same time, they weren't overwhelming. They didn't distract from the story. 
 I've gotta say one thing on language, though. Let's talk about race, Daniel. Let's talk about some of the weird stuff you have in here that, frankly, I don't know how it made it in. Especially after the National Book Awards. You made a good apology, you put your money where your mouth was, and you didn't phrase it as "sorry if you were offended"--it was legitimately "sorry I said a racist thing." But? But? A woman "screamed the way the appearance of a black man makes everything suddenly scary." What the actual christ, Daniel. Yes, Manny is black, yes, he shows up, yes, the woman screams because of piracy, but just... dear lord. I hate that sentence. There are a few others, a strange comment about (black) police officers working "twice as hard, due to injustice,"one about a "knocking, clasping ritual believed at the time to be favoured by black people," and there's one other. The first sentence I've mentioned is absolutely not okay, and it bothered me throughout. The others were just... strange. They felt unnecessary. Unneeded. Why did you put those in there, Daniel? Why? 
 Okay. Now to the actual plot of the book: 
 The basic plot is there's a dad who's in radio and he's floundering in life. His infinitely more interesting daughter, Gwen, has been caught stealing. As punishment, she's has to go to an old folks home and talk to old people there. Suddenly, piracy happens. And we watch that unfold. 
 Interesting plot. I found this a really gripping story, and I had to keep reading to find out what would happen next. 
 Character-building was weird. I didn't like Phil a whole lot; he's kind of a sleazebucket and I never quite trusted him. Yet he shares equal screen-time with his daughter, Gwen. I found myself less interested in Phil's parts, partially because I had a hard time following what was happening, but also because he reads as a terrible person. I don't quite know if he's supposed to be sympathetic. Part of me doesn't think he is, mainly because of the way he treats Levine and ignores Marina, HIS WIFE, and is a bit of a snooper. See also: him reading Levine's personal file on her computer, where she's writing an erotic note, and he Gets Ideas . On the other hand, he's billed first on the book blurb, so he's clearly one of the protagonists. No doubt he's flawed, and I really don't mind flawed protagonists, but on the whole he turned out kind of bleh. 
 Gwen, though. Gwen's intriguing. Fourteen-year-old who's frustrated with everything, alter-ego who commits crimes, suddenly swept up in ideas of piracy? Yes, that's more like it. To be honest, I found myself wishing this were more overtly her story, rather than flipping back and forth between the two. I felt bad for Phil once or twice (when Gwen goes missing, but that was more regarding the horror of a missing child ) but Gwen I sympathized more with. This isn't because I read a lot of YA, although maybe it is--she was just more interesting overall. 
 As for other characters: they didn't feel as defined. In some, that's okay. In some, that's not. I wanted more Marina, Phil's wife, Gwen's mum--she intrigued me more than her husband did. The Glassermans were occasionally sketchy, although I was okay with that. Amber was fascinating, perhaps a little thin but nonetheless amusing. I also thought this was going to be a tale of reconciliation between Gwen and Naomi, and I never quite got why Gwen broke off her friendship with Naomi. Oh well. Can't win 'em all.  
 As for the actual piracy: Okay. I should've seen bloodshed coming, but I was absolutely shocked that Gwen was prepared to kill. That's such a drastic action, especially for a fourteen-year-old. Yes, I've read TBE, I know Handler writes this grand tradition of teenage murderesses, but also, that's... that's so big... and it didn't ring true, not quite, not for me. I also didn't get Gwen's sudden PIRACY!!! obsession. It happens as soon as she meets Errol, but I really would've loved to watch it expand. It felt, eh, not quite shoe-horned in, but dealt with too quickly. There was a lot that worked, a lot that didn't. Eh.  
 Oh, and there's a twist at the end that makes you want to re-read the book. I guess I should've seen it coming that Gwen and Errol were related, that Errol was grandfather, that he would die, but I didn't. Don't know how I felt about it, although I didn't feel like it was a cheapo plot device. So that's good.  
 Aaaaaand one last thing that I loved: I shipped Gwen/Amber all the way through and then they KISS on the BOAT and it's described as ROMANTIC and it was actually pretty glorious. SO THAT WAS REALLY NICE.  
 OVERALL: I don't regret reading this, I had a lot of fun with it, although it's less of a fun romp than I would've liked. Be prepared for strangeness and terror and feelings.

Labels were what he fought against from the beginning, constantly reinventing himself and trying to figure out/decide who he wanted to be or who he really was. Bipolar was the label he ran from the most. He didn't want that to define him, and because of that, he let it destroy him. Following him through the manic stage was very interesting. It was easy to see why Violet would latch on and let him pull her along. He was able to pull her out of her funk and help her to start living again. I loved watching her come back to herself and start to get over her sister's death. While Violet was surrounded by loving parents, Finch had nothing really. I didn't envy him his home life. He had a horrible family. If they had been more attentive and caring from the beginning, perhaps Finch would have had it easier. Perhaps he would have gotten help. I loved the wandering. It was such a fun way for Violet and Finch to get to know each other and make memories. Finch is one of those characters I will continue to think about even after the story ended. I do wonder what his life would have been like if more people had truly cared about him. Violet seems to be the only one to have done so. He tried his hardest to avoid the darkness for her. This really was a powerful and impactful story. It is one I will think about for awhile to come. That is not true of a lot of books. Even ones I love are often forgot a couple days later. This one will leave a lasting impression.

Short Review 
 A one off book dealing with characters that we're not likely to really see again. Not one of the best Discworld books, but the time spent in the Assassin's guild makes up for most of the shortcomings. Also does a decent job of making fun of religion. 
 Long Review 
 I have mixed feelings on this Discworld installment. On one hand, I found the protagonist Teppic to be kind of forgettable. Sandwiched in literary order between Granny Weatherwax and Commander Vimes he has tough competition when it comes to memorability and ultimately loses out. Many of the other characters are a bit tedious, like our main 'antagonist' Dios. All in all the last half of the book has a fair number of good jokes but was a little flat to me. 
 On the other hand, the time Pratchett spends at the start of the book fleshing out the Assassin's Guild was fantastic. Rather than just letting it be kind of a goofy self-parodying place he crafts a really believable (within the context of the Discworld universe anyway) institution that fits in a believable way into Ankh-Morpork. I think I would've enjoyed the book a lot more if we'd stayed in the realm of the Assassin's Guild the whole time. 
 I also enjoyed the parodies of ancient Egyptian and Greek culture, and the thorough manner in which he ridicules religion - a topic I think doesn't get made fun of enough considering how ludicrous it all is. 
 In the end then you're left with half of a great book, and then half of a so-so book with some good jokes peppered about in it. 
 If you like Discworld in general, or ancient Egypt and Greece as general topics, you'll enjoy it - you just probably won't rave about it like people do for Wyrd Sisters or Mort. If you're kind of on the fence with the series though, you might want to skip it and come back to it later once you're more hooked. You won't be missing out on anything huge.

This book made me mad. Not at Corey Whaley, who wrote a book I didn't particularly like. That's common enough, and I am well aware that I'm not the only reader out here. But I'm tweaked at all these folks who've been lauding this as top-shelf material. A.J. Jacobs, for one, made favorable comparisons to John Green. And I just don't see it. The best thing about "Noggin" is the concept: part cancer story, part Rip Van Winkle. And everything else was kinda ho-hum. The funny wasn't so funny, the poignant wasn't pointed, the protagonist wasn't particularly sympathetic. The central conflict revolves around Travis wanting to return to boyfriend-status with the girl he had been dating. That Kate is older, obviously changed, and engaged doesn't deter him. His mooning about her is several clicks past annoying. 
 There are many other unsatisfyimg bits that could have worked but just don't. Need examples? How about the title? The titular nick- name Travis gets upon his return to school appears to be some sort of embrace of his new identity, but it only gets mentioned again in passing, leaving narrative chips on the table. Or how about the importance of Kate's artistic pursuits? That she's dropped them is never explored. There seems to be some noise about making peace with the past and accepting the present, but it never came into focus. The positive LGBTQ thread is an idea I usually favor, but here it didn't connect to themes of relationship and affection that could have made it powerful. 
 I'll add this to the list of so-so books that maybe, some day, one reader may like. Note I don't say love.

I feel like most YA books that feature people of color are focused on navigating racial politics in a serious and sobering way. I think that it's incredibly important to tell those stories, but sometimes you just want an angsty teen novel about how horrible your parents are and how you don't know how to talk to the boy you like. The Education of Margot Sanchez delivers both. This isn't a frothy book (it covers weighty topics like gentrification, class division, prejudice, drugs, and more), but the serious stuff is wrapped in a package that feels light. It was refreshing to see a summery teen drama with a Latina heroine when so often those kinds of books are limited to white, female protagonists.

 I read the print book and immediately turned around and listened to the audiobook. I feel as though this re-read helped me absorb a few things better. 
 1.  I do think the book would have benefited greatly by telling the reader much closer to the beginning that it was a demon that Piper and Neeve had woken in the cave at the end of the previous book. We do not learn this until we get a Piper chapter halfway through this book, but by that point we'd already seen the corruption of the trees in Cabeswater, Adam's hands and eye going rogue, and the possession of Noah. The characters had casually mentioned maybe it was a demon before, but we were really in the dark about what was truly causing this until we get that first Piper scene. I understood those earlier scenes and how they tied into the overall story much better upon the reread. That Piper/demon chapter really should have been moved up in the book.  
 2.  The fact that Noah had passed on is marked only by the line "he quietly slipped from time." With all of the time loops in this story, I thought that meant he went back to the present, not that his ghost disappeared forever (reviving Gansey as his last act). I spent the rest of the book waiting to see Noah again and was QUITE enraged when there was no mention of him in the epilogue. I do think his passing should have been stated more concretely because I totally did not get that that's what happened until I re-read it knowing we'd never see him after that scene.  
 3. Glendower did not resurrect Gansey the first time with the bee incident because Glendower was already dead. It was Noah's voice that Gansey heard, but did Noah have the power to resurrect him? Cabeswater exists outside of ordinary time. When it healed him at the end, I believe it was simultaneously healing him at that other point in time through Noah, whose spirit had been blessed by the ley line since he died as a sacrifice. And that's why Gansey had the ability to command small things in Cabeswater with his words. Because he'd had a part of the ley line in him all along. Yes, yes! This is the kind of wibbly wobbly timey wimey stuff I wanted!  
 Overall, I felt there were too many new characters being introduced for a finale, and not enough closure for the ones we'd known all along (Maura, Grey Man, NOAH).  Although that felt like a lot of loose threads, I don't hate it because Maggie's characters are so unusual and so interesting. She really shows the bigger picture of this town and how things have a larger impact. I do appreciate that, I just wish more time had been spent with our main group. In particular, I felt the women of Fox Way were brushed aside too much in the end. 
 As a finale, I felt this was imperfect in how open to interpretation it was (not to be confused with an open ended plot). The meaning I got above in point 3 was mindblowing for me, but was I just making an assumption? Is this really what Maggie intended? It was never stated implicitly so even if this was 100% correct, what's the likelihood of everyone catching it? It took me reading it 3 times to really grasp on. I think a finale should be a bit more absolute. 
 However, it was a delight to spend time with these characters again. Even on my first read I thought there was a fairly obvious meaning to the plot that  chasing dreams and favors from others won't solve your problems, or give meaning to your life. In the end these characters were the kings of their own lives with the power to change their destinies.  And that's lovely.

This book is cool, but didn't really make an impression on me. I liked the back and forth storytelling, but kind of got annoyed that I had to keep flipping the comic book over. *This review has been brought to you by 12-year-old me*
